  • (D) Independent per-thread scheduling is exactly what the kernel needs to know about the threads to do, which user-level threads deny it.

Common misconception. Assuming cheaper means better. The cheap switch is paid for with the loss of parallelism and of independent blocking.

Takeaway. User-level threads: cheap switch, no parallelism. Kernel threads: real parallelism, expensive switch.

OS-U1-Q62MCQhard

A process uses the many-to-many model with 4 kernel threads and 10 user-level threads. All 10 user threads are CPU-bound and make no system calls. On an 8-core machine, how many of the user threads can be executing at the same instant?

  1. 1
  2. 4
  3. 8
  4. 10
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. In the many-to-many model the kernel schedules the kernel threads and the library multiplexes user threads onto them. Only a user thread that currently has a kernel thread can be on a CPU, so the instantaneous parallelism is bounded by the smaller of the kernel-thread count and the core count.

Step by step.

  1. Kernel threads available: 4.
  2. Cores available: 8.
  3. User threads can occupy at most one kernel thread each, so at most min(4, 8) = 4 run at once.
  4. The other 6 user threads are runnable inside the library but have no kernel thread to run on.

Answer: Option (B), 4.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) One would be the many-to-one answer; here there are 4 kernel threads.
  • (C) 8 is the core count, but there are only 4 kernel threads to occupy them.
  • (D) 10 is the user-thread count, which no model can run in parallel beyond its kernel threads.

Common misconception. Reading the many-to-many model as unlimited. The multiplexing ratio bounds concurrency from above; the kernel thread count is the real ceiling.

Takeaway. Parallelism = min(kernel threads, cores); the user-thread count only decides how much work is queued behind them.

OS-U1-Q81MCQeasy

In the many-to-one threading model, one thread of a process issues a blocking read on a file. What happens to the other threads of the same process?

  1. They keep running, because each thread has its own kernel thread.
  2. They all block, because the one kernel thread that backs the process is blocked inside the kernel.
  3. They keep running, but none of them can make a system call until the read returns.
  4. The kernel creates a new kernel thread for each of them on demand.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Concept. In the many-to-one model the whole process is known to the kernel as a single schedulable entity. Every blocking call made by any user-level thread blocks that one kernel thread, and with it every user-level thread of the process.

Step by step.

  1. The library maps all user-level threads onto one kernel thread.
  2. The read traps to the kernel and the kernel blocks the only thread it knows about.
  3. No user-level thread can be scheduled while the kernel thread is blocked, because the library runs on that same thread.
  4. Hence all threads of the process stop until the read completes.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the one-to-one model.
  • (C) the threads do not run at all, so the question of further calls does not arise.
  • (D) the many-to-one model never creates a second kernel thread.

Common misconception. Assuming threads are always independent. Independence in the kernel requires one kernel thread per blocking unit of work.

Takeaway. Many-to-one: one blocking call stops the process.

OS-U1-Q82MCQmedium

Which one of the following is naturally kept in thread-local storage rather than in a variable shared by every thread of the process?

  1. the process's heap
  2. errno, the error code of the last failed library call, one copy per thread
  3. the process's open file descriptor table
  4. the program's global variables
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Concept. Thread-local storage gives each thread its own instance of a variable while keeping the same name. It exists precisely for state that is meaningless if shared, and errno is the classic case: two threads failing differently must not overwrite each other's error code.

Step by step.

  1. Sharing errno would make the value depend on which thread ran last, which is a race.
  2. POSIX therefore defines errno as a macro that expands to a per-thread location.
  3. The heap, the file descriptor table and globals are process-wide by design, and all threads address them directly.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) the heap is shared, which is why two threads can corrupt it without synchronisation.
  • (C) file descriptors are process-wide, which is why closing a file in one thread closes it for all.
  • (D) globals are shared by definition.

Common misconception. Believing each thread has a private copy of every variable. Only its registers, stack and thread-local storage are private.

Takeaway. Shared: heap, globals, file descriptors. Private: registers, stack, thread-local storage.

OS-U1-Q83MSQhard

Which of the following statements about forking a multithreaded process, thread pools, a shared counter and kernel-thread switches are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. After fork() in a multithreaded process, the child contains only the thread that called fork().
  2. In a thread pool a worker that finishes a task returns to the pool instead of being destroyed, so thread creation is paid only for the pool's initial workers.
  3. Two threads of one process can safely update a shared counter with an unsynchronised read-modify-write.
  4. A switch between two user-level threads needs no trap into the kernel, whereas a switch between two kernel threads does.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Concept. Threads share an address space but not a kernel identity. Anything that changes the set of runnable kernel entities — fork, a switch between kernel threads — costs a trip into the kernel; a switch inside a user-level library does not.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. POSIX fork() duplicates only the calling thread, so the child is single-threaded even though the parent is not.
  2. (B) True. A pool amortises creation over many requests; the workers are created once and reused.
  3. (C) False. A read-modify-write is three machine steps, and the scheduler can switch between any two of them, so the increment can be lost.
  4. (D) True. The user-level switch saves and restores registers inside the library; the kernel-level switch needs the kernel scheduler, hence a mode switch.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing that two threads of one process cannot race because they are "the same program". They share memory, so they race exactly as two processes sharing a segment would.

Takeaway. Shared memory means races; kernel identity means mode switches.

OS-U1-Q84NATmedium

A program has a fraction s of its work that must be executed serially, and the remaining 1 − s parallelises perfectly. With s = 0.2 on 4 cores, the maximum speedup over the single-core execution is 1 / (s + (1 − s)/n). What is that speedup?
(Enter a decimal value.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 2.5

Detailed solution

Concept. Amdahl's law: the serial part is not divided by the number of cores, so it bounds the speedup no matter how many threads are used. This is why the many-to-many and one-to-one models do not make a program with a serial section scale without limit.

Step by step.

  1. Serial term: s = 0.2 of the work stays on one core.
  2. Parallel term: (1 − s)/n = 0.8/4 = 0.2 of the original time.
  3. Total time on 4 cores is 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4 of the single-core time.
  4. Speedup = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5.

Answer: 2.5

Common misconception. Reporting 4, the core count. Four cores give a speedup of 4 only when s = 0; with 20% serial work the ceiling is 5, and 4 cores reach just 2.5.

Takeaway. Serial work is never divided; add the serial share to the divided parallel share, then invert.

OS-U1-Q85MCQeasy

Which one of the following statements about the stack of a thread is TRUE?

  1. All threads of a process share one stack, so a deep recursion in one thread disturbs the others.
  2. Each thread has its own stack, yet a pointer to a local variable of one thread can still be dereferenced by another thread of the same process.
  3. Each thread has its own stack in a separate address space that no other thread can address.
  4. A thread's stack is kept in kernel memory, so user-mode code cannot address it.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Concept. A thread has its own stack and its own registers, but the stack lives in the process's single address space. So the stack is private by convention, not by protection: another thread can address it if it has a pointer.

Step by step.

  1. The thread library reserves a separate region of the address space for each thread's stack.
  2. Since all regions belong to the same address space, a pointer into one thread's frame is a valid address for every other thread.
  3. Nothing in the MMU stops the access, so the danger is a dangling pointer after the owning thread returns.
  4. Hence the stack is private only in the sense that no other thread uses it automatically.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) sharing one stack would make independent calls impossible; that is the definition of separate stacks.
  • (C) threads share one address space by definition; separate address spaces would make them processes.
  • (D) the stack is ordinary user memory, mapped by the process itself.

Common misconception. Treating a private stack as protected memory. It is not: passing the address of a local variable to another thread compiles and runs.

Takeaway. Private stack, shared address space — private by use, not by protection.

OS-U1-Q107MCQeasy

A process has two threads and runs on a machine with a single core. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. The threads run concurrently but never in parallel, because at any instant at most one of them is executing.
  2. The threads run in parallel, because each of them has its own stack and its own register set.
  3. The threads cannot run at all until a second core becomes available.
  4. The threads run in parallel provided the scheduler is non-preemptive.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Concurrency means several activities are in progress over an interval; parallelism means several are progressing at the same instant. On one core only one instruction stream can execute at any instant, so two threads interleave — they are concurrent but not parallel. Parallelism needs as many cores as simultaneously running threads, and kernel-level threads to place on them.

Step by step.

  1. Two threads exist and both make progress, so the program is concurrent.
  2. There is one core, so only one thread can be executing at any given instant.
  3. The other thread waits in the ready queue and is switched in when the first is preempted or blocks.
  4. Hence concurrency without parallelism.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Separate stacks and registers are what makes two threads possible; they do not create a second execution unit.
  • (C) Threads run perfectly well on one core; they simply take turns.
  • (D) Non-preemption reduces interleaving, it does not create hardware parallelism.

Common misconception. Treating "two threads" as "twice the speed". On one core the total CPU work is unchanged; only the interleaving changes.

OS-U1-Q108MCQmedium

A user-level thread library runs on the many-to-many model and uses scheduler activations — upcalls from the kernel into the library. Which one of the following problems does that mechanism solve?

  1. It keeps each user thread's stack in the kernel, so that switching between user threads becomes free.
  2. When a user thread blocks inside the kernel, the kernel upcalls the library and hands it a fresh virtual processor, so the library can run another of its user threads instead of stalling the whole process.
  3. It removes the need for kernel threads, giving the speed of many-to-one with the parallelism of one-to-one.
  4. It allows two user threads of the same process to execute on the same core at the same instant.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. In a pure many-to-one model the kernel sees only one schedulable entity, so a blocking system call in one user thread stalls every thread of the process. Scheduler activations fix that: the kernel treats each virtual processor as a schedulable unit and notifies the library through an upcall whenever a virtual processor blocks or is preempted, so the library can schedule another user thread on the processors it still has.

Step by step.

  1. The library multiplexes its user threads over a set of virtual processors (kernel threads).
  2. A user thread blocks in the kernel; the kernel knows the whole virtual processor is now idle.
  3. The kernel upcalls the library, which marks that user thread blocked and dispatches another user thread.
  4. When the blocked thread is ready again, the kernel upcalls once more and the library resumes it.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Stacks stay in user space; kernel-resident stacks would not make switching free.
  • (C) Virtual processors are kernel threads, so the model still needs them.
  • (D) Two threads cannot execute simultaneously on one core under any model.

Common misconception. Believing the library can detect a blocking call by itself. It cannot — only the kernel knows — which is exactly why an upcall is needed.

OS-U1-Q109MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about threads are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Two threads of one process can execute at the same instant on two cores only if the kernel knows about both of them.
  2. Thread-local storage gives each thread its own copy of a variable, while an ordinary global variable is shared by every thread of the process.
  3. Switching between two user-level threads of one process needs no switch into kernel mode.
  4. A thread that blocks in a system call always blocks every other thread of its process.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The kernel schedules what it can see. If it sees only one entity per process, the process can occupy at most one core, whatever its thread library believes. Thread-local storage is the standard way to give each thread its own instance of a variable. A switch between user-level threads is a library call: save registers, swap stacks, return — no trap. And whether a blocking call stalls the process depends entirely on the model: it does under many-to-one, it does not under one-to-one or many-to-many.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: parallelism requires one kernel-schedulable entity per simultaneously running thread.
  2. (B) True: that is the definition of thread-local storage, the usual fix for accidental sharing of a global.
  3. (C) True: the kernel is not involved, which is why a user-level switch is much cheaper.
  4. (D) False: the word "always" fails. Under one-to-one only the blocked thread waits; under many-to-one the whole process waits.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Generalising from the many-to-one model. Almost every claim of the form "a thread blocking blocks the process" is true only for many-to-one.

OS-U1-Q110NATeasy

A process uses the many-to-many threading model: 6 user-level threads are multiplexed over 4 kernel threads, on a machine with 8 cores. At some instant 2 of the kernel threads are blocked in system calls and the other 2 are runnable.
What is the largest number of user-level threads that can be executing at that instant? (Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 2

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. In the many-to-many model each runnable kernel thread can carry at most one user-level thread at a time. The number of cores is irrelevant once it exceeds the number of runnable kernel threads; the binding constraint is the number of virtual processors the library still has.

Step by step.

  1. 4 kernel threads exist; 2 are blocked in system calls, so 2 are runnable.
  2. Each runnable kernel thread can execute one user-level thread.
  3. 6 user threads are available, which is more than the 2 slots, so the library fills both slots.
  4. Maximum executing at that instant = 2. The 8 cores cannot help, because only 2 kernel threads are runnable.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Answering 6 (all user threads), 4 (all kernel threads) or 8 (the core count). The blocked kernel threads hold their user threads but cannot execute them, and the library cannot create execution units the kernel does not have.

OS-U1-Q111MCQhard

Which one of the following statements about reentrant and thread-safe functions is TRUE?

  1. Every thread-safe function is reentrant.
  2. A function that touches only its own parameters and its own local (stack) variables is reentrant, and therefore thread-safe.
  3. A reentrant function cannot be called recursively by the same thread.
  4. A function can be made thread-safe only by wrapping every call to it in one global lock.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A function is reentrant when it keeps no state outside its own stack frame — no static or global data, no shared buffer, no pointer to such storage — so several invocations can be in flight at once, or one invocation can be suspended in the middle of another. A function is thread-safe when it is correct under concurrent calls, which may be achieved with locking instead. Reentrancy implies thread safety; thread safety does not imply reentrancy.

Step by step.

  1. Using only parameters and locals means each invocation works on its own copy of everything.
  2. Two threads then cannot interfere, so the function is thread-safe as well as reentrant.
  3. Locking makes a function thread-safe but not reentrant if it uses a single static lock, since a recursive call would deadlock on it.
  4. So the implication runs one way only: reentrant ⇒ thread-safe.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) reverses the implication; a locked function is thread-safe but not reentrant.
  • (C) recursion is a normal use of a reentrant function; each call gets a fresh frame.
  • (D) locking is one technique, not the only one: local state, atomic operations and per-thread data all work.

Common misconception. Using the two terms interchangeably. Remember the direction: reentrant is the stronger property.

OS-U1-Q112MCQeasy

A thread calls pthread_join(t, &status) on another thread t of the same process. Which one of the following does that call do?

  1. It blocks the caller until t terminates, then collects t's return value and releases its resources.
  2. It terminates t immediately and returns t's thread identifier.
  3. It detaches t, so that t's resources are freed automatically the moment it finishes.
  4. It returns at once whether or not t has finished, placing t's identifier in status.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. pthread_join is the thread analogue of wait(). It waits for the target thread to terminate, stores that thread's return value where the caller asks, and reaps the thread's resources (its stack, its thread-control block). A joinable thread that is never joined leaks its resources, exactly like a zombie process.

Step by step.

  1. The calling thread blocks until t returns from its start routine.
  2. The return value of that routine is copied into the caller's status pointer.
  3. The kernel or library then frees t's stack and control block.
  4. Joining twice on the same thread is undefined behaviour; that is what detaching avoids.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Cancellation is pthread_cancel, a different call with different semantics.
  • (C) Detaching is pthread_detach; a detached thread cannot be joined.
  • (D) A non-blocking probe would be a try-join, not pthread_join.

Common misconception. Confusing join with cancel, or believing a finished thread frees itself. A joinable thread keeps its resources until somebody joins it.

preemptive-nonpreemptive-scheduling 28
OS-U1-Q14MCQeasy

Which one of the following CPU scheduling algorithms is inherently non-preemptive?

  1. Round robin
  2. Shortest remaining time first
  3. First come first served
  4. Preemptive priority scheduling
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Preemption needs a rule that can remove a running process. FCFS has none: it dispatches the oldest ready process and lets it run until it blocks or terminates.

Step by step.

  1. FCFS hands the CPU to the process that arrived earliest and never takes it back; the only exits are blocking and termination.
  2. Round robin preempts on quantum expiry — that is its whole mechanism.
  3. SRTF preempts whenever a new arrival has a shorter remaining time.
  4. Preemptive priority preempts whenever a higher-priority process becomes ready.

Answer: Option (C) — first come first served.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A), (B) and (D) are all defined by their preemption rule.

Common misconception. Students sometimes call FCFS preemptive because an arriving process with a short burst 'should' run first. FCFS ignores burst lengths entirely.

Takeaway. Non-preemptive algorithms in the GATE syllabus: FCFS and non-preemptive SJF. Everything with 'remaining time', a quantum, or a preemptive priority is preemptive.

OS-U1-Q15MCQmedium

Which one of the following does NOT by itself cause the running process to be preempted?

  1. The interval timer expires the running process's time quantum.
  2. A process with a higher priority becomes ready.
  3. The I/O request of a blocked process completes, so that process becomes ready.
  4. Under SRTF, a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining burst than the running process.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Preemption means the running process is displaced by the scheduler's policy. A process merely becoming ready is not enough; the policy must also rank it above the running one.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Quantum expiry is the round-robin preemption trigger.
  2. (B) Under preemptive priority a higher-priority arrival outranks the running process, so it preempts.
  3. (C) I/O completion only moves a process from Waiting to Ready. Whether it then preempts depends on the policy; in FCFS or non-preemptive SJF it simply waits.
  4. (D) SRTF compares remaining times, so a shorter newcomer does preempt.

Answer: Option (C) — an I/O completion by itself does not preempt.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A), (B) and (D) are each a defined preemption trigger under the stated policy.

Common misconception. Students treat 'becomes ready' as synonymous with 'preempts'. Becoming ready is a state change; preemption is a scheduling decision on top of it.

Takeaway. Ask which policy is in force. A ready process preempts only if that policy ranks it above the running one.

OS-U1-Q16MSQmedium

Which of the following scheduling algorithms can be preemptive? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Shortest remaining time first (SRTF)
  2. Round robin
  3. Non-preemptive shortest job first (SJF)
  4. Priority scheduling in its preemptive form
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An algorithm is preemptive if it can remove a running process before that process blocks or finishes. SRTF compares remaining times, round robin uses a quantum, and preemptive priority compares priorities — all three can displace a running process.

Step by step.

  1. (A) SRTF is preemptive by definition: the shortest remaining time always runs.
  2. (B) Round robin preempts on quantum expiry.
  3. (C) Non-preemptive SJF, as its name states, lets the chosen job run to completion.
  4. (D) The preemptive form of priority scheduling displaces the running process when a higher-priority process becomes ready.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) is explicitly non-preemptive; SJF has a separate preemptive version called SRTF.

Common misconception. SJF and SRTF are treated as one algorithm, so SJF is marked preemptive. They are two algorithms: SJF is non-preemptive, SRTF is its preemptive counterpart.

Takeaway. SJF ↔ SRTF is the standard non-preemptive/preemptive pair. Priority scheduling has the same pair, and round robin is preemptive by construction.

OS-U1-Q17MSQeasy

Under non-preemptive scheduling, which of the following can take the CPU away from the running process? (Select all that apply.)

  1. The process terminates.
  2. The process issues a blocking I/O request.
  3. A process with a higher priority arrives in the ready queue.
  4. The process's time quantum expires.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A) and (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. In a non-preemptive scheme the running process gives up the CPU voluntarily. Only two events are voluntary: finishing, and blocking on something.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Termination releases the CPU, so the scheduler picks the next process.
  2. (B) A blocking request moves the process to Waiting and releases the CPU.
  3. (C) A higher-priority arrival is exactly what preemption would act on — and non-preemptive scheduling refuses to act.
  4. (D) There is no time quantum to expire in a non-preemptive algorithm.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) is the definition of preemption, which is absent here.
  • (D) A quantum belongs to round robin, which is preemptive.

Common misconception. Option (D) is chosen because students think every algorithm has a quantum. A quantum is a round-robin parameter, not a universal one.

Takeaway. Non-preemptive = the process keeps the CPU until it blocks or exits. Nothing else can take it away.

OS-U1-Q18NATmedium

Four processes are scheduled on one CPU by preemptive priority scheduling, where a smaller priority number means a higher priority. All times are in milliseconds.

ProcessArrivalBurstPriority
P10205
P2211
P3412
P4613
How many times is a running process preempted by a newly arrived process?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 3

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Preemptive priority compares the priority of the running process with that of every ready process, at every arrival. A preemption happens only when the newcomer outranks the process currently on the CPU.

Step by step.

  1. t = 0: only P1 has arrived, so P1 runs.
  2. t = 2: P2 (priority 1) arrives and outranks P1 (priority 5) — P1 is preempted. Preemption 1. P2 runs for its 1 ms and finishes at t = 3.
  3. t = 3: P1 is the only ready process, so P1 resumes and runs from t = 3.
  4. t = 4: P3 (priority 2) arrives and outranks P1 (priority 5) — P1 is preempted. Preemption 2. P3 runs 1 ms and finishes at t = 5; P1 resumes.
  5. t = 6: P4 (priority 3) arrives and outranks P1 (priority 5) — P1 is preempted. Preemption 3. P4 runs 1 ms and finishes at t = 7.
  6. t = 7: P1 runs its remaining 17 ms and finishes at t = 23.
  7. Total preemptions = 3.

Answer: 3.

Common misconception. Counting the dispatches of P3 and P4 as preemptions is right here only because P1 happened to be running each time. The trap is the opposite error: counting a preemption when the CPU was idle or when a process had just finished, which is a fresh dispatch, not a preemption.

Takeaway. A preemption needs a victim that is actually running. Trace the timeline second by second and ask, at each arrival, whether the newcomer outranks whoever holds the CPU.

OS-U1-Q39MCQeasy

Preemptive scheduling is essential for which one of the following?

  1. Maximising the throughput of a batch system
  2. Letting an interactive process obtain the CPU promptly, because no process can hold the CPU until it blocks or exits
  3. Eliminating context switches
  4. Guaranteeing that no process ever starves
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Without preemption the running process keeps the CPU until it blocks or terminates. A single CPU-bound process would then be able to hold the CPU for seconds at a time, and an interactive process would wait that long. Preemption — by quantum expiry or by a higher-priority arrival — is what bounds that wait.

Step by step.

  1. The benefit of preemption is bounded response time, which is what an interactive system needs — option (B).
  2. Batch throughput usually favours fewer switches, so preemption does not help it.
  3. Preemption increases context switches rather than removing them.
  4. Preemption can itself cause starvation (a stream of high-priority arrivals); it does not prevent it.

Answer: Option (B) — prompt response for interactive processes.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Preemption adds switches, which costs throughput.
  • (C) It adds switches.
  • (D) Priority-based preemption is a classic cause of starvation; aging is the cure.

Common misconception. Equating preemption with fairness. Preemption bounds how long a process can hold the CPU; it says nothing about whether a particular process ever gets it.

Takeaway. Preemption buys response time and costs switch overhead. Those two are the trade-off in every preemptive design.

OS-U1-Q40MCQeasy

Which one of the following is a difficulty that preemptive scheduling introduces and non-preemptive scheduling does not?

  1. A process can be stopped in the middle of an update to shared data, so the operating system must protect its own data structures against concurrent access.
  2. A ready queue has to be maintained.
  3. Each process needs a process control block.
  4. A dispatcher has to exist.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. When a process can be displaced at an arbitrary instant, the kernel itself may be interrupted while it is modifying a shared structure such as the ready queue. That is why kernels disable interrupts or use locks around such critical sections, and why user-level code needs synchronisation primitives. Non-preemptive scheduling only switches at well-defined points.

Step by step.

  1. The new hazard of preemption is an interruption at an arbitrary instant — option (A).
  2. A ready queue exists in both schemes.
  3. Every process has a PCB in both schemes.
  4. A dispatcher exists in both schemes.

Answer: Option (A) — a process may be interrupted mid-update of shared data.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B), (C) and (D) are common to both preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling.

Common misconception. Thinking preemption is free. It costs switches and it forces the kernel to treat its own data structures as critical sections.

Takeaway. Preemption is the reason a kernel needs interrupt disabling and locks around scheduler data structures — a direct link to the synchronisation unit.

OS-U1-Q41MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Under a strictly non-preemptive policy, a process that has started running cannot be starved of the CPU before it finishes.
  2. For the same workload, preemptive scheduling can perform more context switches than non-preemptive scheduling.
  3. Under non-preemptive SJF, a newly arrived short process may have to wait for a long process that is already running.
  4. A preemptive scheduler can never starve a process.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Non-preemptive means the CPU is released only voluntarily, so once a process is running it completes. The corollary is that a short arrival may wait behind a long runner. Preemption adds forced switches, so it can only increase the switch count. Preemption does not guarantee fairness: a stream of higher-priority arrivals can starve a low-priority process indefinitely.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true — release is voluntary only, so the runner finishes.
  2. (B) is true — quantum expiry and priority arrivals are extra switch triggers.
  3. (C) is true — that is precisely the weakness of non-preemptive SJF.
  4. (D) is false — preemptive priority scheduling without aging starves low-priority processes.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Believing preemption implies fairness. Preemption bounds a process's turn on the CPU, not its waiting time; only aging or a fair-share policy bounds the latter.

Takeaway. Non-preemptive = no starvation once running, but bad response. Preemptive = good response, but starvation is possible and switches cost more.

OS-U1-Q42NATmedium

Four processes are scheduled on one CPU by preemptive shortest remaining time first (SRTF). All times are in milliseconds.

ProcessArrivalBurst
P109
P223
P346
P482
If a newly arrived process has exactly the same remaining time as the running process, the running process continues. How many times is the running process preempted by a newly arrived process? (Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 2

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. SRTF preempts the running process only when a newly arriving process has a strictly shorter remaining time. Count only those forced displacements; a process that finishes normally, or that is merely passed over at the moment of a dispatch, is not a preemption.

Step by step.

  1. t = 0: only P1 has arrived, so P1 runs. At t = 2 its remaining time is 7.
  2. t = 2: P2 arrives with 3 ms, which is less than 7 — P1 is preempted (count 1). P2 runs 2 → 5 and finishes.
  3. t = 5: ready are P1 (7) and P3 (6). P3 is shorter, but this is a dispatch decision after P2 finished, not a preemption.
  4. P3 runs 5 → 8. At t = 8 its remaining time is 3.
  5. t = 8: P4 arrives with 2 ms, which is less than 3 — P3 is preempted (count 2). P4 runs 8 → 10 and finishes.
  6. t = 10: P3 (3) then P1 (7) run to completion with no further arrivals.
  7. Total preemptions = 2.

Answer: 2 preemptions.

Common misconception. Counting every change of the running process. A switch made because the previous process finished or blocked is not a preemption; only an arrival that displaces a running process is. Here the P2 → P3 change at t = 5 is of that harmless kind.

Takeaway. Preemption counting is a separate skill from completion times. Fix the rule (strictly shorter remaining time) and walk the timeline once, marking only displacements.

OS-U1-Q43MCQhard

Three processes are scheduled by preemptive priority scheduling, where a smaller priority number means a higher priority. All times are in milliseconds.

ProcessArrivalBurstPriority
P1063
P2241
P3422
What is the completion time of P1?

  1. 8 ms
  2. 10 ms
  3. 12 ms
  4. 14 ms
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Under preemptive priority the process with the smallest priority number runs whenever it is ready, and a newly arriving higher-priority process displaces the runner immediately.

Step by step.

  1. t = 0: only P1 is present, so P1 runs. At t = 2 it has used 2 ms and 4 ms remain.
  2. t = 2: P2 arrives with priority 1, higher than P1's 3 — P2 preempts P1 and runs 2 → 6, finishing at 6.
  3. t = 4: P3 arrives with priority 2. P2 has priority 1, which is higher, so P3 does not preempt.
  4. t = 6: ready are P1 (priority 3, 4 ms left) and P3 (priority 2, 2 ms). P3 is higher, so P3 runs 6 → 8 and finishes.
  5. t = 8: only P1 remains; it runs its last 4 ms, 8 → 12.
  6. P1 completes at 12 ms.

Answer: Option (C) — P1 completes at 12 ms.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 8 ms is when P3 completes.
  • (B) 10 ms results from letting P3 preempt P2 at t = 4, which priority 1 forbids.
  • (D) 14 ms results from running P1 to completion before P3 is considered at all.

Common misconception. Letting any new arrival preempt. Preemption needs a strictly higher priority; P3's priority 2 cannot displace P2's priority 1.

Takeaway. Trace preemptive priority arrival by arrival and compare the newcomer's priority with the runner's each time; do not assume every arrival preempts.

OS-U1-Q44NAThard

Four processes are scheduled by preemptive priority scheduling, where a smaller priority number means a higher priority. All times are in milliseconds.

ProcessArrivalBurstPriority
P1084
P2141
P3293
P4352
What is the average waiting time? (Enter a number; decimals are allowed.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 7 ms

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Waiting time = completion time − arrival time − burst time. Under preemptive priority the highest priority ready process always runs, so the timeline has to be built one arrival at a time.

Step by step.

  1. t = 0: only P1 is present, so P1 runs. At t = 1 it has used 1 ms and 7 ms remain.
  2. t = 1: P2 arrives with priority 1, higher than 4 — P2 preempts and runs 1 → 5, finishing at 5.
  3. t = 2: P3 (priority 3) arrives, but P2's priority 1 is higher, so nothing changes.
  4. t = 3: P4 (priority 2) arrives, again lower than P2's 1, so nothing changes.
  5. t = 5: ready are P1 (priority 4, 7 ms left), P3 (priority 3, 9 ms) and P4 (priority 2, 5 ms). P4 has the highest priority, so P4 runs 5 → 10 and finishes at 10.
  6. t = 10: P3 (priority 3) beats P1 (priority 4); P3 runs 10 → 19 and finishes.
  7. t = 19: P1 runs 19 → 26 and finishes.
  8. Waiting times: P1 = 26 − 0 − 8 = 18; P2 = 5 − 1 − 4 = 0; P3 = 19 − 2 − 9 = 8; P4 = 10 − 3 − 5 = 2.
  9. Average = (18 + 0 + 8 + 2) / 4 = 28 / 4 = 7 ms.

Answer: 7 ms.

Common misconception. Forgetting the arrival times when computing waiting time. P2 arrives at t = 1, so its waiting time is 5 − 1 − 4 = 0, not 5 − 4 = 1.

Takeaway. Build the Gantt chart first, read off completion times, then apply WT = C − A − B to every process in one pass.

OS-U1-Q63MCQeasy

Which one of the following is TRUE of non-preemptive scheduling?

  1. A process keeps the CPU until it blocks or terminates.
  2. A process is removed from the CPU as soon as a higher-priority process becomes ready.
  3. It needs a periodic timer interrupt in order to function.
  4. It always produces a lower average waiting time than preemptive scheduling.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Non-preemptive means the scheduler runs only when the running process gives up the CPU voluntarily — by blocking on I/O, by calling exit(), or by yielding.

Step by step.

  1. The dispatcher hands the CPU to a process.
  2. The process keeps it; no arrival of another process can displace it.
  3. Only a voluntary relinquish returns control to the scheduler.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Displacing a running process on a higher-priority arrival is precisely preemption.
  • (C) A timer is what enables preemption; a non-preemptive scheduler does not need one.
  • (D) No such general claim holds; preemptive SRTF has the minimum average waiting time.

Common misconception. Believing non-preemptive means no interrupts. Device interrupts still occur; they just do not cause a scheduling decision for the running process.

Takeaway. Preemption is about who may take the CPU away — only the running process itself, or the kernel as well.

OS-U1-Q64MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about response time are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Response time is measured from submission of the process to the first instant it gets the CPU.
  2. For a long queue of CPU-bound jobs, preemptive round robin bounds the worst-case response time, while first come first served does not.
  3. Response time and waiting time are the same quantity.
  4. Under a non-preemptive scheduler the response time of a newly arrived process can be as large as the longest remaining burst in the system.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Response time is the delay before the first CPU service; waiting time is the total time spent in the ready queue. For a process that is dispatched once and never preempted they coincide, which is why they are so often confused.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: that is the definition.
  2. (B) True: with quantum q and n ready processes, a new arrival waits at most (n − 1)·q before its first slice; under FCFS it waits for every burst queued ahead of it.
  3. (C) False: a process preempted many times has a large waiting time but its response time was small.
  4. (D) True: a new arrival cannot start until the running process gives up the CPU, which may take as long as its remaining burst.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (C) They differ exactly when preemption occurs, which is the interesting case.

Common misconception. Treating response time as an average. It is usually quoted as a worst case, because an interactive user cares about the longest stall, not the mean.

Takeaway. Response time = first service; waiting time = all ready-queue time. Preemption improves the first and can worsen the second.

OS-U1-Q65NATmedium

Four processes arrive as shown and are scheduled by preemptive shortest remaining time first (SRTF). All times are in milliseconds. How many times is a running process preempted? Do not count the initial dispatch of the first process.

P109
P225
P342
P461
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 2

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. SRTF compares remaining times at every arrival instant. A preemption occurs only when a newly arrived process has strictly less remaining time than the running one; the running process is never displaced by one that is merely equal or longer.

Step by step.

  1. t = 0: only P1 exists, so P1 runs. Remaining: P1 = 9.
  2. t = 2: P2 arrives with burst 5. P1 has 7 left, and 5 < 7, so P2 preempts P1. Preemption 1.
  3. t = 4: P2 has 3 left; P3 arrives with burst 2, and 2 < 3, so P3 preempts P2. Preemption 2.
  4. t = 6: P3 completes. P4 arrives at t = 6 with burst 1. Waiting are P2 with 3 left and P1 with 7 left; 1 is the smallest, so P4 runs — but P3 had already finished, so this is a dispatch, not a preemption.
  5. t = 7: P4 completes. P2 (3 left) runs to t = 10.
  6. t = 10: P1 runs its remaining 7 ms and completes at t = 17.

Answer: 2 preemptions.

Common misconception. Counting every change of the running process. A dispatch after the previous process completed is not a preemption; the count is only of processes displaced while still runnable.

Takeaway. Draw the Gantt chart and mark only those boundaries at which the outgoing process still had work left.

OS-U1-Q66MCQeasy

Why does a preemptive scheduler need a hardware timer?

  1. To measure the burst time of each process.
  2. To regain control of the CPU from a process that neither blocks nor terminates.
  3. To choose the next process when several are ready.
  4. To save the context of the preempted process.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The kernel runs only when it is entered — by a system call, an exception or an interrupt. A CPU-bound process that makes no system calls never enters the kernel on its own, so without a periodic timer interrupt the kernel could never take the CPU back.

Step by step.

  1. The timer is programmed to interrupt after the quantum.
  2. The interrupt transfers control to the kernel's handler.
  3. The handler charges the running process, marks the quantum expired and invokes the scheduler.
  4. The scheduler may then switch to another process.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Burst times are not measured by the timer; they are observed or predicted.
  • (C) Selection is the scheduler's job, not the timer's.
  • (D) The context switch routine saves the context; the timer only triggers it.

Common misconception. Thinking the timer chooses the next process. It only guarantees the kernel gets a chance to choose.

Takeaway. The timer is the mechanism that makes preemption possible; the scheduler is the policy that uses it.

OS-U1-Q67MCQhard

Which one of the following statements comparing preemptive shortest remaining time first (SRTF) with non-preemptive shortest job first (SJF) is TRUE?

  1. For the same set of processes, SRTF never has a larger average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.
  2. For the same set of processes, non-preemptive SJF never has a larger average waiting time than SRTF.
  3. The two always give the same average waiting time, because both always pick the shortest job.
  4. SRTF can only be implemented as one level of a multilevel feedback queue.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. SRTF is the optimal algorithm for average waiting time among all schedulers that must decide without knowing future arrivals. It re-decides at every arrival, so its set of feasible schedules contains every schedule non-preemptive SJF can produce, and it always takes the best of them.

Step by step.

  1. Non-preemptive SJF fixes an order when the CPU is free; a long job that starts cannot be interrupted by a short arrival.
  2. SRTF interrupts it, which can only move short jobs earlier.
  3. Shortening the jobs that run early cannot increase the total waiting time, so SRTF's average is at most SJF's — and strictly smaller whenever a short job arrives during a long one.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the containment: SJF cannot beat the optimum.
  • (C) They differ whenever an arrival has a shorter remaining time than the running process.
  • (D) SRTF is an ordinary priority scheduler with remaining time as the key; a multilevel feedback queue only approximates it when bursts are unknown.

Common misconception. Assuming optimality carries over to turnaround time. SRTF minimises average waiting time; it can increase turnaround for long jobs.

Takeaway. SRTF ≤ SJF on average waiting time, always, and SRTF can starve the long job that SJF would at least have started.

OS-U1-Q68MCQmedium

Two processes update a shared counter with an ordinary read-modify-write sequence and no synchronisation. Which one of the following failures becomes possible only because the scheduler is preemptive?

  1. A page fault on the page holding the counter.
  2. A deadlock in which each process waits for a resource the other holds.
  3. A process being stopped because its time quantum has expired.
  4. A lost update: both processes read the same old value and one of the increments is overwritten.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A read-modify-write is not atomic. If the scheduler can stop a process between the read and the write, another process can read the same old value, and one of the two increments disappears. Under non-preemptive scheduling a process runs that sequence to completion, so the interleaving cannot occur.

Step by step.

  1. Both processes read the counter, say 5.
  2. P1 is preempted before it writes.
  3. P2 computes 6 and writes 6.
  4. P1 resumes, computes 6 from its stale 5 and writes 6. One increment is lost.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Page faults arise from memory access patterns, not from the scheduling policy.
  • (B) Deadlock needs each process to hold one resource and wait for another; it can happen with or without preemption.
  • (C) Quantum expiry is the normal operation of preemption, not a failure caused by it.

Common misconception. Believing that a single machine instruction is automatically atomic with respect to other processes. Only genuinely atomic instructions, or critical sections, give that guarantee.

Takeaway. Preemption turns any non-atomic shared update into a race; that is why critical sections exist.

OS-U1-Q86MCQeasy

Which one of the following process-state transitions is possible only when the scheduler is preemptive?

  1. Running → Waiting
  2. Running → Ready
  3. Waiting → Ready
  4. New → Ready
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Concept. Preemption is exactly the ability to take the CPU away from a process that has not asked to give it up. In state terms that is the edge Running → Ready: the process is runnable but no longer running.

Step by step.

  1. Running → Waiting happens when the process itself blocks; the process initiates it, so it needs no preemption.
  2. Waiting → Ready happens when the awaited event completes; an interrupt or another process causes it, but the process was not running.
  3. New → Ready is the long-term scheduler's admission decision.
  4. Only Running → Ready removes the CPU from a running process against its will.

Answer: Option (B) — Running → Ready.

Common misconception. Confusing Waiting → Ready with preemption because both are asynchronous. A blocked process holds no CPU, so nothing is being taken away.

Takeaway. Preemption adds exactly one edge to the state diagram: Running → Ready.

OS-U1-Q87MCQmedium

A round-robin scheduler is given a time quantum so small that it is comparable to the cost of a context switch. Which one of the following best describes the result?

  1. The CPU spends most of its time switching, so throughput falls even though every process gets the CPU often.
  2. Average turnaround time improves without limit as the quantum shrinks.
  3. The scheduler behaves exactly like FCFS.
  4. The scheduler behaves exactly like SJF.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Concept. Round robin trades two costs against each other: a large quantum wastes little on switching but behaves like FCFS, and a tiny quantum gives excellent response time but pays a context switch per quantum.

Step by step.

  1. Useful work per quantum is at most q, and overhead per quantum is the switch cost c.
  2. The fraction of the CPU doing useful work is q / (q + c).
  3. When q ≈ c that fraction is about one half, so half the machine is spent saving and restoring state.
  4. Response time does improve, but turnaround time and throughput get worse, so (B) fails.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) each process is dispatched more often, but each dispatch costs more, so turnaround does not keep improving.
  • (C) FCFS is the limit of a quantum larger than every burst, not smaller.
  • (D) SJF needs burst lengths, which round robin never uses.

Common misconception. Thinking a smaller quantum is always better. It improves response time only; it degrades efficiency.

Takeaway. Useful fraction = q/(q + c). Keep the quantum far above the switch cost.

OS-U1-Q88NATeasy

Two CPU-bound processes arrive at t = 0. P1 needs 10 ms and P2 needs 6 ms, and P1 is ahead of P2 in the ready queue. The scheduler is round robin with a time quantum of 4 ms. At what time, in ms, does the last process terminate?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 16

Detailed solution

Concept. Under round robin a process that has not finished when its quantum expires goes to the tail of the ready queue. Both processes are CPU-bound, so neither ever blocks and the CPU is never idle.

Step by step.

  1. 0–4: P1 runs, 6 ms left, and is re-queued behind P2.
  2. 4–8: P2 runs, 2 ms left, and is re-queued behind P1.
  3. 8–12: P1 runs, 2 ms left, and is re-queued behind P2.
  4. 12–14: P2 runs its last 2 ms and terminates at 14.
  5. 14–16: P1 runs its last 2 ms and terminates at 16.

Answer: 16

Common misconception. Finishing P1 first because it started first. With 16 ms of work and no idle time the last completion is at 16 whatever the order, so the trap is really the queueing: after each expiry the preempted process goes behind the other.

Takeaway. Total work plus total idle = last completion time; track the queue to get the order.

OS-U1-Q89MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about the timer, a non-preemptible kernel, a read-modify-write and the average waiting time are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Preempting a CPU-bound process that never blocks requires a hardware timer interrupt.
  2. A kernel that is not preemptible makes a newly runnable higher-priority process wait until the running process leaves kernel mode.
  3. Under non-preemptive scheduling a process can never lose the CPU in the middle of a read-modify-write on a shared variable, so no synchronisation is needed.
  4. Preemption always reduces the average waiting time of a workload.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A) and (B)

Detailed solution

Concept. Preemption needs a trigger that the running process cannot refuse, and for a process that never blocks the only such trigger is the timer interrupt. Where the kernel cannot be preempted, the switch is deferred to the next point at which the kernel is safe to leave.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. A process that neither blocks nor yields gives the scheduler no opportunity to run, so only an interrupt can take the CPU.
  2. (B) True. In a non-preemptible kernel the running process is not displaced inside a system call; the reschedule happens on the way out.
  3. (C) False. A process can still be switched out in the middle of a read-modify-write by blocking inside it — on a page fault, for example — and with two CPUs the interleaving happens regardless of preemption.
  4. (D) False. Preemption can make the average waiting time worse: round robin is generally worse than SJF on average waiting time.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. Reading "non-preemptive" as "atomic". It only means the scheduler is not invoked by the timer; blocking and multiprocessors still interleave.

Takeaway. Preemption needs a timer, a preemptible kernel, and it buys response time, not necessarily waiting time.

OS-U1-Q90MCQhard

An operating system has a non-preemptible kernel. A low-priority process L is inside a long system call, copying a large buffer, when a high-priority process H becomes runnable. Which one of the following happens?

  1. H preempts L at once, because H has the higher priority.
  2. H waits until L returns from the system call and the kernel is ready to return to user mode; only then can the switch be made.
  3. The kernel migrates H to an idle CPU even when the machine has a single CPU.
  4. L is killed so that H can run.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Concept. In a non-preemptible kernel a process is not displaced while it executes kernel code, because the kernel's own data structures may be in an inconsistent state. The reschedule is deferred to the safe point at which the process is about to return to user mode.

Step by step.

  1. H becomes ready and the scheduler marks a reschedule as needed.
  2. The check cannot be honoured inside the kernel, so it is postponed.
  3. L finishes the copy, reaches the exit path of the system call, and only then is H dispatched.
  4. The delay to H is therefore bounded by the length of L's system call, not by its whole CPU burst.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) that is precisely what a non-preemptible kernel forbids.
  • (C) with one CPU there is no idle CPU to migrate to, and migration does not help a single-CPU machine.
  • (D) priority never licenses killing a process that is doing legitimate work.

Common misconception. Believing higher priority means immediate. Priority decides the next dispatch, and the dispatch point is set by whether the kernel can be preempted.

Takeaway. Priority orders the queue; kernel preemptibility decides when the order is consulted.

OS-U1-Q113MCQeasy

Which one of the following is NOT an instant at which a preemptive scheduler can take the CPU away from the running process?

  1. The instant the running process's time quantum expires.
  2. The instant a process with a higher priority becomes ready.
  3. Inside a critical section of the kernel in which interrupts are disabled on that CPU.
  4. The instant the running process issues a blocking I/O request.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Preemption needs a mechanism to interrupt the CPU: the timer interrupt for quantum expiry, an interrupt or a scheduling check when a higher-priority process becomes ready, or the process's own trap on a blocking call. With interrupts disabled the CPU will not take the timer interrupt at all, so the scheduler cannot run until the critical section ends. Such regions are the reason a kernel has non-preemptible stretches.

Step by step.

  1. Quantum expiry is delivered as a timer interrupt, so it is a preemption point.
  2. A higher-priority arrival triggers a scheduling check at the next safe point, so it is one too.
  3. With interrupts masked, the timer interrupt stays pending; no scheduling decision can be taken.
  4. Blocking I/O is a voluntary exit from the CPU, which happens immediately but is not a preemption in the strict sense; it is certainly not the answer to "NOT possible", because the CPU is indeed released.

Answer: Option (C) — inside a critical section with interrupts disabled the CPU cannot be taken away.

Common misconception. Believing preemption can occur at any instruction boundary. It can occur only where the hardware and the kernel allow an interrupt to be taken or a scheduling point to be reached.

OS-U1-Q114MCQmedium

A process is executing a system call, so it is inside the kernel. Which one of the following is TRUE about its preemption?

  1. It can never be preempted once it has entered the kernel, on any operating system.
  2. With a preemptible kernel it can be preempted, but only at points where the kernel's own data structures are in a consistent state.
  3. It is preempted at every timer tick, whatever the kernel happens to be doing at that instant.
  4. Preemption inside the kernel is impossible on a multiprocessor, because another CPU is always free to run the next process.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A kernel that is not preemptible delays every other process until the running process returns from the kernel, which hurts response time. A preemptible kernel allows a switch inside kernel mode, but only at explicit preemption points (safe points) where no lock is held and no data structure is half-updated. Preempting in the middle of a list insertion would leave the kernel's own state corrupt.

Step by step.

  1. A non-preemptible kernel defers the switch until the system call returns — that is the historical UNIX behaviour, not a universal rule.
  2. A preemptible kernel checks whether a switch is due at safe points inside the kernel.
  3. Between those points, locks may be held and invariants broken, so preemption is deferred.
  4. Hence preemption inside the kernel is possible but constrained, not unconditional.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Modern general-purpose kernels are preemptible in kernel mode.
  • (C) Unconditional preemption at every tick would break the kernel's own invariants.
  • (D) Having another CPU changes nothing about whether this CPU's kernel code may be preempted.

Common misconception. Thinking preemption is a property of the hardware alone. It is a policy the kernel implements at points it chooses to consider safe.

OS-U1-Q115MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about the cost of preemptive scheduling are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. For a set of CPU-bound processes that never block, adding preemption increases the number of context switches compared with running them non-preemptively.
  2. Preemption can lower throughput, because the switching overhead is time during which no user process makes progress.
  3. To stop the running process and later resume it exactly where it stopped, the scheduler relies on the saved CPU context held in the PCB.
  4. Preemptive scheduling always produces a lower average turnaround time than non-preemptive scheduling for the same set of processes.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Preemption buys responsiveness with switching overhead. Every preemption of a CPU-bound process costs a context save and restore that does no user work, so throughput can fall even though response time improves. Correct resumption depends on the PCB holding the complete CPU context.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: without preemption a CPU-bound process runs to completion, giving n − 1 switches for n processes; preemption adds a switch at every quantum.
  2. (B) True: the switch time is overhead, so useful work per unit time falls.
  3. (C) True: the program counter, registers and memory-management state saved in the PCB are exactly what makes resumption possible.
  4. (D) False: preemption can increase turnaround time by adding overhead and by delaying long jobs. Turnaround is not monotone in preemption.

Common misconception. Treating preemption as a strict improvement. It is a trade: better response time and fairness, usually worse throughput and more overhead.

OS-U1-Q116NATmedium

Four processes are scheduled by preemptive shortest remaining time first (SRTF). All times are in milliseconds. A newly arrived process displaces the running one only if its remaining time is strictly smaller; on a tie the running process continues.

P108
P214

P431

Show answer & solution

Answer: 2

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Under SRTF a preemption is counted only when a process that is actually running is replaced by another process that has not yet run to completion. A process that finishes and hands over to the next one has not been preempted, and a tie does not displace the running process.

Step by step.

  1. t = 0: only P1 is present, remaining 8. It runs.
  2. t = 1: P2 arrives with 4 < 7 remaining of P1 → preemption 1; P2 runs.
  3. t = 2: P3 arrives with 2 < 3 remaining of P2 → preemption 2; P3 runs.
  4. t = 3: P4 arrives with 1, but P3 has exactly 1 left. A tie does not displace, so P3 continues and completes at t = 4.
  5. t = 4: ready P2 (3), P4 (1), P1 (7). P4 runs 4→5 and completes; P2 runs 5→8 and completes; P1 runs 8→15.
  6. None of those three handovers is a preemption: each follows a completion.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Counting every change of the running process, which gives 5 here (the three handovers after completions included), or letting P4 displace P3 on the tie, which would give 3. A preemption is only the involuntary displacement of a process that still has work left.

OS-U1-Q117MCQhard

A system runs one long CPU-bound process together with many short I/O-bound processes on a single CPU, and CPU utilisation is poor. Which one of the following changes is most likely to raise CPU utilisation and shorten the average response time?

  1. Increase the round-robin quantum until it exceeds the CPU-bound process's burst.
  2. Give the I/O-bound processes a higher priority, so that each of them leaves the CPU quickly and the disk can work in parallel with the CPU-bound process.
  3. Replace preemptive round robin with non-preemptive first come first served.
  4. Disable the timer interrupt, so that context switches cost nothing.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Utilisation is poor when the CPU is idle waiting for I/O that has not been started, or when short interactive jobs queue behind a long one. I/O-bound processes need the CPU only briefly before issuing their next request, so favouring them keeps the disk busy and returns the CPU almost at once. This is the standard argument for giving I/O-bound work a higher priority or a shorter quantum.

Step by step.

  1. A long quantum lets the CPU-bound process monopolise the CPU, delaying every I/O request and leaving the disk idle — worse, not better.
  2. Prioritising the I/O-bound processes lets each issue its request in a few milliseconds, then block.
  3. The CPU-bound process then runs during those I/O operations, so CPU and disk work in parallel.
  4. Average response time also falls, because the short jobs are no longer stuck behind the long one.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) A long quantum reproduces FCFS and worsens both metrics here.
  • (C) Non-preemptive FCFS is the worst case for this mix: the long process holds the CPU to completion.
  • (D) The timer is what makes preemption possible; removing it removes the fix.

Common misconception. Assuming "fair" means "equal share of the CPU". For a mixed workload, giving the short I/O-bound jobs priority raises total throughput because it keeps every device busy.

OS-U1-Q118MCQeasy

Under a non-preemptive scheduler, a process that never blocks and never terminates starts running. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  2. The timer preempts it when its time quantum expires.
  3. The medium-term scheduler swaps it out as soon as another process becomes ready.
  4. It is moved to a lower-priority queue once it has used one time slice.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A non-preemptive scheduler changes the running process only when that process gives up the CPU — by blocking, by terminating, or by a yield. A process that never does any of these therefore runs for ever. That is the classic argument that batch systems without preemption rely on the goodwill of their jobs, and why interactive systems must be preemptive.

Step by step.

  1. Only a voluntary event removes a process from the CPU under non-preemptive scheduling.
  2. This process blocks never and terminates never, so no such event occurs.
  3. Nothing else can take the CPU, so the rest of the system waits indefinitely.
  4. The situation is a livelock for the others: they are ready but never dispatched.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) There is no quantum to expire when the scheduler is non-preemptive.
  • (C) A running process cannot be swapped out; swapping applies to processes off the CPU.
  • (D) Queue demotion belongs to a feedback queue, which is a preemptive mechanism.

Common misconception. Believing that a higher-priority arrival still displaces the running process. Without preemption it does not, however urgent it is.

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Under FCFS the processes run in arrival order without interruption. Waiting time is turnaround time minus burst time, and turnaround time is completion time minus arrival time.

Step by step.

  1. P1 runs from 0 to 3: completion 3, waiting time 3 − 0 − 3 = 0.
  2. P2 runs from 3 to 9: completion 9, waiting time 9 − 1 − 6 = 2.
  3. P3 runs from 9 to 13: completion 13, waiting time 13 − 2 − 4 = 7.
  4. Average = (0 + 2 + 7) / 3 = 9 / 3 = 3 ms.

Answer: Option (A) — 3 ms.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) comes from forgetting to subtract the arrival time of P2 and P3.
  • (C) and (D) come from adding arrival times instead of subtracting them.

Common misconception. Using arrival time as the start time for every process. P2 does not start at t = 1; it starts when P1 releases the CPU.

Takeaway. Waiting time = completion − arrival − burst. Always compute completion times first.

OS-U1-Q20MCQeasy

The convoy effect — several short CPU-bound processes queued behind one long CPU-bound process, producing a poor average waiting time — is most closely associated with which algorithm?

  1. Round robin
  2. First come first served
  3. Shortest remaining time first
  4. Multilevel feedback queue
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The convoy effect is a direct consequence of serving processes in arrival order regardless of length, which is exactly what FCFS does.

Step by step.

  1. Under FCFS one long job at the head of the queue makes every short job behind it wait.
  2. The short jobs also hold up the I/O device they use only briefly, so device utilisation suffers too.
  3. SRTF would move the short jobs ahead, and round robin would interleave them, so neither produces the convoy.
  4. Hence the convoy effect belongs to FCFS.

Answer: Option (B) — first come first served.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Round robin interleaves jobs and bounds the wait by the quantum.
  • (C) SRTF always runs the shortest remaining job, which dissolves the convoy.
  • (D) Multilevel feedback queues promote short jobs, which also dissolves it.

Common misconception. The convoy effect is sometimes attached to SJF because SJF is 'the fix'. SJF avoids the convoy; FCFS causes it.

Takeaway. Convoy effect = FCFS + one long job at the head. The standard remedies are SJF, SRTF and round robin.

OS-U1-Q21MCQmedium

Three processes arrive at time t = 0 with CPU bursts of 12 ms, 18 ms and 30 ms. The scheduler knows the burst lengths in advance. What is the minimum achievable average waiting time for these three processes under a non-preemptive scheduler?

  1. 12 ms
  2. 14 ms
  3. 16 ms
  4. 18 ms
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. For a fixed set of processes with no arrival spread, the non-preemptive algorithm that minimises average waiting time is shortest job first: run the shortest burst first and the longest last.

Step by step.

  1. Order the bursts: 12, 18, 30.
  2. SJF runs them in that order. Waiting times: first job 0, second 12, third 12 + 18 = 30.
  3. Average = (0 + 12 + 30) / 3 = 42 / 3 = 14 ms.
  4. Any other order increases the sum, so 14 ms is the minimum.

Answer: Option (B) — 14 ms.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 12 ms is the waiting time of the second job alone.
  • (C) and (D) come from averaging turnaround times, or from running the jobs in arrival order and dividing incorrectly.

Common misconception. Averaging turnaround times instead of waiting times. With all arrivals at t = 0 the turnaround times are 12, 30, 60, whose average is 34 ms — a different quantity.

Takeaway. All arriving together + non-preemptive + 'minimum average waiting time' means sort the bursts ascending and accumulate: 0, b₁, b₁ + b₂.

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Simulate round robin one quantum at a time. Keep a FIFO ready queue and note that the completion time is the instant the last unit of a process's burst finishes.

Step by step.

  1. t = 0–2: P1 runs its first quantum, 2 ms, leaving 3 ms. P2 arrived at t = 1 and is already queued.
  2. t = 2–4: P1's quantum has expired and it goes to the back, so P2 runs 2 ms, leaving 1 ms. P3 arrived at t = 2 and is queued behind P1.
  3. t = 4–6: P1 runs its second quantum, 2 ms, leaving 1 ms.
  4. t = 6–7: P3 runs its 1 ms and completes at t = 7.
  5. t = 7–8: P2 runs its last 1 ms and completes at t = 8.
  6. t = 8–9: P1 runs its last 1 ms and completes at t = 9.
  7. Completion time of P1 = 9 ms.

Answer: Option (C) — 9 ms.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 7 ms is the completion time of P3.
  • (B) 8 ms is the completion time of P2.
  • (D) 11 ms comes from giving P1 an extra quantum somewhere in the trace.

Common misconception. Charging the first quantum from t = 0 to t = 1 for P1. The quantum is 2 ms, so P1 runs from 0 to 2, and P2 — which arrives at t = 1 — must wait.

Takeaway. Write the queue state after every quantum. For round robin, the answer is in the bookkeeping, not in the formula.

OS-U1-Q23MSQhard

Which of the following statements about CPU scheduling algorithms are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. SRTF can starve a long process indefinitely if short processes keep arriving.
  2. Increasing the time quantum of round robin increases the number of context switches.
  3. Among non-preemptive algorithms, SJF minimises the average waiting time.
  4. FCFS always gives the minimum average turnaround time for a given set of processes.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Starvation, quantum size and SJF optimality are the three classic scheduling properties; FCFS optimality is the classic false claim.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: SRTF always picks the shortest remaining time, so a long job loses to every short arrival and may never run.
  2. (B) False: a larger quantum means fewer expiries, hence fewer context switches — with a quantum larger than every burst, round robin degenerates into FCFS.
  3. (C) True: SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time among non-preemptive algorithms, by an exchange argument on adjacent jobs.
  4. (D) False: FCFS can be arbitrarily bad — the convoy effect — so it cannot be optimal.

Answer: Options (A) and (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the relationship: the number of switches falls as the quantum grows.
  • (D) is false; SJF, not FCFS, is the optimal non-preemptive rule for waiting time.

Common misconception. Option (B) is chosen because a smaller quantum is associated with 'more responsive', which students turn into 'more switches when the quantum grows'. It is the other way round.

Takeaway. Quantum up → switches down, response worse. Quantum down → switches up, overhead up. SJF is optimal for waiting time; nothing is optimal for turnaround in general except in special cases.

OS-U1-Q24NATmedium

Four processes arrive as shown and are scheduled by preemptive shortest remaining time first (SRTF). All times are in milliseconds.

ProcessArrivalBurst
P107
P224
P341
P454
What is the average waiting time?
(Enter a number; decimals are allowed.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 3

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Under SRTF the process with the smallest remaining burst always holds the CPU, and the comparison is repeated at every arrival. Waiting time = completion − arrival − burst.

Step by step.

  1. t = 0: P1 runs. At t = 2 its remaining time is 5.
  2. t = 2: P2 arrives with burst 4 < 5, so P2 preempts P1.
  3. t = 4: P3 arrives with burst 1 < P2's remaining 2, so P3 preempts P2.
  4. t = 5: P3 completes. Remaining: P2 = 2, P1 = 5, P4 = 4 (P4 arrived at t = 5). P2 runs.
  5. t = 7: P2 completes. Remaining: P4 = 4, P1 = 5. P4 runs.
  6. t = 11: P4 completes. P1 runs its remaining 5 ms and completes at t = 16.
  7. Completion times: P1 = 16, P2 = 7, P3 = 5, P4 = 11.
  8. Waiting times: P1 = 16 − 0 − 7 = 9; P2 = 7 − 2 − 4 = 1; P3 = 5 − 4 − 1 = 0; P4 = 11 − 5 − 4 = 2.
  9. Average = (9 + 1 + 0 + 2) / 4 = 12 / 4 = 3 ms.

Answer: 3 ms.

Common misconception. Letting P1 finish its first stretch because it started first. SRTF is preemptive: P2's burst of 4 beats P1's remaining 5 at t = 2, so P1 is displaced.

Takeaway. Re-evaluate the shortest remaining time at every arrival instant, not only at completions.

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Turnaround time is completion time minus arrival time; it includes both the waiting and the execution of the process. Under SRTF the schedule is rebuilt at every arrival.

Step by step.

  1. t = 0: P1 runs. At t = 1 its remaining time is 5.
  2. t = 1: P2 arrives with burst 2 < 5, so P2 preempts P1.
  3. t = 2: P3 arrives with burst 1, which ties P2's remaining time of 1. The running process P2 continues (the tie does not change the totals either way).
  4. t = 3: P2 completes. Ready: P3 = 1, P4 = 3 (arrived at t = 3), P1 = 5. P3 runs.
  5. t = 4: P3 completes. P4 = 3 < P1 = 5, so P4 runs from t = 4 to t = 7.
  6. t = 7: P4 completes. P1 runs its remaining 5 ms and completes at t = 12.
  7. Completion times: P1 = 12, P2 = 3, P3 = 4, P4 = 7.
  8. Turnaround times: P1 = 12 − 0 = 12; P2 = 3 − 1 = 2; P3 = 4 − 2 = 2; P4 = 7 − 3 = 4.
  9. Average = (12 + 2 + 2 + 4) / 4 = 20 / 4 = 5 ms.

Answer: 5 ms.

Common misconception. Reporting the average waiting time instead. Here the waiting times are 6, 0, 1, 1, whose average is 2 ms — a different number, and the usual wrong answer.

Takeaway. Turnaround = completion − arrival. Waiting = turnaround − burst. Read which one the question asks for before dividing.

OS-U1-Q47MSQhard

Which of the following statements about multilevel and multilevel feedback queue scheduling are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. In a multilevel feedback queue, a process that has used a great deal of CPU time is usually moved to a lower-priority queue.
  2. A multilevel queue with absolute priority between its queues can starve the lower-priority queues.
  3. In a multilevel feedback queue, a process that has been demoted to a lower queue can never return to a higher one.
  4. Aging — gradually raising the priority of a waiting process — can prevent starvation in a priority-based multilevel queue.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A multilevel feedback queue lets processes move between queues. The usual rule is that a process which exhausts its quantum is demoted, so CPU-bound work sinks and interactive work stays high. With absolute priority between queues, lower queues run only when higher ones are empty, which starves them; aging, or time slicing between queues, is the standard cure.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true — demotion on quantum exhaustion is the defining feedback rule.
  2. (B) is true — absolute priority means the low queue waits for every high-queue arrival.
  3. (C) is false — promotion is normally allowed (by aging or by a return to interactive behaviour), and it is what makes the scheme starvation-free.
  4. (D) is true — that is exactly what aging does.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Reading "feedback" as "one-way". The feedback in the name is the movement of processes between queues, and it normally runs in both directions; a scheme that only ever demotes would starve its bottom queue.

Takeaway. Multilevel queue = fixed assignment, absolute priority, starvation possible. Multilevel feedback queue = migration between queues, and the cure for starvation is aging.

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Round robin gives each process at most one quantum, then sends it to the back of the FIFO ready queue. Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time.

Step by step.

  1. t = 0: only P1 has arrived, so P1 runs. It uses its quantum 0 → 4 with 2 ms left.
  2. t = 4: the queue holds P2 (arrived 1) and P3 (arrived 2), and P1 is put back behind them — order P2, P3, P1.
  3. P2 runs 4 → 7 and finishes (burst 3 is less than the quantum).
  4. P3 runs 7 → 11 and uses its full quantum, with 3 ms left.
  5. P1 runs 11 → 13 and finishes.
  6. P3 runs 13 → 16 and finishes.

Common misconception. Putting the preempted process back at the front of the queue, or admitting arrivals only at the start of the next quantum. The stated rule puts arrivals first and the preempted process last; that is what makes P2 run before P1 at t = 4.

Takeaway. Write the ready queue down at every quantum boundary. Round robin is a queue discipline before it is an arithmetic problem.

OS-U1-Q49MCQmedium

A two-level multilevel feedback queue gives the top queue a time quantum of 8 ms and runs the bottom queue by FCFS.
