Takeaway. Fixed-capacity container with inserters and removers = bounded buffer.

OS-U2-Q08MCQeasy

In the dining-philosophers problem with five philosophers seated around a circular table, how many forks must a philosopher hold in order to eat?

  1. One
  2. Two — the fork on the left and the fork on the right
  3. Three
  4. Five
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A philosopher needs both adjacent forks, which is what makes the problem interesting: the resources are shared between neighbours, so a philosopher can hold one fork and still be unable to proceed.

Step by step.

  1. Five forks are placed on the table, one between each pair of neighbouring philosophers.
  2. A philosopher can pick up only the two forks that are adjacent to their own place.
  3. Eating requires both, so two forks are needed.
  4. This is option (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the naive reading, but then no contention would arise and the problem would be trivial.
  • (C) and (D) exceed the two forks that are adjacent to any one philosopher.

Common misconception. The common mistake is to forget that the two forks are shared with the neighbours, which is the whole source of deadlock.

Takeaway. Two forks per philosopher, each shared with one neighbour — that sharing is the problem.

OS-U2-Q13MCQmedium

In the producer–consumer problem with a bounded buffer of capacity N, which invariant must always hold?

  1. full + empty = N
  2. full − empty = N
  3. full × empty = N
  4. full = empty
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. full counts the items present and empty counts the free slots. Between them they always account for the whole buffer, so their sum is the capacity N at every instant.

Step by step.

  1. Initially full = 0 and empty = N, so the sum is N.
  2. A producer inserts an item: it decrements empty and increments full, so the sum is unchanged.
  3. A consumer removes an item: it increments empty and decrements full, again unchanged.
  4. The sum is therefore the invariant N, which is option (A).

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) would force full above N.
  • (C) is dimensionally meaningless here and fails for full = 0.
  • (D) would hold only for a half-full buffer.

Common misconception. Candidates confuse empty with 'the buffer is empty'. empty is a count of free slots, not a Boolean.

Takeaway. full = items present, empty = slots free, and they always sum to N.

OS-U2-Q16NATmedium

A producer–consumer system uses a bounded buffer of capacity 9 together with the counting semaphores full and empty. At some instant full = 4 and no producer is blocked. How many further items can be inserted before a producer blocks? (Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 5

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The number of free slots is empty, and empty = capacity − full.

Step by step.

  1. Capacity N = 9.
  2. full = 4, so 4 slots are occupied.
  3. Free slots = 9 − 4 = 5, and this equals the current value of empty.
  4. Each insertion consumes one free slot, so 5 more insertions are possible before empty reaches 0 and the next producer blocks.

Answer: 5.

Common misconception. Candidates sometimes answer 4, reading full as the number of free slots. full is the number of items present.

Takeaway. empty = N − full is the number of insertions still possible.

OS-U2-Q22NAThard

Seven philosophers sit around a circular table with seven forks, one between each pair of neighbours. Each philosopher needs both adjacent forks in order to eat. Using the asymmetric solution, in which one designated philosopher picks up the right fork first while every other philosopher picks up the left fork first, what is the maximum number of philosophers that can be eating at the same time? (Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 3

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each eating philosopher occupies two forks, and every fork sits between exactly two philosophers, so at most ⌊7/2⌋ = 3 can eat at once. The asymmetric rule guarantees that this maximum is actually reachable without deadlock.

Step by step.

  1. There are 7 forks and each eating philosopher needs 2 distinct forks.
  2. Forks are never shared between two eating philosophers, so the number eating is at most ⌊7 / 2⌋ = 3.
  3. That bound is achievable: philosophers 1, 3 and 5 can hold forks (7,1), (2,3) and (4,5) respectively, and none of them blocks the others.
  4. The asymmetric rule removes the circular wait, so this configuration is actually reached. Answer: 3.

Answer: 3.

Common misconception. Candidates often answer 7, thinking every philosopher can hold one fork simultaneously — but holding one fork is not eating.

Takeaway. Maximum simultaneous eaters = ⌊forks / 2⌋; the asymmetric (hierarchy) rule only makes that maximum reachable without deadlock.

OS-U2-Q23MCQmedium

In the first readers–writers solution, in which readers are never made to wait, what is the main hazard?

  1. Readers can starve.
  2. Writers can starve, because a continuous stream of readers keeps the resource occupied.
  3. A reader and a writer can be inside the critical section at the same time.
  4. Two readers can deadlock against each other.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The first readers–writers solution gives readers priority: a reader waits only while a writer is actually writing. If new readers keep arriving, the count of active readers never falls to zero, so a waiting writer is never admitted.

Step by step.

  1. A writer waits until the reader count reaches 0.
  2. Every arriving reader increments the count without regard to waiting writers.
  3. If readers arrive faster than the existing ones leave, the count never reaches 0.
  4. The writer therefore waits indefinitely: writer starvation. Option (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the hazard of the second (writer-priority) solution.
  • (C) is prevented by the semaphores in both solutions.
  • (D) is impossible: readers never block one another in this solution.

Common misconception. The two readers–writers solutions have mirror-image starvation hazards. Read the priority direction carefully before answering.

Takeaway. First solution → writers starve. Second solution → readers starve.

OS-U2B-Q20MCQeasy

In the bounded-buffer producer–consumer problem with capacity N, the counting semaphore full counts the items in the buffer and empty counts the free slots. A producer blocks when:

  1. full = 0.
  2. empty = 0.
  3. mutex = 0.
  4. empty = N.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The producer consumes a free slot before it produces; it blocks when no free slot is left.

Step by step.

  1. The producer executes P(empty) before inserting and V(full) after.
  2. It can only block inside P(empty), which happens when empty has reached 0.
  3. At that instant the buffer holds N items, so full = N as well; the two statements describe the same state, which is why only one of them appears in the options.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the state in which a consumer blocks.
  • (C) means another process is inside the buffer update.
  • (D) is the initial state, with an empty buffer.

Common misconception. Swapping the two semaphores is the classic bug: a producer that waits on full blocks as soon as the buffer is empty, which is exactly when it should be producing.

OS-U2B-Q21MCQmedium

In the second readers–writers solution, a writer that arrives while readers are active blocks new readers from entering. The main hazard of this solution is that:

  1. two writers can enter the shared data at the same time.
  2. readers and writers can deadlock on the shared mutex.
  3. a reader can be kept waiting indefinitely while new writers keep arriving.
  4. readers can no longer read concurrently with one another.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Giving writers priority removes writer starvation by creating reader starvation.

Step by step.

  1. When a writer is waiting, arriving readers are made to queue behind it, so writers are served promptly.
  2. If writers arrive continuously, each new writer re-blocks the readers before the previous queue drains.
  3. A reader can therefore wait without any bound, which is starvation rather than deadlock — the system keeps making progress, just not for that reader.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (B) are prevented by the writer mutex and the read-count protocol.
  • (D) is false: the first reader still holds the mutex on behalf of all readers, so readers continue to share the data.

Common misconception. The two readers–writers solutions are mirror images: the first starves writers, the second starves readers. Neither is 'the correct one' without a stated priority policy.

OS-U2B-Q22MCQhard

In the dining-philosophers problem with five philosophers and five forks, the solution that admits at most four philosophers to compete for forks at any time prevents deadlock. Which one of the following is the reason?

  1. Four philosophers cannot all be hungry at the same time, so contention disappears.
  2. The fifth philosopher permanently holds the extra fork, which breaks the cycle.
  3. It removes the mutual-exclusion requirement on the forks.
  4. With at most four competitors for five forks, at least one philosopher can always obtain both neighbours' forks, so the circular-wait condition cannot hold.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions; the four-at-a-time rule removes circular wait.

Step by step.

  1. If each of four philosophers held one fork, that accounts for four of the five forks.
  2. The fifth fork is free and belongs to one of those four philosophers as its second fork, so that philosopher can pick it up and eat.
  3. Eating releases both forks, which lets the others proceed in turn; a cycle in which every philosopher waits for a neighbour can therefore never close.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is false: hunger has nothing to do with the bound.
  • (B) invents a fork that does not exist.
  • (C) is false: each fork is still used by one philosopher at a time.

Common misconception. The bound is not about politeness; it is a structural argument that some philosopher always has both forks available. Without that argument the rule looks arbitrary.

OS-U2B-Q23MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about the classic synchronisation problems are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. The dining-philosophers problem with one fork between neighbours models both deadlock and starvation.
  2. The first readers–writers solution allows several readers to be inside the shared data at the same time.
  3. A monitor is a semaphore with an associated counter of the processes waiting on it.
  4. With counting semaphores full and empty in a bounded buffer of capacity N, the relation full + empty = N holds at every instant.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each of these three statements is a standard structural fact about the classical problems.

Step by step.

  1. Dining philosophers: if every philosopher picks up the left fork first, all five can hold one fork and wait for ever — deadlock; a philosopher can also be overtaken indefinitely — starvation.
  2. First readers–writers: the first reader takes the mutex, later readers only increment a count, so readers share the data concurrently.
  3. In the bounded buffer every slot is either full or empty, so the two counters always sum to the capacity.
  4. A monitor is a language-level construct with mutual exclusion built in plus condition variables; it is not a semaphore with a counter.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) is the statement to reject: condition variables and semaphores are different primitives, and a monitor is a module, not a counter.

Common misconception. Monitors are often introduced right after semaphores, which invites the idea that one is a renamed version of the other. They differ in where the mutual exclusion lives.

OS-U2B-Q24NATeasy

A bounded buffer has capacity 8 and is managed with the counting semaphores full and empty. At some instant full = 3 and no process is blocked. What is the value of empty?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 5

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Every slot of the buffer is either occupied or free, so the two counters partition the capacity.

Step by step.

  1. The capacity is N = 8.
  2. Three slots hold items, so full = 3.
  3. The remaining slots are free: empty = N - full = 8 - 3 = 5.

Answer: 5.

Common misconception. Reporting 3 by symmetry with full, or 8 by treating empty as the capacity.

OS-U2B-Q25NATmedium

Five philosophers sit around a circular table with one fork between each pair of neighbours, and the solution admits at most four philosophers to compete for forks at any instant. What is the maximum number of philosophers that can be eating at the same instant?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 2

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each eater needs two distinct forks, and a table of five has five forks.

Step by step.

  1. Two eaters use four forks and cannot be adjacent, because neighbours would share a fork.
  2. Three eaters would need six forks, which the table does not have.
  3. The bound is therefore ⌊5 / 2⌋ = 2, and it is achievable: philosophers 1 and 3 eat while 2, 4 and 5 wait.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Answering 4 by reading the four-at-a-time rule as a count of eaters rather than of competitors.

OS-U2-Q69MCQeasy

In the bounded-buffer producer–consumer solution with n buffer slots, protected by a mutex and two counting semaphores, what are the correct initial values?

  1. mutex = 1, empty = n, full = 0.
  2. mutex = 1, empty = 0, full = n.
  3. empty = 1, full = n, and no mutex is needed.
  4. mutex = n, empty = 0, full = 0.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. empty counts free slots and full counts filled ones, so they start at n and 0. The mutex protects the buffer itself and starts unlocked, at 1.

Step by step.

  1. Producer: wait(empty), wait(mutex), insert, signal(mutex), signal(full).
  2. Consumer: wait(full), wait(mutex), remove, signal(mutex), signal(empty).
  3. With n free slots at the start, the producer may fill the whole buffer before blocking.
  4. The mutex is needed because the buffer update itself must be atomic, even though the semaphores already order producer against consumer.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) starts with no empty slot and n full ones, i.e. a full buffer with nothing in it.
  • (C) a single slot semaphore cannot express both counts, and without a mutex two producers can corrupt the buffer index.
  • (D) a mutex does not take the value n.

Common misconception. Thinking the counting semaphores make the mutex redundant. They order the two roles; they do not protect the shared buffer from two producers at once.

Takeaway. mutex 1, empty n, full 0 — and always wait on the counting semaphore before the mutex.

OS-U2-Q70MCQeasy

In the dining-philosophers problem with five philosophers and five forks, each philosopher picks up the left fork and then the right one. Allowing at most four philosophers to sit at the table at any time prevents deadlock by removing which of the four necessary conditions?

  1. Mutual exclusion of the forks.
  2. Hold and wait.
  3. No preemption of a fork already picked up.
  4. Circular wait.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The classic deadlock arises because every philosopher holds one fork and waits for the next: a cycle of five waiters around the table. With at most four seated, one fork is always free, so the cycle of five cannot close.

Step by step.

  1. Deadlock requires a cycle of processes each waiting for a resource held by the next.
  2. Each philosopher holds exactly one fork and needs exactly one more, so the wait-for graph is a cycle of the seated philosophers.
  3. With only four seated, at most four forks are held, so at least one fork is free and some seated philosopher can proceed; no cycle can include all four.
  4. Hence the condition removed is circular wait.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) forks are still held exclusively; mutual exclusion remains.
  • (B) each philosopher still holds one fork while waiting for another.
  • (C) a fork is still not taken away from a holder.

Common misconception. Believing the seating limit adds preemption. It only removes the possibility of a full cycle.

Takeaway. Ordering the forks globally or limiting the seated count both break circular wait.

OS-U2-Q71MCQeasy

In the readers–writers solution, the first reader locks wrt and increments readcount, later readers only increment readcount, and the last reader unlocks wrt. Suppose the first reader forgets to lock wrt. What is the consequence?

  1. The readers deadlock among themselves on readcount.
  2. A writer can acquire wrt and modify the data while readers are still reading.
  3. readcount becomes negative.
  4. The last reader will be unable to unlock wrt, so it stays locked for ever.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. wrt is the semaphore shared between the reader group and the writers. Readers as a group must hold it while any reader is inside; the first reader takes it on behalf of the group and the last one returns it.

Step by step.

  1. If the first reader does not take wrt, the semaphore remains free at value 1.
  2. A writer arriving then succeeds in wait(wrt) and enters.
  3. Readers are inside concurrently, because they never gate themselves on wrt after the first.
  4. So a read and a write overlap: mutual exclusion between readers and writers is violated.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) readers only serialise on mutex around readcount, which is untouched.
  • (C) the counter is still incremented and decremented once per reader.
  • (D) the last reader's signal(wrt) would simply be an extra signal, which is harmless for a semaphore but indicates a protocol error.

Common misconception. Thinking each reader must hold wrt. Only the group does, which is exactly why the first and last readers are special.

Takeaway. wrt is a group lock: first in takes it, last out releases it.

OS-U2-Q72MCQmedium

In the bounded-buffer producer–consumer solution, suppose the producer executes wait(mutex) before wait(empty). Which failure can result?

  1. Deadlock: a producer that finds the buffer full blocks while holding the mutex, so no consumer can enter to free a slot.
  2. A lost update on the buffer index, but the system still makes progress.
  3. Only a performance loss, because the producer spins instead of blocking.
  4. Nothing changes, because the two semaphores commute.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A process must never block while holding a lock that the process able to unblock it also needs. The buffer-full condition is resolved by the consumer, and the consumer needs the mutex to work, so holding the mutex while waiting for a free slot deadlocks the pair.

Step by step.

  1. Buffer full: empty = 0, full = n.
  2. Producer executes wait(mutex), taking the mutex.
  3. Producer executes wait(empty) and blocks, because there is no free slot.
  4. The consumer tries wait(full), succeeds, then blocks on wait(mutex), which the blocked producer holds. Neither can proceed: deadlock.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) there is no interleaving of the index updates; the failure is liveness, not consistency.
  • (C) a semaphore blocks; it does not spin.
  • (D) the two operations do not commute: the order decides whether a lock is held while blocking.

Common misconception. Believing the mutex only needs to cover the buffer statement. It does, but it must not be held across a blocking wait.

Takeaway. Always take the counting semaphore first, the mutex last, and release the mutex first.

OS-U2-Q73NATmedium

In the standard dining-philosophers setup there are five philosophers around a circular table and exactly five forks, one between each pair of neighbours; a philosopher needs both adjacent forks to eat. What is the maximum number of philosophers who can be eating at the same time, whatever protocol they follow?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 2

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each eating philosopher consumes two distinct forks, and a fork cannot be shared. With five forks the count is bounded by the number of disjoint pairs of adjacent forks, which is floor(5/2) = 2.

Step by step.

  1. Each of the five forks can serve at most one eating philosopher.
  2. Each eating philosopher needs exactly two forks.
  3. So at most floor(5 / 2) = 2 philosophers can be eating.
  4. Two is achievable: philosophers 1 and 3 use forks (1,2) and (3,4), leaving fork 5 idle.

Answer: 2 philosophers.

Common misconception. Answering 5 by counting one fork per philosopher, or answering 1 by assuming any eating philosopher blocks all neighbours. Only the two immediate neighbours are blocked, so two non-adjacent philosophers can eat together.

Takeaway. Concurrency here is a matching problem: floor(forks / 2).

OS-U2-Q74MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about the readers–writers problem are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. The readers-preference solution can starve a writer that is waiting.
  2. A writer-preference solution can starve readers.
  3. Under readers-preference, a reader that arrives while a writer is already waiting is still allowed to enter.
  4. Guarding the whole database with a single mutex gives readers-preference behaviour.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The two classical variants trade one form of starvation for the other. Readers-preference lets any reader in whenever no writer is inside, so a stream of readers can hold the lock for ever. Writer-preference blocks new readers as soon as a writer is waiting, so a stream of writers can starve readers.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. The writer waits on wrt, which the readers as a group hold continuously while any reader is inside.
  2. (B) True. With writer-preference a waiting writer blocks new readers, and successive writers can keep the lock busy.
  3. (C) True. In the readers-preference code a new reader only tests wrt, which the waiting writer has not yet acquired.
  4. (D) False. A single mutex serialises everyone, so readers do not proceed concurrently at all; that is not readers-preference.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (D) removes concurrency between readers, which is the whole point of distinguishing readers from writers.

Common misconception. Assuming one of the two variants is “correct”. Both are correct solutions to different requirements; starvation-freedom needs a fair policy such as FIFO ordering of arrivals.

Takeaway. Preference decides who starves. Fairness needs an arrival order, not a preference.

OS-U2-Q75MSQhard

Which of the following statements about the classical synchronisation problems are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Allowing at most four philosophers to sit at the table removes the possibility of a circular wait.
  2. With one binary semaphore per fork and no other mechanism, deadlock is possible in the dining-philosophers problem.
  3. In the producer–consumer problem with n slots, replacing the two counting semaphores by a single mutex still preserves correctness.
  4. In the readers–writers solution, a semaphore wrt initialised to 1 ensures that at most one writer is inside at a time.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each classical problem isolates one failure mode: circular wait for the philosophers, a full or empty buffer for the producer and consumer, and writer exclusion for the readers and writers.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. With four seated, at most four forks are held, so at least one is free and no cycle of all five can form.
  2. (B) True. If all five pick up their left fork at once, each waits for the right one held by a neighbour: a cycle.
  3. (C) False. A single mutex gives exclusion but no way to block a producer on a full buffer or a consumer on an empty one; busy-waiting inside the mutex deadlocks, and blocking outside it loses the count.
  4. (D) True. Writers hold wrt for the whole write, so two writers cannot overlap.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (C) confuses mutual exclusion with condition synchronisation. The counting semaphores carry state about the buffer that a mutex does not represent.

Common misconception. Believing one mutex is a universal fix. A mutex answers “may I touch this?”; a counting semaphore answers “is there room, or an item?”.

Takeaway. Exclusion and condition synchronisation are different jobs and need different primitives.

OS-U2-Q95MCQeasy

In the readers–writers solution, the shared variable readcount records how many readers are currently reading, and a semaphore mutex guards it. What is mutex protecting?

  1. The file itself, so that only one reader reads at a time.
  2. The writer's access to the file.
  3. The queue of waiting writers.
  4. The readcount variable, so that two readers cannot update it at the same time.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. There are two different shared objects in this problem and they are guarded by two different semaphores. wrt is the file (shared between readers as a group and writers individually); mutex is the counter.

Step by step.

  1. A reader executes P(mutex), increments readcount, and releases mutex.
  2. If it was the first reader it also executes P(wrt) before releasing mutex, so that no writer is active while readers read.
  3. The last reader to leave decrements readcount and executes V(wrt).
  4. So mutex is held only while the counter is being read and changed, and readers themselves run concurrently.

Answer: Option (D) — mutex guards readcount.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Readers are meant to read concurrently; wrt, not mutex, excludes writers.
  • (B) A writer's exclusive access is enforced by wrt.
  • (C) There is no explicit queue semaphore; the waiting writers simply block on wrt.

Common misconception. Assuming one semaphore per problem. The readers–writers solution needs two, and knowing which guards which is the whole of the analysis.

Takeaway. Name the shared object each semaphore protects before reasoning about the code. A counter and a file are different objects with different exclusion requirements.

OS-U2-Q96NATeasy

Six philosophers sit around a circular table with six forks, one between each pair of neighbours, and each needs both adjacent forks to eat. Under the asymmetric solution, in which one designated philosopher picks up the right fork first while every other philosopher picks up the left fork first, what is the maximum number of philosophers that can be eating at the same time?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 3

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Two bounds apply: a fork cannot be held by two philosophers, and each eating philosopher needs two distinct forks. The answer is the smaller of what the forks allow and what the asymmetric rule actually permits.

Step by step.

  1. There are 6 forks and each eating philosopher holds 2 of them, so at most 6 / 2 = 3 can eat at once.
  2. That bound is reachable: philosophers 0, 2 and 4 hold the fork pairs {5, 0}, {1, 2} and {3, 4} respectively, which are disjoint.
  3. The asymmetric rule does not lower it, because the three philosophers chosen above are not neighbours, so no two of them contend for the same fork.
  4. Hence the maximum is 3.

Answer: 3

Common misconception. Answering 2 because that is the answer for five philosophers. With an even number of seats the table splits into two independent sets and half the philosophers can eat; with an odd number one fork is always left over.

Takeaway. For a ring of n philosophers the naive maximum is ⌊n/2⌋. The asymmetric rule changes which philosophers may proceed, not this ceiling.

OS-U2-Q97MCQeasy

Which one of the following describes the access rule of the readers–writers problem?

  1. Any number of readers may read at the same time, but a writer needs exclusive access to the file.
  2. At most one reader and one writer may be active at the same time.
  3. Readers must wait for one another, and a writer may run alongside them.
  4. A writer may share the file with readers provided it only appends.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The problem is defined by which pairs of operations may overlap. Two readers never change the file, so they may overlap freely; a writer changes it, so nothing else may run with it.

Step by step.

  1. Reader–reader: allowed, any number at once.
  2. Reader–writer: forbidden.
  3. Writer–writer: forbidden.
  4. Writer–anything: forbidden, which is exactly what the semaphore wrt enforces.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) allows one reader with one writer, which the problem forbids.
  • (C) is the reverse of the rule: readers are the ones allowed to overlap.
  • (D) an append still modifies the file, so a writer needs exclusivity regardless of where it writes.

Common misconception. Thinking that any two operations that do not write the same bytes may overlap. The problem's rule is stated on the file as a whole, not on the region being touched.

Takeaway. Readers–writers is the standard model for a shared object read by many and written by few: concurrent readers, exclusive writer.

OS-U2-Q98MSQmedium

A bounded buffer of capacity N is managed with the counting semaphores full and empty and a mutex. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. full counts the items in the buffer and empty counts the free slots, so full + empty = N at every instant.
  2. The producer must execute P(empty) before P(mutex); reversing the two can deadlock.
  3. When N = 1 the mutex is unnecessary, because the counting semaphores already serialise the producer and the consumer.
  4. A consumer that executes V(mutex) before removing the item lets another consumer remove the same item.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The two counting semaphores describe the state of the buffer; the mutex protects the buffer's indices while they are being changed. Keeping those roles separate is what makes the solution correct.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Every item inserted decrements empty and increments full, and every item removed does the reverse, so the two always sum to N.
  2. (B) True. If the producer takes the mutex first and then blocks on empty, the consumer cannot take the mutex to free a slot, so both wait for ever. The counting semaphore must be acquired first.
  3. (C) True. With one slot, at most one producer can hold empty and at most one consumer can hold full, so the insertion and the removal can never overlap.
  4. (D) False. Releasing the mutex before removing the item lets a second consumer enter while the item is still there, so it removes the same item; the mutex must be held for the whole of the removal.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (D) is the false statement: the mutex must cover the read of the buffer as well as the change of the index.

Common misconception. Believing the mutex can be dropped early to shorten the critical section. It must cover every access to the shared structure, not only the index update.

Takeaway. Acquire the counting semaphore before the mutex, and hold the mutex across the whole buffer operation. Reverse either rule and the solution breaks.

OS-U2-Q99MCQhard

In a bounded-buffer solution the producer executes P(empty); P(mutex); and the consumer executes P(full); P(mutex);, with V(mutex) executed before V(full) and before V(empty) respectively. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. The solution deadlocks as soon as the buffer becomes full.
  2. The solution deadlocks whenever two producers run at the same time.
  3. The solution is deadlock-free: the mutex is always acquired last and released first, so no cycle of waiting can form.
  4. The mutex is unnecessary because the counting semaphores already exclude concurrent access to the buffer.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Deadlock needs a cycle of processes each holding one resource and waiting for another. Show that no such cycle can form, given the order in which the resources are acquired.

Step by step.

  1. A process holds at most two semaphores: a counting semaphore, then the mutex.
  2. It never holds the mutex and then waits for a counting semaphore, because the counting semaphore is always acquired first.
  3. So the only waiting edge is “holds a counting semaphore, wants the mutex”, and the mutex is held only by a process that already has a counting semaphore — which will release it.
  4. With all resources acquired in one global order and released in the reverse order, no cycle can form, so the solution cannot deadlock. The buffer may fill up, but a blocked producer is simply waiting for a consumer, which is not deadlock.

Answer: Option (C) — the solution is deadlock-free.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) A full buffer blocks producers by design; consumers still run, so progress continues.
  • (B) Producers serialise on the mutex, which is exactly the intended behaviour.
  • (D) Two producers or two consumers do touch the same index, so the mutex is needed.

Common misconception. Confusing blocking with deadlock. A producer waiting on empty is waiting for work that the consumer will do; a deadlock is a wait that nothing can ever satisfy.

Takeaway. Deadlock freedom is an ordering argument: acquire all resources in one global order, release them in the reverse order, and no cycle of waiting can exist.

OS-U2-Q100MSQmedium

In the dining-philosophers solution that keeps a state array and one semaphore per philosopher, a hungry philosopher eats only when neither neighbour is eating. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A philosopher takes both forks or neither, so the solution cannot deadlock.
  2. The test of the neighbours' states and the change of the philosopher's own state are performed while holding a mutex, so the two steps are atomic.
  3. The solution deadlocks if all five philosophers become hungry at the same instant.
  4. A philosopher who is hungry is not guaranteed to eat before a neighbour who becomes hungry later, so starvation is not ruled out.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The state-array solution removes deadlock by never letting a philosopher hold one fork while waiting for the other; it does not add any ordering among hungry philosophers, so it does not remove starvation.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Forks are not picked up one at a time. A philosopher whose neighbours are idle is signalled and takes both; otherwise it takes neither and blocks on its own semaphore. There is no hold-and-wait, so no circular wait.
  2. (B) True. Without the mutex, two neighbours could each test the other, both see EATING as false, and both start eating — so the test and the state change must be one atomic step.
  3. (C) False. If all five become hungry, each finds at least one neighbour hungry, so none is signalled; every philosopher waits on its own semaphore and the system simply waits until someone eats. No one holds a fork, so nothing is deadlocked — the first philosopher to be released by a neighbour eating and finishing proceeds.
  4. (D) True. The per-philosopher semaphores carry no priority and no arrival order, so a philosopher whose two neighbours keep alternating can be passed over repeatedly.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) is the false statement: with no forks held while waiting, the “everyone hungry at once” situation cannot produce a circular wait. It is the naive left-then-right protocol that deadlocks in that situation.

Common misconception. Assuming that removing deadlock also removes starvation. They are different failures: deadlock is a cycle that nothing can break, starvation is a wait that is always outbid.

Takeaway. Deadlock freedom needs the hold-and-wait or circular-wait condition removed; starvation freedom needs a fairness rule on top, such as FIFO ordering of the waiting semaphores.

Unit 3 — Deadlocks · 100 solved questions (2026-10-27)
four-conditions-resource-allocation-graph 25
OS-U3-Q01MCQeasy

Which one of the following is NOT one of the four necessary conditions for a deadlock to occur?

  1. Mutual exclusion
  2. Hold and wait
  3. Preemption of resources
  4. Circular wait
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Each is necessary, and deadlock requires all four to hold at the same time.

Step by step.

  1. Mutual exclusion: at least one resource must be held in a non-shareable mode, so a second requester must wait.
  2. Hold and wait: a process must be holding at least one resource while it waits for another.
  3. No preemption: a resource can be released only voluntarily, by the process that holds it.
  4. Circular wait: there is a closed chain of processes in which each waits for a resource held by the next.
  5. Option (C) states the negation of the third condition. Deadlock needs preemption to be impossible, so “preemption of resources” is not a condition — it is the escape route.

Answer: Option (C) — preemption of resources is the opposite of the required condition, which is no preemption.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Mutual exclusion is the first Coffman condition.
  • (B) Hold and wait is the second.
  • (D) Circular wait is the fourth.

Common misconception. Many candidates tick “preemption” because the word does appear in the standard list. The list says no preemption: if the system could preempt a resource from a waiting process, the wait could never be permanent.

Takeaway. All four conditions must hold simultaneously. Denying any one of them makes deadlock impossible — that is exactly what deadlock prevention does.

OS-U3-Q02MCQeasy

A resource allocation graph contains exactly one instance of every resource type. Which of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. A cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock.
  2. A cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock.
  3. A cycle is sufficient but not necessary for deadlock.
  4. A cycle is neither necessary nor sufficient for deadlock.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. When every resource type has a single instance, each resource node has at most one outgoing edge, so the graph collapses into a wait-for graph on processes. In that graph deadlock and cycle are the same thing.

Step by step.

  1. Merge each resource node with its holder: draw Pᵢ → Pⱼ exactly when Pᵢ is waiting for a resource held by Pⱼ.
  2. Deadlock ⇒ cycle. If a set of processes is deadlocked, each member waits for a resource held by another member; following the waits around the set closes a cycle.
  3. Cycle ⇒ deadlock. Take a cycle P₁ → P₂ → … → Pₖ → P₁. Each Pᵢ waits for the single instance held by its successor, and that successor cannot release it, because it is itself waiting. No member can ever proceed.
  4. Hence with single instances the cycle test is a complete decision procedure.

Answer: Option (B) — with one instance per resource type, a cycle is necessary and sufficient for deadlock.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the correct statement only when a resource type may have several instances.
  • (C) reverses the quantifiers: a deadlock always contains a cycle, so a cycle cannot be merely sufficient.
  • (D) denies a standard theorem.

Common misconception. Candidates learn “cycle is necessary, not sufficient” as a slogan and apply it everywhere. That slogan belongs to the multi-instance case; with single instances the cycle test decides.

Takeaway. Single instance → wait-for graph → cycle test. Multiple instances → graph reduction.

OS-U3-Q06MCQmedium

A system has two resource types: R₁ with 2 instances and R₂ with 1 instance. Three processes hold and request them as follows. Allocated : R₁ → P1 , R₁ → P2 , R₂ → P3 Requested : P1 → R₂ , P2 → R₂ , P3 → R₁ Which of the following statements about the current state is TRUE?

  1. The system is deadlocked.
  2. The system is not deadlocked, because R₁ has two instances in total.
  3. The system is not deadlocked, because each process holds at most one resource.
  4. The system is not deadlocked, because a cycle in a graph with multiple instances never implies deadlock.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With more than one instance per resource type a cycle is only a necessary condition, so the verdict comes from graph reduction: repeatedly let a process whose outstanding request can be met finish, and add all of its resources back to the pool.

Step by step.

  1. Compute what is free. R₁: 2 − 2 = 0 available. R₂: 1 − 1 = 0 available.
  2. P1 and P2 both request R₂, whose only instance is held by P3. P3 requests R₁, whose two instances are held by P1 and P2.
  3. No process's request can be satisfied from the available pool, so no process can finish and no edge can be removed. Reduction stalls immediately.
  4. The processes left behind wait only on one another, so they are deadlocked. The cycle is P1 → R₂ → P3 → R₁ → P1.

Answer: Option (A) — the graph cannot be reduced, so the system is deadlocked.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Two instances in total is irrelevant once both are already allocated; the free count is zero.
  • (C) Holding one resource each is exactly the arrangement that closes the cycle.
  • (D) States the correct general rule but misapplies it: here reduction confirms the deadlock rather than dissolving it.

Common misconception. Candidates stop at “multiple instances, so a cycle proves nothing” and never run the reduction. The rule is a warning to check further, not a licence to answer “no deadlock”.

Takeaway. Always compute the free counts first, then reduce. If nothing can finish, the remaining processes are deadlocked regardless of how many instances exist.

OS-U3-Q15MCQeasy

Which of the following statements about denying the mutual-exclusion condition is TRUE?

  1. It can be denied for every resource by declaring all resources shareable.
  2. It cannot be denied for intrinsically non-shareable resources such as a printer or a tape drive, so it is rarely usable as a general prevention technique.
  3. Denying mutual exclusion also denies circular wait.
  4. It is the only condition that cannot be denied in any system.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A resource is non-shareable when concurrent use would corrupt it. For such resources mutual exclusion must hold, so denying it is not a general prevention strategy.

Step by step.

  1. Mutual exclusion is required whenever simultaneous access is unsafe — a printer, a tape drive, a write lock on a file.
  2. For these resources the condition cannot be denied at all, so prevention must attack hold-and-wait or circular wait instead.
  3. The classic partial workaround is spooling: several processes write to a disk queue and one spooler process owns the printer. The printer is then shared only in the sense that the queue is.
  4. Spooling works only for resources whose output can be buffered; it does not generalise to a tape drive or a shared memory region.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Declaring a printer shareable does not make it shareable.
  • (C) The two conditions are independent; denying one says nothing about the other.
  • (D) Mutual exclusion is not the only condition that resists denial, and the phrasing of the option is too absolute.

Common misconception. Assuming every condition is equally deniable. In practice prevention targets hold-and-wait and circular wait, because mutual exclusion usually cannot be removed.

Takeaway. Spooling is the one well-known attack on mutual exclusion, and it applies only to bufferable resources.

OS-U3-Q16MSQeasy

Which of the following are among the four necessary conditions for deadlock? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Mutual exclusion
  2. Hold and wait
  3. No preemption
  4. Priority inversion
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. They must hold simultaneously for deadlock to be possible.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Mutual exclusion — a resource is held in a non-shareable mode. Condition.
  2. (B) Hold and wait — a process holds one resource while waiting for another. Condition.
  3. (C) No preemption — a resource is released only voluntarily. Condition.
  4. (D) Priority inversion — a scheduling anomaly in which a low-priority task holding a lock blocks a high-priority one. It is a real-time scheduling problem, not a deadlock condition. Not a condition.
  5. The fourth Coffman condition, circular wait, is absent from the list, so three of the four appear here.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Priority inversion is often grouped with deadlock because both involve blocking. Inversion concerns who gets the CPU while a lock is held; deadlock concerns a closed wait set.

Takeaway. Four conditions, all necessary, all simultaneously required: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.

OS-U3-Q20MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about a resource allocation graph are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A cycle is a necessary condition for deadlock, whatever the number of instances per resource type.
  2. If every resource type has exactly one instance, a cycle implies deadlock.
  3. If the graph contains no cycle, the system is deadlock-free.
  4. A cycle in a graph in which some resource type has several instances always implies deadlock.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A cycle is always necessary; it is sufficient only when every resource type has a single instance.

Step by step.

  1. (A) In a deadlock every blocked process waits for a resource held by another blocked process; following those waits around the set closes a cycle. TRUE
  2. (B) With single instances no process outside the cycle can release the needed resource, so the cycle can never be broken. TRUE
  3. (C) This is the contrapositive of (A): no cycle ⇒ no deadlock. TRUE
  4. (D) With several instances a process outside the cycle may hold a spare instance and release it, dissolving the cycle; only graph reduction decides. FALSE

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. The pair (B) and (D) is where marks are lost. The correct summary is one sentence: necessary always, sufficient only for single instances.

Takeaway. Cycle ⇒ check further, never a verdict — unless every resource has exactly one instance.

OS-U3B-Q01MCQeasy

A resource allocation graph may contain more than one instance of a resource type. The graph contains a directed cycle. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. A cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock in such a graph.
  2. A cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock in such a graph.
  3. A cycle is sufficient but not necessary for deadlock in such a graph.
  4. A cycle has no bearing on deadlock once a resource type has several instances.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A cycle in the resource allocation graph is always a necessary condition for deadlock. It becomes a sufficient condition only when every resource type has exactly one instance.

Step by step.

  1. Every deadlock corresponds to a closed chain of waiting, which appears as a cycle. So a cycle is necessary.
  2. With multiple instances, several processes may hold different instances of the same resource type, and a cycle can be formed while another free instance still exists.
  3. That free instance can satisfy one of the requests, breaking the apparent chain, so no process need wait forever.
  4. Hence a cycle is necessary but not sufficient; the exact test in that case is graph reduction, not cycle detection.

Answer: Option (B) — a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.

Common misconception. Carrying over the single-instance rule. 'Cycle means deadlock' is valid only when each resource type has one instance; with several instances a cycle can be harmless.

OS-U3B-Q02MCQeasy

In a resource allocation graph, an assignment edge is directed:

  1. from a process to a resource type, showing what the process has asked for.
  2. from a resource instance to the process that holds it.
  3. from one process to another process.
  4. from one resource type to another resource type.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The graph has two edge kinds: a request edge Pᵢ → Rⱼ and an assignment edge Rⱼ → Pᵢ. The direction always runs from the holder of the authority to the receiver.

Step by step.

  1. A request edge leaves the requesting process and points at the resource type it wants: Pᵢ → Rⱼ.
  2. An assignment edge leaves the resource instance and points at the process holding it: Rⱼ → Pᵢ.
  3. So an assignment edge runs resource → process. Option B.
  4. Options C and D describe edges that do not exist in a resource allocation graph; process-to-process edges appear only in the derived wait-for graph.

Answer: Option (B) — from the resource instance to the process holding it.

Common misconception. Reversing the two edge kinds. Request goes process → resource; assignment goes resource → process. Swapping them inverts every cycle you then read off the graph.

OS-U3B-Q03MCQeasy

A resource allocation graph has exactly one instance of every resource type and contains the cycle `P₁ → R₁ → P₂ → R₂ → P₁`. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. Both `P₁` and `P₂` are deadlocked.
  2. Neither process is deadlocked; a cycle of even length is harmless.
  3. Only `P₁` is deadlocked, because it started the cycle.
  4. Nothing can be concluded without the arrival times of the two processes.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With a single instance per resource type, a cycle in the resource allocation graph is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock, and every process on the cycle is deadlocked.

Step by step.

  1. P₁ → R₁ is a request edge: P₁ is waiting for R₁.
  2. R₁ → P₂ is an assignment edge: the only instance of R₁ is held by P₂.
  3. P₂ → R₂ means P₂ is waiting for R₂, and R₂ → P₁ means the only instance of R₂ is held by P₁.
  4. P₁ waits for a resource held by P₂, and P₂ waits for a resource held by P₁. Neither can proceed, and neither will release. Both are deadlocked.
  5. The length or parity of the cycle is irrelevant; with single instances any cycle is a deadlock.

Answer: Option (A) — both processes are deadlocked.

Common misconception. Reading the cycle in the wrong direction, or believing the process that 'started' the chain is the only victim. In a closed chain every member waits on the next, so every member is deadlocked.

OS-U3B-Q04MCQmedium

Resource type `R₁` has two instances and `R₂` has one. The graph contains `P₁ → R₂`, `R₂ → P₂`, `P₂ → R₁` and `R₁ → P₁`. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. There is a deadlock, because the graph contains a cycle.
  2. There is no deadlock: a cycle exists, but a free instance of `R₁` can still satisfy `P₂`.
  3. There is no deadlock, because `R₂` is not part of any cycle.
  4. The state cannot be decided without knowing the CPU burst times of `P₁` and `P₂`.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With multiple instances a cycle is only necessary, not sufficient. You must check whether any request on the cycle can be met from the currently free instances.

Step by step.

  1. R₁ has 2 instances and only one is assigned (R₁ → P₁), so one instance of R₁ is free.
  2. R₂ has 1 instance and it is held by P₂.
  3. The cycle is P₁ → R₂ → P₂ → R₁ → P₁: P₁ waits for R₂, P₂ waits for R₁.
  4. P₂'s request is for R₁, and a free instance of R₁ exists, so P₂ can be granted it. P₂ then finishes and releases R₂, which unblocks P₁.
  5. The cycle is therefore broken by an available instance, and there is no deadlock.

Answer: Option (B) — a cycle exists but the system is not deadlocked.

Common misconception. Applying the single-instance rule to a multi-instance graph. Always count the free instances before concluding from a cycle.

OS-U3B-Q05MSQhard

Which of the following statements about resource allocation graphs are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. In a graph with a single instance of every resource type, a knot implies deadlock.
  2. If the graph contains no cycle at all, no process is deadlocked.
  3. In a graph where some resource types have several instances, the presence of a cycle guarantees that the system is deadlocked.
  4. Every deadlocked set of processes corresponds to at least one cycle in the graph.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B), (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Cycle and deadlock are linked by a one-way implication that becomes two-way only under the single-instance restriction.

Step by step.

  1. Option A: a knot is a strongly connected subgraph with no edges leaving it. With single instances nothing outside can break it, so every process in the knot is deadlocked. True.
  2. Option B: deadlock implies a closed chain of waiting, which is a cycle. Contrapositively, no cycle means no deadlock. True.
  3. Option C: with multiple instances a cycle can coexist with a free instance that satisfies one of the requests, as in the R₁ with two instances case. The cycle is then not a deadlock. False.
  4. Option D: every deadlocked set has each member waiting for a resource held by another member, and those waits form a closed chain — a cycle. True.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are true. Option (C) is false.

Common misconception. Treating 'cycle' and 'deadlock' as interchangeable. The implication deadlock ⇒ cycle always holds; cycle ⇒ deadlock holds only for single-instance resources.

OS-U3B-Q06NATmedium

Four processes share three resource types, each with exactly one instance. `R₁` is held by `P₁`, `R₂` by `P₂` and `R₃` by `P₃`. The pending requests are `P₁ → R₂`, `P₂ → R₃`, `P₃ → R₁` and `P₄ → R₁`. How many processes are deadlocked, in the sense that each is waiting for a resource held by another member of the deadlocked set?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 3

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A process is deadlocked only if it belongs to a closed chain of waits. A process that merely waits on a deadlocked process is blocked, not deadlocked.

Step by step.

  1. Build the wait-for graph: P₁ waits for R₂ held by P₂, so P₁ → P₂.
  2. P₂ waits for R₃ held by P₃, so P₂ → P₃. P₃ waits for R₁ held by P₁, so P₃ → P₁.
  3. These three edges form the cycle P₁ → P₂ → P₃ → P₁. All three processes are in a closed wait set, so all three are deadlocked.
  4. P₄ waits for R₁, held by P₁, so P₄ → P₁. P₄ lies on no cycle: it is not a member of the deadlocked set.
  5. Count of processes inside the deadlock: 3.

Answer: 3

Common misconception. Counting P₄ as well, giving 4. P₄ is blocked indefinitely but is not part of the closed set, so under the standard definition it is not deadlocked.

OS-U3B-Q07NAThard

Three resource types have `R₁` with 1 instance, `R₂` with 2 instances and `R₃` with 1 instance. The single instance of `R₁` is held by `P₁`; both instances of `R₂` are held, one by `P₂` and one by `P₃`; the single instance of `R₃` is held by `P₄`. The pending requests are `P₁ → R₂`, `P₂ → R₃`, `P₃ → R₁` and `P₄ → R₂`. How many processes are deadlocked?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 4

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. When no instance of any requested resource type is free, every requester is blocked; you must then find the closed chains among the waiters to decide which of them are deadlocked.

Step by step.

  1. Free instances: R₁ = 1 − 1 = 0, R₂ = 2 − 2 = 0, R₃ = 1 − 1 = 0. Nothing is available.
  2. Every pending request is therefore blocked: P₁ needs R₂, P₂ needs R₃, P₃ needs R₁, P₄ needs R₂.
  3. Trace the waits. P₁ waits for R₂, held by P₂ or P₃. P₃ waits for R₁, held by P₁. So P₁ and P₃ wait on each other — a closed chain.
  4. P₂ waits for R₃, held by P₄; P₄ waits for R₂, held by P₂ or P₃. So P₂ and P₄ wait on each other — a second closed chain.
  5. All four processes lie on a closed chain, and with zero free instances nothing can break either chain. All four are deadlocked.

Answer: 4

Common misconception. Assuming a multi-instance graph with no free instances must have every waiter deadlocked — that happens to be true here, but it must be justified by locating the cycles. Conversely, do not assume a cycle is needed in every row of the wait set; it is the closed chain, not the count of waiters, that decides.

OS-U3-Q51MCQeasy

A system has one resource type R₁ with 2 instances and another resource type R₂ with 1 instance. Which one of the following CANNOT appear in a valid resource allocation graph of this system?

  1. Two assignment edges, R₁ → P₁ and R₁ → P₂
  2. Two assignment edges, R₂ → P₁ and R₂ → P₂
  3. A request edge P₁ → R₁ while P₁ already holds an instance of R₁
  4. Two request edges, P₁ → R₁ and P₃ → R₁
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An assignment edge R → P records that one instance of R is held by P. A resource type drawn with k dots can therefore carry at most k assignment edges. Request edges carry no such limit: any number of processes may queue for the same type, because a request is only a claim on a future free instance.

Step by step.

  1. R₁ has 2 instances, so 2 assignment edges are possible — (A) is valid.
  2. R₂ has 1 instance, so at most one process can hold it. Two assignment edges out of R₂ would hand out two units of a one-unit resource — (B) is impossible.
  3. (C) is valid and common: a process holds one unit and asks for another unit of the same type. That is how multi-unit contention arises.
  4. (D) is valid: request edges are unlimited, and two processes competing for R₁ is exactly the state the graph is meant to show.

Answer: Option (B) — R₂ has one instance, so it cannot be assigned to two processes.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) uses both instances of R₁, which is allowed.
  • (C) is the hold-and-request pattern, not an error.
  • (D) request edges are not bounded by the instance count.

Common misconception. Students bound all edges touching a resource type by its instance count. Only assignment edges consume instances; request edges consume nothing yet.

Takeaway. Count dots against outgoing assignment edges. If the assignment edges exceed the dots, the graph is not a picture of any reachable state.

OS-U3-Q52MCQmedium

R₁ has 2 instances and R₂ has 2 instances. P₁ holds one instance of R₁ and requests one instance of R₂; P₂ holds one instance of R₂ and requests one instance of R₁. The graph therefore contains the cycle P₁ → R₂ → P₂ → R₁ → P₁. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. The system is deadlocked, because a cycle in a resource allocation graph always means a deadlock.
  2. The system is not deadlocked: one instance of each type is still free, so a request can be granted and the cycle breaks.
  3. The system is deadlocked only if P₁ and P₂ issue their requests at the same instant.
  4. The system is not deadlocked only because R₁ and R₂ are different resource types.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With several instances per resource type a cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock. The cycle only records who holds and who asks; whether anyone is actually stuck depends on the free instances.

Step by step.

  1. Free instances of R₁ = 2 − 1 = 1.
  2. Free instances of R₂ = 2 − 1 = 1.
  3. P₁'s request for one R₂ can be met immediately, so P₁ is not blocked.
  4. P₁ finishes and releases both its units, so R₁ now has 2 free instances and P₂'s request succeeds.

Answer: Option (B) — a free instance on each side of the cycle means no process on it is blocked.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) treats a necessary condition as a sufficient one — true only when every type has a single instance.
  • (C) deadlock is a property of a state, not of a timing accident. Since both requests are grantable, no interleaving of the two requests produces a deadlock.
  • (D) the identity of the types is irrelevant; only the free instances matter.

Common misconception. Spotting the cycle and stopping. Before calling it a deadlock, check whether every instance on the cycle is held by a process on the cycle.

Takeaway. Cycle = a warning. Deadlock = a cycle with no free instance able to break it.

OS-U3-Q53MCQmedium

In a wait-for graph a knot is a set S of vertices such that every vertex reachable from a vertex of S also lies in S, and no edge leaves S. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. A knot is exactly the same thing as a cycle.
  2. The system is deadlocked if and only if its wait-for graph contains a knot.
  3. A knot is a single vertex whose out-degree is zero.
  4. A knot can exist only when exactly one process is deadlocked.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A knot is a set of processes closed under reachability with no edge leaving it. Every process in a knot waits only on processes inside the knot, so nothing outside can ever release it. For single-instance resources the standard result is: a deadlock exists if and only if the wait-for graph contains a knot.

Step by step.

  1. A simple cycle is not automatically a knot. Take P₁ → P₂ → P₁ together with an edge P₂ → P₃ where P₃ is not blocked: the set {P₁, P₂} is a cycle but an edge leaves it, so it is not a knot.
  2. Here P₃ will run and release what P₂ needs, so the cycle dissolves. Nothing is deadlocked.
  3. Now close the set: if every edge from the set stays inside it, no process in it can ever be released, which is exactly a deadlock.
  4. So the existence of a knot characterises deadlock, while a bare cycle does not.

Answer: Option (B) — a knot is necessary and sufficient for deadlock in a wait-for graph.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) a cycle with an outgoing edge is not a knot.
  • (C) out-degree zero means the process is waiting for nothing — it is runnable, the opposite of a knot.
  • (D) a knot may contain any number of processes.

Common misconception. Using "cycle" and "knot" interchangeably. The distinction is the whole point: a knot is a cycle that nothing can escape.

Takeaway. Reachability closure is the test. If a blocked set can reach a runnable process, it is not a knot and not a deadlock.

OS-U3-Q54MCQhard

Every resource type in a system has several instances. The graph contains the cycle P₁ → R₁ → P₂ → R₂ → P₁, and every instance of R₁ and of R₂ is held by P₁ or by P₂. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. Nothing can be concluded, because a cycle never implies a deadlock once resource types have several instances.
  2. The system is deadlocked, because each process on the cycle waits for a type whose every instance is held by a process on the cycle.
  3. The system is deadlocked only if P₁ and P₂ are the only two processes in the system.
  4. The system cannot be deadlocked, because a deadlock needs at least three processes.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With multiple instances the useful sufficient condition is: a cycle in which every resource type on the cycle has all of its instances held by processes on the cycle. Then no process on the cycle can ever be satisfied from outside, because there is nothing outside to release.

Step by step.

  1. P₁ requests R₁. Every instance of R₁ is held by P₁ or P₂, and P₁ is the requester, so it holds none — all instances are with P₂.
  2. P₂ requests R₂, and by the same argument every instance is with P₁.
  3. Neither can proceed until the other releases, and neither will release before it is satisfied.
  4. No process outside the cycle holds an instance of either type, so no outside event can break the cycle.

Answer: Option (B) — a cycle whose every instance is held inside the cycle is a deadlock.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) over-corrects: a cycle is not sufficient in general, but this extra condition makes it sufficient.
  • (C) processes outside the cycle hold nothing on it, so their existence changes nothing.
  • (D) two processes deadlocking on two resources is the smallest possible deadlock.

Common misconception. Having learned "a cycle does not always mean a deadlock", students reject every cycle. The right test is where the instances on the cycle are held.

Takeaway. Two questions, in order: is there a cycle? Are all instances on it held inside it? Yes to both — deadlock.

OS-U3-Q65MCQeasy

A resource allocation graph in which some resource types have several instances contains no cycle. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. The system may still be deadlocked.
  2. The system cannot be deadlocked.
  3. Exactly one process must be blocked.
  4. Nothing can be concluded, because a cycle is irrelevant when instances are multiple.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A cycle is a necessary condition for deadlock in every resource allocation graph, whatever the instance counts. A graph with no cycle therefore describes a state that is not deadlocked.

Step by step.

  1. In a deadlock every process on the deadlock is blocked, waiting for a resource held by another member.
  2. Following those wait relations must return to the starting process, which traces a cycle.
  3. So a deadlock always leaves a cycle behind; no cycle means no deadlock.
  4. The converse fails only in the other direction: with multiple instances a cycle may exist without a deadlock.

Answer: Option (B) — no cycle means no deadlock.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) contradicts the necessity of a cycle.
  • (C) nothing follows about how many processes are blocked; several may be waiting with no deadlock.
  • (D) the necessity direction is unaffected by instance counts.

Common misconception. Having learned "a cycle is not sufficient with multiple instances", students drop the necessity too. Necessity survives; only sufficiency is lost.

Takeaway. No cycle → definitely safe. Cycle → need the free-instance or reduction check before concluding anything.

OS-U3-Q66MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about resource allocation graphs are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. When every resource type has exactly one instance, a cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock.
  2. When a resource type has several instances, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock.
  3. A graph with no cycle may still describe a deadlocked system.
  4. If the graph can be reduced completely, by repeatedly removing a process whose requests can all be met, then no process is deadlocked.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Three facts govern the graph. A cycle is always necessary for deadlock. With single instances it is also sufficient. With several instances it is not, and there the reduction test is decisive.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: with one instance per type, a cycle means each process on it waits for something held by the next, so none can proceed.
  2. (B) True: a free instance somewhere on the cycle may let a member finish and break the cycle.
  3. (C) False: since a cycle is necessary, no cycle means no deadlock.
  4. (D) True: complete reducibility means every process can, in some order, be satisfied and finish, which is exactly the absence of deadlock.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (C) reverses the necessity of a cycle — the classic misreading of the multi-instance case.

Common misconception. Learning that "cycles do not always mean deadlock" and concluding that cycles are unrelated to deadlock. Only sufficiency is lost.

Takeaway. Necessity always; sufficiency only for single instances; reduction for everything else.

OS-U3-Q71NATeasy

R₁ has 4 instances, R₂ has 3 and R₃ has 2. P₁ holds 2 instances of R₁ and 1 of R₂; P₂ holds 1 instance of R₁ and 1 of R₃. No other instance is allocated. How many instances in the system are currently unallocated?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 4

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Instances are conserved: the unallocated count is the total number of instances minus the number of assignment edges in the graph. Each assignment edge consumes exactly one instance.

Step by step.

  1. Total instances = 4 + 3 + 2 = 9.
  2. Allocated = 2 + 1 (from P₁) + 1 + 1 (from P₂) = 5.
  3. Unallocated = 9 − 5 = 4.

Answer: 4 instances (any integer value 4 is accepted).

Common misconception. Counting resource types instead of instances. Three types hold nine instances; the answer is not 3 − 2.

Takeaway. The available vector is simply total minus the column sums of the allocation matrix. Compute it that way, never by eye.

OS-U3C-Q01MCQeasy

The four necessary conditions for deadlock are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption and circular wait. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. Each of the four conditions is, by itself, sufficient for a deadlock to occur.
  2. All four must hold at the same time before a deadlock is even possible, and their joint holding still does not guarantee that a deadlock exists.
  3. At least one of the four conditions can never be denied, so deadlock prevention is impossible in principle.
  4. Circular wait cannot arise unless at least one resource type has several instances.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The four conditions are jointly necessary: a deadlock needs all four at once. They are not sufficient, and no single one of them causes a deadlock by itself.

Step by step.

  1. A deadlock is a set of processes in which each holds a resource and waits for a resource held by another member of the set. That pattern needs mutual exclusion (the resource is not shareable), hold-and-wait (a process holds one thing while asking for another), no pre-emption (nobody can take it away) and circular wait (the waits close into a loop).
  2. Necessity is not sufficiency. Give five processes five distinct printers that each keeps for ever; all four conditions hold, yet no process ever asks for a second resource, so the circular wait never closes and nothing deadlocks.
  3. Prevention works by designing the system so that at least one condition can never be satisfied — for example by requiring all resources to be requested at once. That removes the possibility of deadlock; it does not detect or cure one that has already formed.
  4. So the only correct statement is (B): the four are necessary together, and even then a deadlock may not exist.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) No single condition is sufficient. A system can satisfy mutual exclusion alone, or hold-and-wait alone, and never deadlock.
  • (C) Every one of the four can be denied in some system, although denying mutual exclusion is impossible for a genuinely non-shareable resource such as a printer.
  • (D) Circular wait needs no multi-instance resource at all: a cycle among single-instance resources is the textbook case.

Common misconception. Treating the four conditions as a test for deadlock. They are a checklist for prevention, not a detector. A running system that satisfies all four may be perfectly healthy.

Takeaway. Necessary is not sufficient. Prevention denies one condition by construction; detection decides whether a deadlock actually exists right now.

OS-U3C-Q02MCQmedium

A system has resource type R₁ with 2 instances and resource type R₂ with 1 instance. Its resource allocation graph contains the assignment edges R₁ → P₁, R₁ → P₂ and R₂ → P₃, and the request edges P₁ → R₂ and P₃ → R₁. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. The graph contains no cycle and the system is not deadlocked.
  2. The graph contains a cycle and the system is deadlocked.
  3. The graph contains a cycle, but the system is not deadlocked.
  4. The graph contains no cycle, but the system is deadlocked.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With more than one instance of a resource type, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock. The graph-reduction algorithm decides the question: repeatedly finish any process whose outstanding requests can all be met from the currently available instances.

Step by step.

  1. Both instances of R₁ are held, so available R₁ = 0; the single instance of R₂ is held, so available R₂ = 0.
  2. P₂ holds an instance of R₁ and requests nothing, so P₂ can finish and releases it: available R₁ = 1.
  3. P₃ requests R₁, which is now available, so P₃ finishes and releases R₁ and R₂: available R₁ = 1, R₂ = 1.
  4. P₁ requests R₂, which is now available, so P₁ also finishes. Every process completes, so there is no deadlock.
  5. The cycle is still present in the graph: P₁ → R₂ → P₃ → R₁ → P₁. A cycle therefore exists while the system is deadlock-free.

Answer: Option (C) — a cycle exists, but the system is not deadlocked.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) The cycle P₁ → R₂ → P₃ → R₁ → P₁ is plainly present, so this is false.
  • (B) Reduction finishes all three processes, so nothing is deadlocked.
  • (D) Both halves of the statement are false: there is a cycle, and there is no deadlock.

Common misconception. Reading a cycle as a deadlock whenever the graph has more than one instance. Only the reduction settles it. A cycle tells you that contention closes into a loop; it does not tell you that the loop can never be broken.

Faster method. Reduce first, read the cycle afterwards. If every process gets marked, the answer is always ‘cycle but no deadlock’.

Takeaway. Single instance: cycle ⇔ deadlock. Multiple instances: cycle ⇒ deadlock is possible, and only graph reduction decides which.

OS-U3C-Q03MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about cycles in a resource allocation graph are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. When a resource type may have several instances, a cycle is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for deadlock.
  2. If the resource allocation graph contains no cycle, then no process is deadlocked.
  3. A cycle guarantees deadlock as soon as every resource type has at least two instances.
  4. In a graph in which every resource type has exactly one instance, a cycle may exist while the system is deadlock-free.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A) and (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. There are exactly two clean theorems. (i) No cycle ⇒ no deadlock, for any number of instances. (ii) Cycle ⇔ deadlock only when every resource type has exactly one instance.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. The graph R₁(2 instances), R₂(1 instance) with the cycle P₁ → R₂ → P₃ → R₁ → P₁ reduces to completion: the cycle is present and no process is deadlocked.
  2. (B) True. A deadlock is a closed loop of waits. If the waits never close into a loop there is nothing to be stuck on, so the absence of a cycle rules deadlock out entirely.
  3. (C) False. Two instances are already enough to break the guarantee, as the graph in (A) shows with 2 and 1 instances.
  4. (D) False. With exactly one instance of every type, a cycle is both necessary and sufficient — that is precisely the case in which the cycle theorem holds.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) reverses the single-instance theorem and applies it to the multi-instance case.
  • (D) denies the single-instance theorem, which is the one case where a cycle is decisive.

Common misconception. Assuming the two theorems are symmetric. They are not: the no-cycle direction holds always, the cycle direction holds only for single-instance resources.

Takeaway. Learn the pair as a single sentence: no cycle means no deadlock; a cycle means deadlock only when no resource type has two instances.

OS-U3C-Q04NATmedium

Resource types R₁ (2 instances), R₂ (1 instance) and R₃ (2 instances) are allocated as follows: P₁ holds one instance of R₁, P₂ holds the other instance of R₁, P₃ holds the single instance of R₂, and P₄ holds one instance of R₃. The outstanding requests are P₁ → R₂, P₂ → R₂ and P₃ → R₁; P₄ has no outstanding request. How many processes are deadlocked?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 3

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Run the graph-reduction algorithm: available instances are whatever is not currently held, and a process is removed as soon as all its outstanding requests can be met, releasing everything it holds.

Step by step.

  1. Available at the start: R₁ = 2 − 2 = 0, R₂ = 1 − 1 = 0, R₃ = 2 − 1 = 1.
  2. P₄ requests nothing, so it is removed and releases its instance of R₃: available R₃ = 2.
  3. P₁ and P₂ both wait for R₂, of which 0 instances are available and none can be released, because the only holder is P₃.
  4. P₃ waits for R₁, of which 0 instances are available; both are held by P₁ and P₂, who are themselves blocked.
  5. So P₁, P₂ and P₃ remain unmarked. Three processes are deadlocked.

Answer: 3

Common misconception. Forgetting that a process with no outstanding request always finishes and hands its instances back. That is what lets a graph reduce at all, and here it is what shows P₄ is not part of the deadlock.

Takeaway. Reduction is mechanical: free instances first, finish what you can, release, repeat. The count left over is the deadlock.

OS-U3C-Q05MCQhard

Resource type R₁ has 3 instances. P₁ holds 2 of them, P₂ holds 1 and P₃ holds none. P₁ now requests one more instance, P₃ requests one instance, and P₂ requests nothing. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. All three processes are deadlocked.
