  2. Adding its rollback count raises its cost each time it is chosen.
  3. Eventually another process becomes the cheapest victim, so the choice rotates.
  4. This is aging applied to victim selection.

Answer: Option (B) — charge each rollback to the victim's cost.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) the largest holder is not necessarily the cheapest to pre-empt; that is what the cost function decides.
  • (C) terminating everyone is the blunt option and loses the most work.
  • (D) new deadlocks would then go undetected.

Common misconception. Thinking recovery ends the problem. Recovery creates a second scheduling problem — which victim — that can itself starve a process.

Takeaway. Every time a system is allowed to choose a victim, add aging or the choice becomes a starvation source.

OS-U3-Q68MSQhard

Which of the following statements about deadlock detection and recovery are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Running the detection algorithm after every allocation request removes the need for prevention and avoidance, but costs O(mn²) per request.
  2. Detection through the wait-for graph is valid only when every resource type has a single instance.
  3. A process left unfinished when the detection algorithm terminates is deadlocked.
  4. Recovery by terminating one process at a time always needs at most one termination.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Detection is an alternative to prevention and avoidance: let deadlock happen, find it, then recover. Its cost is paid per invocation, and the frequency of invocation is a policy choice.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: detecting immediately after every grant means a deadlock is caught the instant it forms, so no structural prevention is needed — at O(mn²) per request.
  2. (B) True: the wait-for graph collapses a resource to a single edge, which only makes sense when the resource has one instance. With several instances a reduction over the allocation and request matrices is required.
  3. (C) True: that is precisely how the algorithm reports a deadlock — the unfinished set.
  4. (D) False: terminating one process may not break every cycle, and the algorithm has to be re-run; several terminations may be needed.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (D) overstates what one termination achieves; recovery is iterative, and each round costs another detection pass.

Common misconception. Assuming detection is free because it is "just a graph search". At O(mn²) per call, invoking it after every request can dominate the system's cost.

Takeaway. Detection frequency trades CPU for the size of the deadlock you may have to undo. Wait-for graphs are single-instance only.

OS-U3-Q73NATmedium

Every resource type in a system has exactly one instance. The wait-for graph has the edges P₁ → P₂, P₂ → P₃, P₃ → P₁, P₄ → P₃, P₅ → P₆ and P₆ → P₅. How many processes lie on a cycle in this graph?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 5

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With single-instance resources the wait-for graph is exact: a cycle is a deadlock. Identify every cycle, then count the distinct processes that lie on one.

Step by step.

  1. P₁ → P₂ → P₃ → P₁ is a 3-cycle: P₁, P₂, P₃.
  2. P₅ → P₆ → P₅ is a 2-cycle: P₅, P₆.
  3. P₄ → P₃ is an edge into the first cycle, not part of any cycle, so P₄ is not counted.
  4. Distinct processes on a cycle: 3 + 2 = 5.

Answer: 5.

Common misconception. Counting P₄ because it is blocked forever too. The question asks for cycle membership; a process that merely waits on a cycle is blocked, but it is not on the cycle.

Takeaway. Read the question's exact wording: "on a cycle" and "blocked" are different counts, and both appear in GATE papers.

OS-U3C-Q13MCQeasy

Every resource type in a system has exactly one instance, so a deadlock is exactly a cycle in the wait-for graph. The graph has one node per process and is stored as an adjacency matrix. If one detection pass uses a depth-first search, what is the worst-case cost of that pass for n processes?

  1. O(n)
  2. O(n log n)
  3. O(n²)
  4. O(2ⁿ)
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The cost of cycle detection is the cost of the graph representation plus the cost of the traversal. An adjacency matrix has n² entries, and a depth-first search that scans a row per visited node touches every entry.

Step by step.

  1. A depth-first search visits each node once and, for each node, inspects its whole row of the matrix to find its successors.
  2. There are n rows, each of length n, so the traversal reads n² entries in the worst case.
  3. The n node visits and the n edge-tree operations are dominated by that n² scan.
  4. Hence one detection pass costs Θ(n²). With an adjacency list the same traversal would cost O(n + e), which is O(n²) only in the worst case.

Answer: Option (C) — O(n²).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) would be the cost of looking at each process once, ignoring the matrix scan.
  • (B) has no source in this computation: nothing is being sorted or halved.
  • (D) is the cost of brute-force enumeration, not of a linear-time traversal.

Common misconception. Quoting O(n) for cycle detection because the wait-for graph has n nodes. The nodes are n; the matrix that stores them is n².

Takeaway. Detection cost is the cost of the representation. Matrix: O(n²). List: O(n + e). Decide which one the question assumes before answering.

OS-U3C-Q14MCQeasy

When a deadlock is broken by terminating processes, the standard measure of the cost of terminating a particular process is

  1. the number of page faults the process has taken.
  2. the process identifier, taking the largest identifier first.
  3. the time since the process last used the CPU.
  4. the amount of work the process has completed and the number of resources it holds.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Victim selection is a cost-minimisation problem. The two costs that matter are the work that would be thrown away and the resources that would be freed.

Step by step.

  1. Terminating a process destroys everything it has computed, so the more work it has already done, the more expensive the choice.
  2. Terminating a process frees everything it holds, so the more resources it holds, the more useful the choice. These two pull in opposite directions, which is why both are counted.
  3. The standard refinement adds the number of times the process has already been rolled back, so that the same victim is not chosen repeatedly.
  4. Page faults, process identifiers and recency of CPU use are not part of this cost measure.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Page faults measure memory behaviour, not the cost of losing the process.
  • (B) A process identifier is an arbitrary label with no relation to cost.
  • (C) Recency of CPU use is a scheduling statistic and says nothing about work lost or resources freed.

Common misconception. Picking the smallest process, or the newest one, as the victim. The criterion is work lost against resources freed, and neither of those is a property of size or age.

Takeaway. Cost = work destroyed + resources released, with repeat rollbacks counted as an extra penalty.

OS-U3C-Q15MCQeasy

Recovering from a deadlock by pre-empting resources from some processes raises three questions: choosing a victim, rolling the victim back to a safe point, and

  1. ensuring that the pre-empted resource is returned to the free pool.
  2. ensuring that the victim is restarted from the beginning of its execution.
  3. ensuring that the same process is not chosen as the victim every time.
  4. ensuring that no process holds more than one resource at a time.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The three questions of pre-emption recovery are victim selection, rollback and starvation. The third is easy to overlook because it is a fairness issue rather than a correctness one.

Step by step.

  1. Choosing the victim decides which resources are taken and how much work is lost.
  2. Rolling back decides how far the victim must be rewound so that it can run again from a consistent point — usually the most recent checkpoint.
  3. If the same process is always the cheapest victim, it is pre-empted again and again and never completes. That is starvation, and it must be guarded against explicitly, typically by adding the number of prior rollbacks to the victim's cost.
  4. So the missing third question is the fairness one.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Returning a resource to the pool is automatic once it is pre-empted, not a separate design question.
  • (B) Restarting from the very beginning is one possible rollback strategy, not a third question; checkpointing exists precisely to avoid it.
  • (D) is a prevention rule about request patterns, unrelated to recovery.

Common misconception. Stopping at two questions. Victim choice plus rollback can still leave a system that makes no progress, because the unlucky process is starved rather than blocked.

Takeaway. Recovery has three parts: whom to take from, how far to rewind them, and how to stop picking on them.

OS-U3C-Q16MCQhard

A system has resource types A (3 instances), B (2) and C (3). The allocation and the outstanding requests are given below. The detection algorithm for resources with several instances repeatedly marks any process whose requests can all be met from the current work vector. Which processes are left unmarked at the end?

ProcessAllocation (A B C)Outstanding request (A B C)
P₁(0, 1, 1)(2, 1, 2)
P₂(1, 1, 1)(1, 1, 2)
P₃(0, 0, 1)(1, 0, 0)
P₄(1, 0, 0)(1, 0, 1)

  1. P₁ and P₂
  2. P₂ and P₃
  3. P₁, P₂ and P₃
  4. No process — the system is not deadlocked.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The detection algorithm for multiple instances is the same reduction as the safety algorithm, run with the current request matrix instead of a need matrix. Work starts as the total minus the sum of the allocations.

Step by step.

  1. Work = (3, 2, 3) − (2, 2, 3) = (1, 0, 0).
  2. P₃ requests (1, 0, 0) ≤ (1, 0, 0), so it is marked and releases (0, 0, 1): Work = (1, 0, 1).
  3. P₄ requests (1, 0, 1) ≤ (1, 0, 1), so it is marked and releases (1, 0, 0): Work = (2, 0, 1).
  4. P₁ requests (2, 1, 2), which needs 1 unit of B — none is free — so it stays unmarked. P₂ requests (1, 1, 2), also needing a unit of B, so it stays unmarked too.
  5. No process can release any B, because both instances of B are held by the two blocked processes themselves. The unmarked set is {P₁, P₂}.

Answer: Option (A) — P₁ and P₂.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) P₃ is marked at the very first step, so it cannot be in the deadlock.
  • (C) includes P₃ for the same reason.
  • (D) ignores that both remaining processes need a unit of B and that no free B can ever appear.

Common misconception. Running the algorithm with the maximum claim instead of the outstanding request. Detection uses what each process is asking for now; only avoidance and safety use the full remaining claim.

Takeaway. Detection and safety use the same reduction with different matrices: requests for detection, need for safety.

OS-U3C-Q17MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about recovering from a detected deadlock are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Terminating every deadlocked process is certain to break the deadlock but is expensive.
  2. Terminating one process at a time and re-running the detection algorithm costs more detection passes but usually terminates fewer processes.
  3. Pre-empting a resource from a victim may require rolling the victim back to a checkpoint taken earlier.
  4. Rolling a victim back always discards all the work it has done since it started.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Recovery trades certainty against cost. Terminating everything is guaranteed and wasteful; terminating one at a time is cheaper in processes and dearer in algorithm invocations.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. If no deadlocked process is left, no cycle is left either, so the deadlock is certainly broken. The cost is every unit of work those processes had done.
  2. (B) True. Each termination is followed by another detection pass, so the number of passes grows, but the loop stops as soon as the deadlock disappears, which usually spares the remaining processes.
  3. (C) True. A pre-empted process cannot simply resume where it was, because the state it had built up may depend on the resource that was taken away. It is rewound to a checkpoint.
  4. (D) False. Rolling back to a checkpoint discards only the work done since that checkpoint. Work before the checkpoint survives, which is the whole reason checkpoints are taken.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (D) overstates rollback. Restarting from the beginning is a fallback used when no checkpoint exists, not what rollback means.

Common misconception. Believing that rollback always means a full restart. Checkpointing exists to bound what a rollback costs.

Takeaway. Prefer one-at-a-time termination with re-detection; roll back only to the last checkpoint.

OS-U3C-Q18NATmedium

Every resource type in a system has exactly one instance. The wait-for graph has the edges P₁ → P₂, P₂ → P₁, P₃ → P₄, P₄ → P₅, P₅ → P₃ and P₆ → P₁. What is the minimum number of processes that must be terminated so that no deadlock remains?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 2

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With one instance per resource type, a deadlock is exactly a directed cycle in the wait-for graph. Terminating one process removes its node and every edge in and out of it, which breaks any cycle through that node.

Step by step.

  1. The edges contain two disjoint cycles: P₁ → P₂ → P₁ and P₃ → P₄ → P₅ → P₃.
  2. P₆ is also deadlocked, because it waits for P₁, which can never release anything while it is inside its own cycle. P₆ is therefore blocked for ever but lies on no cycle of its own.
  3. A single termination cannot break both cycles, because the two cycles share no node. Terminating P₁ or P₂ clears the first cycle and, as a side effect, frees P₆.
  4. Terminating P₃, P₄ or P₅ clears the second. Two terminations therefore suffice, and one never does.
  5. So the minimum is 2.

Answer: 2

Common misconception. Counting the deadlocked processes (all six) instead of the cycles. Killing one process per cycle is enough, and processes that merely wait on a cycle are freed when the cycle breaks.

Takeaway. Minimum victims = number of node-disjoint cycles in the wait-for graph. Processes hanging off a cycle come free.

starvation-vs-deadlock 22
OS-U3-Q03MCQeasy

Which of the following best captures the difference between deadlock and starvation?

  1. In deadlock a set of processes waits forever for resources held by one another; in starvation one process waits indefinitely while the other processes keep making progress.
  2. Starvation always leaves a cycle in the wait-for graph, while deadlock never does.
  3. Deadlock ends as soon as the highest-priority process finishes, while starvation can never end.
  4. Starvation requires mutual exclusion, while deadlock does not.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Deadlock is a closed failure: every member of the blocked set waits for a member of that same set, so nobody can be released. Starvation is an open failure: the system as a whole progresses, but the allocation policy repeatedly passes one process over.

Step by step.

  1. In deadlock, the blocked set is closed under waiting — each process's requested resource is held by another blocked member — so no member can ever be unblocked.
  2. In starvation, other processes acquire and release the contended resource all the time; only the victim is never selected.
  3. A cycle in the wait-for graph is the signature of deadlock, not of starvation: a starving process has no cycle, only a policy that ignores it.
  4. Therefore the distinguishing feature is whether the rest of the system progresses.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the facts: a cycle accompanies deadlock, and starvation needs no cycle.
  • (C) describes no real property of either condition.
  • (D) confuses the resource conditions with the scheduling failure.

Common misconception. The two terms are often used as synonyms. A system can be completely deadlock-free and still starve a low-priority process forever.

Takeaway. Deadlock: nobody progresses. Starvation: everybody except one progresses. Cure deadlock by breaking a wait cycle; cure starvation by aging or fair queueing.

OS-U3-Q10MCQmedium

Which of the following statements about starvation (indefinite blocking) is TRUE?

  1. Starvation implies that a deadlock exists somewhere in the system.
  2. A starving process could in principle be executed, but the resource-allocation policy never selects it while other processes keep making progress.
  3. Starvation can always be removed by adding more instances of the contended resource.
  4. Starvation requires a cycle in the wait-for graph.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Starvation is a fairness failure, not a liveness failure: the victim is eligible and the resource is eventually free, but the policy never chooses the victim.

Step by step.

  1. In starvation the process is runnable, and the resource does become free from time to time.
  2. Other processes progress, so the blocked set is not closed — there is no wait cycle.
  3. The cause is the selection rule: a strict priority policy always prefers a higher-priority waiter, so a steady supply of higher-priority requests keeps the victim waiting forever.
  4. Adding instances reduces contention but does not change the rule; a policy that never selects the victim still never selects it.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Starvation and deadlock are independent failures.
  • (C) More resources ease contention but cannot fix an unfair selection rule; aging or fair queueing does.
  • (D) A cycle is the signature of deadlock, and starvation involves no closed wait set.

Common misconception. Treating more resources as the universal cure. The cure for starvation is a change of policy — aging, FIFO queueing, or a bounded number of overtakes.

Takeaway. Starvation is caused by a policy and cured by a policy. Deadlock is caused by a resource cycle and cured by breaking the cycle.

OS-U3-Q19MSQhard

Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A process can starve even though no deadlock exists anywhere in the system.
  2. Priority-based resource allocation can starve a low-priority process in a system that is completely deadlock-free.
  3. Every starving process belongs to a deadlocked set.
  4. Adding more instances of the contended resource always ends starvation.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A) and (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Starvation is a fairness failure of the selection policy; deadlock is a closed wait cycle. Neither implies the other.

Step by step.

  1. (A) In a strict-priority system with a steady supply of higher-priority requests, a low-priority process is passed over forever while everyone else progresses. No deadlock is involved. TRUE
  2. (B) Same mechanism, stated in the language of priorities. Deadlock-freedom says nothing about which waiter is chosen. TRUE
  3. (C) A starving process is not part of a closed wait set — the resources it needs are granted, just never to it. FALSE
  4. (D) More instances ease contention, but a policy that always prefers a higher-priority waiter will still never select the victim. FALSE

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. “Starvation is a mild deadlock”. They are different failures with different cures: break a cycle for deadlock, change the policy (aging) for starvation.

Takeaway. Deadlock-free does not mean starvation-free. Test them separately: is there a cycle, and is the selection rule fair?

OS-U3-Q24NATeasy

Consider four resource-allocation policies: (i) first-come first-served, (ii) round robin with a fixed quantum, (iii) strict fixed priority without aging, (iv) shortest-job-first in the presence of a continuous stream of new short jobs. How many of these four can leave a process waiting indefinitely while the other processes keep making progress?

Show answer & solution

Answer: Answer: 2

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Starvation arises when a policy lets later arrivals overtake a waiter indefinitely. Any policy that guarantees a bounded number of overtakes is starvation-free.

Step by step.

  1. (i) FCFS. A request is served in arrival order, so the wait is bounded by the requests already queued. No starvation.
  2. (ii) Round robin. Every process is served within one full cycle of the queue, so the wait is bounded by the number of processes. No starvation.
  3. (iii) Strict fixed priority. A continuous supply of higher-priority requests always overtakes the victim, which is never selected. Starvation is possible.
  4. (iv) SJF with continuous short arrivals. A long job is overtaken by every newly arriving short job, forever. Starvation is possible.
  5. Two of the four — (iii) and (iv) — can starve a process.

Answer: 2 (range 2 to 2).

Common misconception. Counting FCFS as starvation-prone. FCFS is the textbook starvation-free policy: the only thing it can be blamed for is a long average wait, not indefinite blocking.

Takeaway. Bounded overtaking ⇒ no starvation. Aging converts an unbounded policy into a bounded one by raising the victim's priority with time.

OS-U3B-Q20MCQeasy

Which one of the following describes a process that is starved but not deadlocked?

  1. A low-priority process that has been runnable for hours while higher-priority processes keep arriving.
  2. A process waiting for a resource held by a process that is itself waiting for a resource this process holds.
  3. A process that has terminated but whose resources have not yet been reclaimed.
  4. A process that holds a resource and is waiting for nothing.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Starvation is indefinite postponement by a scheduling or allocation policy; the process is able to make progress in principle but is never selected.

Step by step.

  1. Option A: the process is runnable and could use the CPU, but the policy never picks it. No resource is held by a blocking cycle. This is starvation.
  2. Option B is a closed wait set — a deadlock, not starvation.
  3. Option C is a reclamation issue, not a scheduling one.
  4. Option D describes a process that is simply running; nothing is blocked.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Calling any long wait starvation. Starvation requires that the process could run if selected; a process blocked on a resource held by a deadlocked peer is deadlocked instead.

OS-U3B-Q21MCQeasy

Aging is used to:

  1. increase the priority of a process the longer it waits, so that it is eventually selected.
  2. reduce the priority of long-running processes so that short ones finish first.
  3. prevent deadlock by imposing an order on resource requests.
  4. detect cycles in the wait-for graph.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Aging makes waiting itself improve a process's position, which bounds the time it can be overtaken.

Step by step.

  1. Starvation arises when a process is repeatedly passed over by a policy that does not account for how long it has waited.
  2. Aging raises the process's priority gradually with waiting time.
  3. Once its priority exceeds that of the competing processes, it is selected and runs.
  4. Options B, C and D describe other mechanisms entirely: SJF-like ordering, prevention, and detection.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Confusing aging with priority scheduling. Aging is a correction applied to a priority scheme; it is not itself a scheduling policy.

OS-U3B-Q22MCQeasy

Which one of the following is TRUE about deadlock and starvation?

  1. Deadlock implies starvation, but starvation does not imply deadlock.
  2. Starvation implies deadlock, but deadlock does not imply starvation.
  3. Deadlock and starvation are two names for the same condition.
  4. Neither condition implies the other.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A deadlocked process waits forever, which is indefinite postponement — so deadlock is a special case of starvation. The converse fails because starvation can arise from policy alone.

Step by step.

  1. Every deadlocked process is blocked forever on a resource held by another member of the closed set. That is indefinite waiting, so it is starved. Deadlock ⇒ starvation.
  2. A starved process may be perfectly runnable and merely never chosen, as with strict fixed priority and a steady supply of higher-priority work. No cycle of waits exists. Starvation ⇏ deadlock.
  3. So the implication holds in one direction only. Option A.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Treating them as equivalent. The distinguishing feature is a closed wait set: present in deadlock, absent in pure starvation.

OS-U3B-Q23MCQmedium

A low-priority process holds a mutex that a high-priority process needs, so the high-priority process blocks. Medium-priority processes keep the CPU busy, so the holder never runs. This situation is called:

  1. priority inversion.
  2. a circular wait.
  3. the convoy effect.
  4. thrashing.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Priority inversion is a high-priority task waiting on a low-priority holder that cannot run because medium-priority tasks occupy the processor.

Step by step.

  1. The high-priority process is blocked on a lock, not on the CPU.
  2. The lock holder has lower priority than the medium-priority processes, so it is never scheduled.
  3. The high-priority process therefore waits for an unbounded time, effectively at the mercy of unrelated medium-priority work.
  4. This inversion of the intended priority order is priority inversion; priority inheritance or a priority ceiling is the standard fix.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Calling it a circular wait. There is no cycle — the holder is not waiting for anything the high-priority process holds; it simply never runs.

OS-U3B-Q24MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about starvation and deadlock are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Starvation can often be removed by aging, whereas a deadlock cannot.
  2. A deadlocked process is blocked; a starved process may be runnable and simply never selected.
  3. A deadlock can always be removed by raising the priority of one of the waiting processes.
  4. A strict fixed-priority scheduler can starve a low-priority process even when no deadlock exists.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B), (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Starvation is a policy failure, deadlock is a structural one; the remedies differ accordingly.

Step by step.

  1. Option A: aging changes the policy so the waiter eventually wins, which fixes starvation. A deadlock needs a process terminated or a resource preempted; priority changes do not break the cycle. True.
  2. Option B: that is the definitional difference between the two. True.
  3. Option C: raising a priority does not release any resource. If every member of a closed wait set still waits on the next, nothing changes. False.
  4. Option D: with strict priorities and a continuous supply of higher-priority work, the lowest-priority process is never chosen, and no cycle need exist. True.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are true. Option (C) is false.

Common misconception. Assuming a scheduling knob can fix a resource cycle. Priorities affect who runs, not who holds a resource.

OS-U3B-Q25NAThard

A system uses strict fixed-priority preemptive scheduling with no priority inheritance. A low-priority process `L` holds a mutex that a high-priority process `H` needs, so `H` blocks. Two medium-priority processes `M₁` and `M₂` then become runnable. How many of the runnable processes are scheduled while `L` still holds the mutex?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 2

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Without priority inheritance, blocking a high-priority process does not raise the holder's priority, so any process ranked above the holder can preempt it.

Step by step.

  1. H is blocked on the mutex, so it is not runnable.
  2. L holds the mutex but has the lowest priority, so both M₁ and M₂ outrank it and preempt it.
  3. M₁ and M₂ therefore run, in priority order, for as long as they are runnable.
  4. L never gets the processor, so it never releases the mutex, and H stays blocked. This is priority inversion.
  5. Runnable processes scheduled while L holds the mutex: M₁ and M₂, that is 2.

Answer: 2

Common misconception. Answering 0 on the assumption that the high-priority process runs first. H cannot run — it is blocked on the mutex, not waiting for the CPU.

OS-U3-Q61MCQeasy

In the readers-preference solution to the readers-writers problem, a writer may wait forever while readers keep arriving. Which one of the following describes that situation?

  1. A deadlock, because the writer holds a resource that the readers need.
  2. Starvation, because the writer is blocked indefinitely without any cycle in the wait-for relation.
  3. A circular wait, because the writer and the readers wait for each other.
  4. Hold and wait, because the writer holds a resource while it waits.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Starvation is indefinite blocking with no cycle: the process is not deadlocked, because the resource it waits for is repeatedly released and immediately re-acquired by others. Deadlock needs a cycle in which each holder waits for another.

Step by step.

  1. The writer waits on the mutual-exclusion semaphore for the data.
  2. Under reader preference, a new reader is never blocked by a waiting writer, so it increments the reader count and enters.
  3. The writer's condition — no reader inside — never becomes true while readers arrive faster than they leave.
  4. Nothing is circular and nothing is permanently held by a blocked process: the resource is being used and released all the time. That is starvation.

Answer: Option (B) — starvation without deadlock.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) the writer holds nothing; it is waiting, not holding.
  • (C) no cycle exists: the writer waits for a resource, and no process waits for the writer.
  • (D) hold and wait requires the process to be holding one resource while requesting another.

Common misconception. Calling every indefinite wait a deadlock. Deadlock is a cycle; starvation is an unfair queue.

Takeaway. Ask two questions: is there a cycle? Is anything permanently held? No and no means starvation.

OS-U3-Q62MCQmedium

A system prevents deadlock by numbering its resource types and requiring every process to request them in strictly increasing order. Which one of the following can still happen?

  1. A circular wait, because two processes may each hold a lower-numbered resource.
  2. A process can wait indefinitely if requests for the higher-numbered resources keep being granted to other processes first.
  3. Two processes can deadlock by each holding an instance of the same resource type.
  4. A process that already holds a resource can be forced to give it up before it finishes.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A total order on resource types removes circular wait, and with it deadlock. It says nothing about fairness: the scheme only forbids certain orderings of requests, not certain outcomes of contention.

Step by step.

  1. A cycle needs a process holding a higher-numbered resource and requesting a lower-numbered one. The rule forbids exactly that edge, so no cycle can form — (A) and (C) are impossible.
  2. Fairness is a different matter. If several processes keep requesting R₅ and each is granted it before a particular waiter, that waiter can be postponed without bound.
  3. Nothing in the scheme preempts a held resource, so (D) is also impossible.

Answer: Option (B) — deadlock-free does not mean starvation-free.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (C) both describe a cycle, which the ordering rules out.
  • (D) ordering is a request discipline; it does not add preemption.

Common misconception. Reading "prevents deadlock" as "guarantees every process finishes". The two guarantees are independent.

Takeaway. Prevention removes cycles; bounded waiting needs a queue or aging on top of it.

OS-U3-Q63MCQeasy

Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. Every starved process is deadlocked.
  2. Every deadlocked process is starved.
  3. Starvation always appears as a cycle in the wait-for graph.
  4. A deadlocked process is not blocked.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Deadlock implies indefinite blocking, and indefinite blocking is starvation. The converse fails: starvation can occur with no cycle at all, for example under strict priority scheduling or reader preference.

Step by step.

  1. If a process is deadlocked it will never receive what it waits for, so it waits forever — it is starved. Hence (B) is true.
  2. A low-priority process can be starved forever while every other process keeps finishing. Nothing is permanently held by a blocked process, so there is no deadlock — (A) is false.
  3. Starvation needs no cycle, so (C) is false.
  4. A deadlocked process is by definition blocked, so (D) is false.

Answer: Option (B) — deadlock is a special case of starvation.

Common misconception. Treating the two as synonyms in either direction. The containment is one-way: deadlock ⊂ starvation.

Takeaway. If a question says "starved but not deadlocked", the answer must involve unfair scheduling with no permanent holder.

OS-U3-Q69MSQeasy

Which of the following statements about starvation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Aging raises the priority of a long-waiting process until it is eventually selected.
  2. First-come first-served scheduling cannot starve a process.
  3. Strict priority scheduling can starve a low-priority process indefinitely.
  4. A deadlocked process will eventually proceed if it waits long enough.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Starvation is indefinite postponement. It is a fairness property of a policy, not a correctness property, and it is cured by bounding the wait, not by removing a cycle.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: aging increases the priority of a waiting process, so its wait is bounded.
  2. (B) True: under FCFS every process is served in arrival order, so the number of processes ahead of any one is fixed and finite.
  3. (C) True: a steady stream of higher-priority work can postpone a low-priority process for ever — the classic case.
  4. (D) False: deadlock is not a waiting-time problem. No amount of waiting releases a resource that is held in a cycle.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (D) confuses starvation with deadlock; the first is cured by fairness, the second only by breaking a cycle.

Common misconception. Believing that a long enough wait fixes everything. For a starved process it may; for a deadlocked one it never will.

Takeaway. Aging and bounded waiting cure starvation. Only preemption, rollback or termination cure deadlock.

OS-U3-Q75NATmedium

A readers-writers solution gives readers preference: a writer waits until no reader is inside the critical section, and a waiting writer never delays a new reader. From t = 0 a writer waits, and readers arrive so that at least one reader is inside the critical section for the whole of the next 500 seconds. How many times does the writer enter its critical section during those 500 seconds?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 0

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Reader preference gives readers priority over any waiting writer. The writer's entry condition — no reader inside — is therefore never satisfied while readers keep arriving.

Step by step.

  1. The writer can enter only when the reader count is zero and no new reader is admitted ahead of it.
  2. Reader preference explicitly allows a new reader to enter even while a writer waits.
  3. Since at least one reader is inside for the entire interval, the count never reaches zero.
  4. So the writer's condition never becomes true and it enters 0 times — indefinite postponement, that is, starvation.

Answer: 0.

Common misconception. Assuming the writer must eventually get a turn. Under reader preference there is no bound on the number of readers that may pass a waiting writer, so no turn is guaranteed.

Takeaway. Preference rules decide who starves. Readers-preference starves writers; writers-preference starves readers; a fair solution bounds the wait for both.

OS-U3C-Q19MCQeasy

Which one of the three requirements for a correct solution to the critical-section problem is the one that rules out starvation of a waiting process?

  1. Mutual exclusion
  2. Bounded waiting
  3. Progress
  4. Atomicity of the entry section
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The three requirements answer three different questions. Mutual exclusion asks whether two processes can be inside at once; progress asks whether the section can stay idle while someone wants it; bounded waiting asks whether a waiter can be overtaken for ever.

Step by step.

  1. Mutual exclusion is a safety property: at most one process inside. It says nothing about how long a waiter waits.
  2. Progress is a liveness property about the system, not about an individual: if the section is free and someone wants it, someone must get in. A protocol can satisfy progress and still let one particular process lose every race.
  3. Bounded waiting is the fairness property: there must be a bound on how many times others may enter after a process has requested entry. That bound is exactly the guarantee against starvation.
  4. Atomicity of the entry section is a mechanism, not one of the three requirements.

Answer: Option (B) — bounded waiting.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Mutual exclusion can hold perfectly while one process starves.
  • (C) Progress guarantees that some process enters, not that every waiting process eventually does.
  • (D) is a property of an instruction, not a correctness requirement of the problem.

Common misconception. Treating progress as a fairness guarantee. Progress is about the section never being wasted; bounded waiting is about no waiter being passed over for ever.

Takeaway. Exclusion, progress, bounded waiting — the third is the anti-starvation clause.

OS-U3C-Q20MCQeasy

A resource is handed out strictly in first-come-first-served order. Can a process that has requested it be starved?

  1. No: every waiter is served in arrival order, so its wait is bounded by the number of processes already ahead of it.
  2. Yes: a process that arrives later can overtake it.
  3. Yes, because first-come-first-served can itself deadlock.
  4. No, because first-come-first-served prevents deadlock as well as starvation.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Starvation is the absence of a bound on waiting. A strict arrival-order queue supplies exactly such a bound: nothing can overtake a waiter.

Step by step.

  1. In a FCFS queue a process joins the tail and is served once every process ahead of it has been served.
  2. New arrivals join behind it, so they cannot overtake. The number of processes ahead of a waiter never increases.
  3. That fixed number is the bound, which is precisely bounded waiting, so starvation is impossible.
  4. FCFS is therefore the simplest anti-starvation device, which is why it appears inside fair locks and fair semaphores.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Overtaking is exactly what a strict queue forbids.
  • (C) Deadlock is a separate failure caused by circular waits across several resources; a single FCFS queue has no cycle.
  • (D) FCFS prevents starvation, but a system of processes each holding one resource while queueing for another can still deadlock.

Common misconception. Assuming any waiting implies starvation. Waiting is bounded in FCFS; only a policy that lets newcomers jump the queue removes the bound.

Takeaway. Arrival-order service = bounded waiting. Fairness comes from the queue, not from the resource.

OS-U3C-Q21MCQeasy

The banker's algorithm has just declared the current state safe. Which one of the following follows?

  1. Every process will eventually finish, whatever order the requests happen to arrive in.
  2. At least one completion order exists, but nothing guarantees that any particular process will ever be served.
  3. The state is deadlocked.
  4. The system can never enter an unsafe state again.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Safety is an existential statement: there exists a sequence in which every process finishes. It is not a universal or a fairness statement.

Step by step.

  1. A safe state means the safety algorithm found some ordering of the processes in which each one's remaining claim is covered at the moment it runs.
  2. That ordering is a witness of possibility. The scheduler is under no obligation to follow it, and a process that is repeatedly unlucky can be overtaken indefinitely.
  3. So safety rules out deadlock but does not rule out starvation; the two guarantees are independent.
  4. Nothing about a safe state says the future states will also be safe — that depends on which requests are granted.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Safety promises one order, not every order, and says nothing about arrival patterns.
  • (C) A safe state is the opposite of a deadlocked one.
  • (D) A safe state can be followed by an unsafe one if a request is granted that the algorithm would have refused.

Common misconception. Reading ‘there exists a safe sequence’ as ‘every process is guaranteed to finish’. Existence is not fairness.

Takeaway. Safety prevents deadlock only. Starvation needs a separate fairness rule on top.

OS-U3C-Q22MCQmedium

Two processes each hold one resource and each needs the other's. Instead of waiting, each releases what it holds as soon as it sees the other waiting, then immediately retries. Both keep running, and neither ever makes progress. This situation is

  1. a deadlock.
  2. starvation of one process.
  3. a violation of bounded waiting.
  4. a livelock.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Three different failures hide behind ‘no progress’. Deadlock means every process is blocked. Starvation means a process is ready but never chosen. Livelock means processes keep running and keep undoing their own progress.

Step by step.

  1. Both processes are executing: they acquire, observe the conflict, release and retry. Neither is blocked, so this is not a deadlock.
  2. Neither process is being passed over by a scheduler; both are being scheduled, and both are busy. So this is not starvation.
  3. The problem is not a missing bound on waiting, because neither process is waiting for long.
  4. The system changes state constantly without ever advancing, which is exactly the definition of a livelock: the processes are not stuck, they are merely uselessly active.

Answer: Option (D) — a livelock.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Deadlock requires blocked processes; these two are running.
  • (B) Starvation is about a ready process never being selected, which is not what happens here.
  • (C) Bounded waiting is a critical-section requirement, and it is not the property being violated — nothing is waiting.

Common misconception. Assuming that ‘no progress’ always means deadlock. A livelock burns CPU while making none, and it is cured by randomised back-off rather than by breaking a cycle.

Takeaway. Blocked for ever = deadlock. Ready but never chosen = starvation. Running but always undoing itself = livelock.

OS-U3C-Q23MCQmedium

Repeatedly choosing the same process as the pre-emption victim can starve it. Which one of the following is the standard safeguard?

  1. Terminate every deadlocked process at the first detection.
  2. Raise the victim's priority after each rollback.
  3. Include the number of times the process has already been rolled back in its victim cost.
  4. Disable pre-emption once the first deadlock has been broken.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Victim selection minimises a cost. Starvation happens when one process is permanently the cheapest victim, so the cure is to make it steadily more expensive.

Step by step.

  1. The base cost counts the work the process has done and the resources it holds.
  2. Adding the number of prior rollbacks means that each time a process is chosen, its cost rises.
  3. Eventually its cost exceeds that of every other candidate, and the algorithm picks somebody else. That is aging applied to victim selection.
  4. So the safeguard is to count previous rollbacks in the cost, not to change the scheduling or to stop pre-empting.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Terminating everything is the most expensive recovery there is and does nothing about fairness.
  • (B) Raising priority affects who gets the CPU, not who is chosen as the victim.
  • (D) Disabling pre-emption would leave later deadlocks unrecoverable.

Common misconception. Thinking of aging only as a CPU-scheduling idea. The same device — make the neglected party steadily more attractive — works in victim selection.

Takeaway. Anti-starvation is always a monotone penalty or bonus. In recovery, count the rollbacks.

OS-U3C-Q24MSQeasy

Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A deadlocked process is always blocked, while a starved process may be runnable.
  2. Aging removes deadlock as well as starvation.
  3. In a system where every resource type has exactly one instance, a cycle in the wait-for graph means that the system is deadlocked.
  4. A starved process is always blocked.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Deadlock and starvation are different failures with different cures, and the single-instance cycle theorem is the one place where the two ideas of ‘blocked’ and ‘stuck’ coincide exactly.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. A deadlocked process has issued a request that can never be granted, so it is blocked. A starved process may be perfectly runnable and merely never selected — for example a low-priority process under strict priority scheduling.
  2. (B) False. Aging raises the priority of a long-waiting process, which cures starvation. It cannot break a circular wait, so a deadlock is untouched.
  3. (C) True. With one instance per type, a cycle means each process in it waits for a resource held by the next, and nobody can release. That is a deadlock, and the cycle is necessary and sufficient.
  4. (D) False. A starved process is frequently runnable. That is what distinguishes starvation from deadlock.

Answer: Options (A) and (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Aging is a scheduling fix and has no effect on a resource cycle.
  • (D) contradicts the definition: starvation is about never being chosen, not about being unable to run.

Common misconception. Using ‘blocked’ as a synonym for ‘not progressing’. Blocking is one way to fail to progress; being passed over is another.

Takeaway. Deadlock blocks. Starvation neglects. Only deadlock needs the cycle broken.

OS-U3C-Q25NATeasy

A waiting process has priority 3. Its priority is raised by 1 for every 50 ms it spends waiting, while a competing process keeps a fixed priority of 9. After how many milliseconds of waiting does the waiting process reach priority 9?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 300

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Aging is a linear ramp: priority rises by a fixed step per fixed interval. The time needed is the size of the gap divided by the step, multiplied by the interval.

Step by step.

  1. The gap to close is 9 − 3 = 6 priority levels.
  2. Each level costs 50 ms of waiting.
  3. Time required = 6 × 50 = 300 ms.
  4. At 300 ms the waiting process has priority 3 + 6 = 9 and can compete on equal terms.

Answer: 300

Common misconception. Multiplying 9 by 50 and answering 450. Aging starts from the process's current priority, so only the gap of 6 levels has to be paid for.

Takeaway. Aging time = (target − current) × interval. Only the gap is paid for.

Unit 4 — Memory Management & Paging · 100 solved questions (2026-10-28)
contiguous-allocation-first-best-worst-fit 26
OS-U4-Q01MCQeasy

A memory manager keeps five free holes in address order: 100 KB, 500 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB and 600 KB. A new process requests 212 KB. Using first fit, which hole is chosen?

  1. the 500 KB hole
  2. the 600 KB hole
  3. the 200 KB hole
  4. none — the request fails
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. First fit scans the free list in address order and takes the first hole that is large enough, without looking further.

Step by step.

  1. The 100 KB hole is smaller than 212 KB, so it is skipped.
  2. The next hole, 500 KB, is at least 212 KB, so the request is satisfied there.
  3. The remainder, 500 − 212 = 288 KB, goes back on the free list.

Answer: Option (A)

Common misconception. Choosing the 600 KB hole (worst fit) or the 300 KB hole (best fit). Both are legitimate policies, but neither is first fit, which never scans past the first adequate hole.

OS-U4-Q02MCQeasy

Which one of the following statements about fragmentation is TRUE?

  1. Contiguous allocation suffers internal fragmentation but not external fragmentation.
  2. Paging suffers external fragmentation but not internal fragmentation.
  3. Contiguous allocation suffers external fragmentation, while a paging system wastes space only inside the last page of a process.
  4. Both contiguous allocation and paging suffer only external fragmentation.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. External fragmentation is free space that exists but is split into pieces too small to be used. Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block.

Step by step.

  1. In contiguous allocation a process gets one run of memory, so when processes finish the free space breaks into holes between the survivors: external fragmentation.
  2. Paging hands a process whole frames, so any free frame can be used and no usable free space is left between allocations: there is no external fragmentation.
  3. The last page of a process is only partly filled, so the unused tail of that frame is lost: internal fragmentation.

Answer: Option (C)

Common misconception. Believing paging removes all waste. It removes external fragmentation only, and it trades it for internal fragmentation that averages half a page per process.

OS-U4-Q03MCQmedium

Free holes of 200 KB, 500 KB, 300 KB and 600 KB are available, in that address order, and a process requests 250 KB. Which placement policy leaves the smallest leftover hole?

  1. first fit, leaving 250 KB
  2. best fit, leaving 50 KB
  3. worst fit, leaving 350 KB
  4. next fit, leaving 250 KB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each policy selects a different hole, and the leftover is the chosen hole minus the request.

Step by step.

  1. First fit takes the first adequate hole, 500 KB, leaving 500 − 250 = 250 KB.
  2. Best fit takes the smallest adequate hole, 300 KB, leaving 300 − 250 = 50 KB.
  3. Worst fit takes the largest hole, 600 KB, leaving 600 − 250 = 350 KB.
  4. Next fit, starting from the beginning of the list here, also takes 500 KB and leaves 250 KB.

Answer: Option (B)

Common misconception. Reading "smallest leftover" as "best overall policy". Best fit does leave the smallest leftover, but that same behaviour shreds memory into holes too small to be reused, which is why it is not automatically the best choice.

OS-U4-Q04MCQhard

A system uses first fit with no compaction. The free holes, in address order, are 100 KB, 500 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB and 600 KB. Requests of 212 KB, 417 KB, 112 KB and 426 KB arrive in that order. Which requests fail?

  1. only the 417 KB request
  2. only the 426 KB request
  3. the 417 KB and 426 KB requests
  4. none — all four requests fit
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. First fit restarts its scan at the beginning of the free list for every request, and a hole is split, never merged with a neighbour that is still in use.

Step by step.

  1. 212 KB: the 100 KB hole is too small; the 500 KB hole is taken and split into 288 KB. Free list: 100, 288, 200, 300, 600.
  2. 417 KB: the first adequate hole is 600 KB, split into 183 KB. Free list: 100, 288, 200, 300, 183.
  3. 112 KB: the first adequate hole is 288 KB, split into 176 KB. Free list: 100, 176, 200, 300, 183.
  4. 426 KB: the largest hole is now 300 KB, so no hole can hold it and the request fails.

Answer: Option (B)

Common misconception. Adding up the free space (100 + 176 + 200 + 300 + 183 = 959 KB, far more than 426 KB) and concluding the request must succeed. First fit needs one contiguous hole, not the total of several.

OS-U4-Q05MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about first fit, best fit and worst fit are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Best fit tends to leave very small holes that are often too small to be reused.
  2. First fit can stop at the first adequate hole, so it is usually faster than best fit.
  3. Worst fit always produces less external fragmentation than best fit.
  4. Next fit resumes the scan where the previous allocation ended, which spreads allocations across memory instead of concentrating them at the low addresses.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The three policies differ only in which adequate hole they choose; the cost of searching and the shape of the holes left behind are the practical consequences.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: best fit minimises the leftover, so it produces many slivers of unusable size.
  2. (B) is true: first fit stops at the first adequate hole, while best fit must scan the whole list to be sure it has the smallest adequate one.
  3. (C) is false: worst fit leaves a large remainder that is more likely to be reusable, but it is not guaranteed to beat best fit on external fragmentation — simulations show it is often worse.
  4. (D) is true: next fit continues from the last allocation point, so it spreads allocations across memory rather than always splitting the low-address holes.

Answer: Options (A), (B), (D)

Common misconception. Treating "worst fit" as the cure for fragmentation. It leaves big remainders, but it also destroys the large holes that big requests need.

OS-U4-Q06MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about contiguous allocation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Compaction can move a running process only if its addresses are translated at run time, that is, with dynamic relocation.
  2. Internal fragmentation is wasted space inside a block that has already been allocated to a process.
  3. When a process terminates, adjacent free blocks must be coalesced, or the free space stays split.
  4. A paging system can suffer external fragmentation.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Contiguous allocation binds a process to one run of physical memory, so the layout of free space and the binding of addresses are both policy questions.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: compaction copies processes to new addresses, which is impossible if the program was bound to absolute addresses at load time; base and limit registers make it possible.
  2. (B) is true by definition: the allocated block is larger than the request, and the surplus is unusable by anyone else.
  3. (C) is true: without coalescing, neighbouring free blocks stay separate, so a later request may fail even though the combined space would satisfy it.
  4. (D) is false: frames are all the same size, so any free frame fits any page. Paging has internal fragmentation but no external fragmentation.

Answer: Options (A), (B), (C)

Common misconception. Assuming compaction is always available. It costs CPU time and needs dynamic relocation, and it is impossible in some systems.

OS-U4-Q07NAThard

Free holes of 300 KB, 600 KB, 350 KB, 200 KB and 450 KB are available. Requests of 250 KB, 400 KB and 200 KB arrive in that order and are placed by worst fit. What is the size, in KB, of the largest hole remaining after all three requests have been placed?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 350

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Worst fit always takes the largest available hole, so the largest hole is consumed first and the remainders are as large as possible.

Step by step.

  1. Holes: 300, 600, 350, 200, 450. The largest is 600, so the 250 KB request takes it and leaves 350. Holes: 300, 350, 350, 200, 450.
  2. The largest hole is now 450, so the 400 KB request takes it and leaves 50. Holes: 300, 350, 350, 200, 50.
  3. The largest hole is 350, so the 200 KB request takes it and leaves 150. Holes: 300, 150, 350, 200, 50.
  4. The largest hole remaining is 350 KB.

Answer: 350

Common misconception. Sorting the holes once and using that order throughout. The list must be re-examined after every placement, because the hole just split is no longer the largest.

OS-U4-S2-Q01MCQeasy

A memory manager keeps four free holes in address order: 250 KB, 600 KB, 400 KB and 300 KB. A process requests 380 KB. Using best fit, which hole is chosen?

  1. the 250 KB hole
  2. the 600 KB hole
  3. the 400 KB hole
  4. none — the request fails
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Best fit scans the whole free list and takes the smallest hole that is at least as large as the request. Only holes that can hold the request are candidates.

Step by step.

  1. The 250 KB hole is smaller than 380 KB, so it is not a candidate.
  2. The 600 KB hole fits, leaving 220 KB.
  3. The 400 KB hole fits, leaving 20 KB, and the 300 KB hole does not fit at all.
  4. Of the candidates 600 KB and 400 KB, the smaller is 400 KB, so best fit chooses it.

Option (C)

Common misconception. Answering 600 KB, which is what worst fit would choose, or scanning for the hole whose address is closest to the request. Best fit compares sizes, never addresses.

OS-U4-S2-Q02NATeasy

Free holes of 500 KB, 200 KB, 700 KB and 300 KB lie in address order. Two requests of 450 KB and 260 KB arrive in that order and are placed by first fit, each scan restarting at the beginning of the list, with remainders split off and no coalescing. What is the size, in KB, of the largest hole remaining after both requests?

Show answer & solution

Answer: Answer: 440

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. First fit takes the first hole in address order that is large enough, splits off the remainder and leaves it in place. Each new request restarts the scan at the beginning of the list.

Step by step.

  1. The 450 KB request meets the 500 KB hole first and it is large enough, so it is taken at once, leaving 500 − 450 = 50 KB. Free list: 50, 200, 700, 300.
  2. The 260 KB request scans from the start: 50 is too small and 200 is too small, so the 700 KB hole is taken, leaving 700 − 260 = 440 KB. Free list: 50, 200, 440, 300.
  3. The largest hole is therefore 440 KB.

Answer: 440

Common misconception. Scanning the holes from the largest instead of from the lowest address. That is worst fit, and it would have placed the 450 KB request in the 700 KB hole.

OS-U4-S2-Q03MCQmedium

Free holes of 400 KB, 250 KB, 550 KB and 300 KB are available. Requests of 200 KB, 350 KB and 150 KB arrive in that order and are placed by worst fit. What is the size, in KB, of the largest hole remaining after all three requests?

  1. 300 KB
  2. 350 KB
  3. 200 KB
  4. 250 KB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Worst fit always allocates from the largest hole, so the largest hole must be recomputed after every placement.

Step by step.

  1. 200 KB takes the 550 KB hole, leaving 350. Holes: 400, 250, 350, 300.
  2. 350 KB takes the 400 KB hole, leaving 50. Holes: 50, 250, 350, 300.
  3. 150 KB takes the 350 KB hole, leaving 200. Holes: 50, 250, 200, 300.
  4. The largest hole left is 300 KB.

Option (A)

Common misconception. Sorting the holes once and then walking that order. The 350 KB remainder created by the first placement becomes the largest hole at the next step, so the order must be rebuilt each time.

OS-U4-S2-Q04MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about contiguous-allocation policies are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Worst fit leaves a remainder at least as large as best fit would leave for the same hole set and request.
  2. Best fit tends to leave many holes so small that they cannot be reused.
  3. Compaction is possible only when a process can be relocated at run time.
  4. First fit always produces less external fragmentation than best fit.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B), (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Best fit picks the smallest adequate hole, worst fit the largest. Since the largest adequate hole is at least as big as the smallest one, worst fit always leaves a remainder at least as large.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: remainder = chosen hole − request, and the largest adequate hole ≥ the smallest adequate hole, so worst fit leaves the bigger remainder.
  2. (B) is true: shaving the request off the closest-fitting hole produces slivers too small to be reused.
  3. (C) is true: compaction moves processes, which is impossible unless addresses are bound at run time (base and limit registers or page tables).
  4. (D) is false: no policy dominates. Simulation shows first fit is usually faster and often as good, but there are sequences on which best fit fragments less.

Options (A), (B) and (C)

Common misconception. Treating best fit as the policy that wastes least memory. It wastes least per allocation and therefore creates the most unusable slivers.

OS-U4-S2-Q05MCQhard

Free holes of 200 KB, 600 KB, 150 KB and 400 KB lie in address order. Two requests, 500 KB then 250 KB, are placed by first fit, each scan restarting at the beginning of the list, with remainders split off and no coalescing. What is the largest single request, in KB, that can still be satisfied afterwards?

  1. 100 KB
  2. 150 KB
  3. 200 KB
  4. 600 KB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The answer is the largest hole that survives, because a request must fit inside a single contiguous hole. The total of all free holes is irrelevant.

Step by step.

  1. 500 KB scans 200 (too small), then takes the 600 KB hole and leaves 100 KB. Holes: 200, 100, 150, 400.
  2. 250 KB scans 200 (too small), 100 (too small), 150 (too small), then takes the 400 KB hole and leaves 150 KB. Holes: 200, 100, 150, 150.
  3. The largest surviving hole is 200 KB.

Option (C)

Common misconception. Adding the free holes (200 + 100 + 150 + 150 = 600 KB) and concluding a 600 KB request fits. First fit needs one hole large enough, not the sum of several.

OS-U4-S2-Q06NATmedium

Holes of 300 KB, 150 KB, 500 KB and 250 KB are available. Requests of 140 KB, 480 KB, 200 KB and 260 KB arrive in that order and are placed by best fit. What is the size, in KB, of the largest hole remaining after all four requests?

Show answer & solution

Answer: Answer: 50

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Best fit takes the smallest adequate hole at every step, so the leftover is always as small as the free list allows. The largest surviving hole must be recomputed after each of the four placements.

Step by step.

  1. 140 KB: the smallest adequate hole is 150, leaving 10. Holes: 300, 10, 500, 250.
  2. 480 KB: the smallest adequate hole is 500, leaving 20. Holes: 300, 10, 20, 250.
  3. 200 KB: the smallest adequate hole is 250, leaving 50. Holes: 300, 10, 20, 50.
  4. 260 KB: the smallest adequate hole is 300, leaving 40. Holes: 40, 10, 20, 50.
  5. The largest hole left is 50 KB.

Answer: 50

Common misconception. Reading the holes in address order. Best fit compares every hole on each request, so the 500 KB hole is passed over for the 480 KB request only because no smaller hole fits it.

OS-U4-Q51MCQeasy

A process is loaded into a contiguous region whose base register holds 8000 and whose limit register holds 600. The memory unit adds the base to every offset it is given, but only after the limit check. Which one of the following offsets is rejected with a trap?

  1. 0
  2. 350
  3. 599
  4. 600
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A base–limit pair defines the legal window of a process. The limit register holds the size of the region, not its last address, so the legal offsets are 0 ≤ offset < limit. The hardware compares the offset with the limit before it forms base + offset.

Step by step.

  1. The window is [8000, 8000 + 600) = [8000, 8600) in physical memory.
  2. Offset 0 gives physical address 8000 — legal.
  3. Offset 350 gives 8350 — legal.
  4. Offset 599 gives 8599, the last byte of the region — legal.
  5. Offset 600 gives 8600, one byte past the region. The comparison 600 < 600 is false, so the reference traps.

Answer: Option (D) — offset 600 is the first offset that fails the limit check.

Common misconception. Treating the limit as the highest legal address. It is a length, so the highest legal offset is limit − 1. Reading the limit as an inclusive bound makes 600 look legal and also lets a one-byte overrun through.

OS-U4-Q52MCQeasy

Which one of the following schemes can suffer internal fragmentation but can never suffer external fragmentation?

  1. Contiguous allocation with first fit
  2. Fixed-size partitions
  3. Pure segmentation
  4. Dynamic contiguous allocation with compaction
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Internal fragmentation is space wasted inside an allocated block, because the block is larger than the request. External fragmentation is free space wasted outside the allocated blocks, in holes too small to serve a request. A scheme in which every block is the same fixed size always wastes the tail of the block and never produces holes of varying size, so it has the first and not the second.

Step by step.

  1. Fixed partitions are of one size. A request smaller than the partition wastes the remainder inside the partition — internal fragmentation.
  2. Every free partition is exactly one partition in size, so any request that fits the partition size fits some free partition. No free space is stranded in odd-sized holes — no external fragmentation.
  3. First fit, worst fit and the rest allocate variable-size blocks from variable-size holes, so they can strand space externally.
  4. Pure segmentation allocates variable-size segments, which also strands space externally.

Answer: Option (B) — fixed-size partitions.

Common misconception. Believing that paging-style schemes have neither kind. Paging and fixed partitions have internal fragmentation only; pure segmentation and dynamic contiguous allocation have external fragmentation only; paged segmentation has internal fragmentation and no external fragmentation.

OS-U4-Q53MCQmedium

Four free holes of 100 KB, 500 KB, 300 KB and 600 KB lie in that address order. A request for 250 KB arrives. Which one of the following states correctly which hole first fit and best fit choose?

  1. First fit takes the 500 KB hole; best fit also takes the 500 KB hole.
  2. First fit takes the 500 KB hole; best fit takes the 300 KB hole.
  3. First fit takes the 300 KB hole; best fit also takes the 300 KB hole.
  4. First fit takes the 600 KB hole; best fit takes the 300 KB hole.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. First fit scans the free list in address order and stops at the first hole that is large enough. Best fit scans the whole list and takes the smallest hole that is large enough. Worst fit takes the largest hole.

Step by step.

  1. First fit meets 100 KB (too small) and then 500 KB, which is the first hole that fits 250 KB. It takes 500 KB and leaves a 250 KB remnant.
  2. Best fit compares every hole that fits: 500 KB, 300 KB and 600 KB. The smallest is 300 KB.
  3. Best fit therefore takes the 300 KB hole and leaves a 50 KB remnant.

Answer: Option (B) — first fit takes 500 KB, best fit takes 300 KB.

Common misconception. Thinking first fit and best fit coincide whenever the first hole that fits is also a good fit. Here the first fitting hole is 500 KB while the smallest fitting hole is 300 KB, so the two policies split different holes and leave different remnants (250 KB against 50 KB).

OS-U4-Q54NATmedium

Free holes of 300 KB, 150 KB, 500 KB and 250 KB lie in that address order. Three requests arrive in the order 200 KB, 120 KB and 400 KB. The allocator uses first fit with no compaction. What is the total size of all free memory remaining, in KB, after the three requests have been placed?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 480

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. First fit walks the holes in address order and splits the first hole that is large enough, leaving the remainder in place. The remainders of earlier requests are therefore still candidates for later requests, and the order of the requests changes the outcome.

Step by step.

  1. Request 200 KB: 300 KB is the first hole that fits. It becomes 100 KB. Holes: 100, 150, 500, 250.
  2. Request 120 KB: 100 is too small, 150 fits. It becomes 30 KB. Holes: 100, 30, 500, 250.
  3. Request 400 KB: 100 and 30 are too small, 500 fits. It becomes 100 KB. Holes: 100, 30, 100, 250.
  4. Total free memory = 100 + 30 + 100 + 250 = 480 KB.

Answer: 480 KB.

Common misconception. Subtracting the request sizes from the total and reporting 1200 − 720 = 480 as if it were a check on the allocation. The arithmetic agrees here only because every request was placed; it would not detect a request that failed for want of a large enough hole. Track the holes, not just the totals.

OS-U4-Q55MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about dynamic contiguous allocation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Under the 50-percent rule, if N blocks have been allocated, about N/2 further blocks are expected to be lost to fragmentation.
  2. Next fit restarts its scan at the beginning of the free list on every request.
  3. Worst fit tends to leave behind holes that are too small to be useful.
  4. Compaction removes external fragmentation but costs processor time and requires that every process be able to move at run time.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The four facts that decide these options are the 50-percent rule, the difference between next fit and first fit, the remnant each policy leaves, and the price of compaction.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. The statistical result is that for every N allocated blocks roughly N/2 more blocks are lost to fragmentation, so about a third of memory is unusable. The reason is that the average remnant is half the average request.
  2. (B) False. That describes first fit. Next fit continues the scan from the point where the previous allocation finished, wrapping to the start of the list, so that the search does not always begin at low addresses.
  3. (C) False. Worst fit takes the largest hole, so the remnant it leaves is the largest of the three policies. It is best fit that leaves tiny, unusable remnants.
  4. (D) True. Compaction slides the allocated blocks together, which is a copy of memory and therefore processor time, and it is only possible if addresses can be relocated at run time — which is why base–limit or paging hardware is a precondition.

Answer: Options (A) and (D).

Common misconception. The names invite the error in (C): "worst" suggests the worst outcome. Worst fit is the policy that leaves the best remnants; it is merely wasteful because it never preserves a large hole for a large request.

OS-U4-Q56MCQhard

Free holes of 120 KB, 150 KB and 400 KB lie in that address order. Three requests arrive in the order 260 KB, 140 KB and 150 KB, and no compaction is available. Which allocation policy can satisfy all three requests?

  1. First fit only
  2. Best fit only
  3. Both first fit and best fit
  4. Neither first fit nor best fit
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. No policy dominates. First fit is faster and usually at least as good, but it can consume a large hole that a later request needs while best fit happens to leave that hole untouched. The only way to answer is to simulate both.

Step by step.

  1. First fit. 260 KB: the first hole that fits is 400 KB, which becomes 140 KB. Holes: 120, 150, 140. Next, 140 KB: the first hole that fits is 150 KB, which becomes 10 KB. Holes: 120, 10, 140. Next, 150 KB: no hole is large enough — the request fails.
  2. Best fit. 260 KB: the only hole that fits is 400 KB, which becomes 140 KB. Holes: 120, 150, 140. Next, 140 KB: the smallest fitting hole is the 140 KB remnant, which becomes 0. Holes: 120, 150, 0. Next, 150 KB: the 150 KB hole fits exactly and becomes 0. All three requests are placed.
  3. So the sequence is feasible under best fit and infeasible under first fit.

Answer: Option (B) — best fit only.

Common misconception. Remembering "first fit is generally better than best fit" as a theorem. It is an empirical average over workloads, not a guarantee: the counterexample above shows a request sequence on which first fit fails and best fit succeeds.

OS-U4-Q76MCQeasy

A memory system uses fixed-size partitions, and every process is bound to absolute addresses when it is loaded (static relocation). Why can such a system not compact memory to remove the space wasted between partitions?

  1. Because moving a loaded process would leave every absolute address inside it pointing at the old location, and no run-time hardware exists to adjust them.
  2. Because compaction is needed only in paging systems, where pages move between frames.
  3. Because fixed partitions never waste space, so there is nothing to compact.
  4. Because compaction would have to move the operating system itself, which is never permitted.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Compaction slides the occupied regions of memory together and closes the holes. The copy itself is trivial; what makes compaction possible is that every address a process uses is translated at run time, so a move costs one change of a base register.

Step by step.

  1. Compaction changes the physical location of a process.
  2. Under static relocation the loader has already written absolute addresses into the instructions and data of the process. After a move, every one of those addresses still names the old place.
  3. With dynamic relocation — a base (or relocation) register added to every logical address by the memory unit — the process can be moved anywhere by rewriting one register.
  4. A system with static binding therefore has to refuse compaction and live with the wasted space. Option (C) is false: fixed partitions waste the tail of every partition, and a process can be refused even when the total free space is large enough. Option (D) is false: the operating system can be relocated at boot or protected by the memory unit; it is not the obstacle.

Answer: Option (A) — without run-time relocation, a moved process keeps addressing its old home.

Common misconception. Treating compaction as a copy loop. Copying the bytes is easy; rewriting every address that referred to them is the whole problem, and only translation hardware makes that free.

Takeaway. Compaction needs relocation hardware, not a faster memcpy.

OS-U4-Q77MCQeasy

Under the 50-percent rule for first fit, which one of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. About half of every allocated block is lost to internal fragmentation.
  2. For every two blocks that are allocated, one further hole is expected, so roughly a third of memory is lost to fragmentation.
  3. First fit leaves the largest possible remainder after every allocation, so it is the policy that wastes the least memory.
  4. The number of holes stays constant as processes are allocated and released.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The 50-percent rule is a statistical statement about first fit: when many processes have been allocated and released, the free memory is broken into about half as many holes as there are allocated blocks, and the unusable remainder approaches a third of memory.

Step by step.

  1. Every allocation splits a hole into a used part and a smaller hole; every release merges neighbours back.
  2. Simulation and analysis of first fit give the steady-state result: N allocated blocks come with roughly N/2 holes.
  3. Those holes are individually small, so the memory they hold is largely unusable — the rule of thumb is that about one third of memory is lost this way.
  4. Option (A) confuses this with internal fragmentation, which is the waste inside a fixed partition or a page, not between blocks. Option (C) describes worst fit: first fit takes the first hole that fits, not the largest, and it is precisely because the remainders are arbitrary that the holes accumulate. Option (D) is contradicted by the rule itself, which says the number of holes grows with the number of blocks.

Answer: Option (B) — holes grow as half the number of blocks, and about a third of memory is lost.

Common misconception. Reading the rule as a statement about internal fragmentation, or as a guarantee about the quality of the fit. It is an average over a long run of allocations and releases, not a bound on any single request.

Takeaway. First fit is the fastest of the three policies and pays for that speed in fragmentation, not in speed.

OS-U4-Q78MCQeasy

A first-fit allocator currently holds 400 allocated blocks. Under the 50-percent rule, how many free holes are expected?

  1. 100
  2. 400
  3. 200
  4. 800
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)
