Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The 50-percent rule states that the expected number of holes is half the number of allocated blocks.

Step by step.

  1. Allocated blocks N = 400.
  2. Expected holes = N/2 = 200.
  3. The option 800 would be the result of doubling instead of halving; 100 is a quarter of N; 400 is N itself, which the rule explicitly does not say.

Answer: Option (C) — 200 holes.

Common misconception. Assuming one hole per allocated block. The rule says the count of holes is about half the count of blocks, which is why so much memory ends up in fragments too small to use.

Takeaway. Holes ≈ blocks / 2, and roughly a third of memory becomes unusable.

OS-U4-Q79MCQeasy

Next fit differs from first fit in that the free-list search resumes from the position of the last allocation instead of from the start of the list. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. Next fit scans the whole free list on every request, so it is strictly slower than first fit.
  2. Next fit always leaves less external fragmentation than best fit.
  3. Next fit needs compaction after every allocation, because it never reuses the low holes.
  4. Next fit usually scans less of the free list, but it tends to break up the large holes near the top of memory and so fragments memory more than first fit.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Next fit is first fit with a moving start pointer. It spreads allocations over the whole address range instead of packing them at the bottom, which shortens the average search and worsens the fragmentation.

Step by step.

  1. First fit always begins at the low end, so the low holes are consumed and reused first and the list of holes near the top stays large.
  2. Next fit resumes where it stopped, so consecutive requests walk upward through memory and each tends to split a different large hole.
  3. The average search is shorter — the pointer rarely has to travel the whole list — but the largest holes are broken up sooner, and the worst-case fragmentation is worse than first fit.
  4. Options (A), (B) and (C) misdescribe the policy: it does not scan the whole list, it has no advantage over best fit in fragmentation, and it needs no compaction at all.

Answer: Option (D) — faster search, worse fragmentation.

Common misconception. Assuming that a shorter search implies a better allocation. Search cost and fragmentation quality are separate axes: next fit improves the first and damages the second.

Takeaway. First fit packs low, next fit spreads high, best fit minimises the remainder, worst fit preserves big holes.

OS-U4-Q80NATmedium

Three free partitions of 16 KB, 24 KB and 8 KB are available. Requests of 12 KB, 7 KB and 20 KB arrive in that order, and each is placed by best fit into one whole partition. What is the total internal fragmentation, in KB?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 9

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With fixed-size partitions a request occupies a whole partition, so the internal fragmentation of one placement is partition size − request size. Best fit chooses the smallest partition that is large enough.

Step by step.

  1. Free set {16, 24, 8}; request 12 KB: partitions that fit are 16 and 24; best fit takes 16, wasting 16 − 12 = 4 KB. Free set becomes {24, 8}.
  2. Request 7 KB: partitions that fit are 24 and 8; best fit takes 8, wasting 8 − 7 = 1 KB. Free set becomes {24}.
  3. Request 20 KB: only 24 fits; it takes 24, wasting 24 − 20 = 4 KB. Free set is empty.
  4. Total internal fragmentation = 4 + 1 + 4 = 9 KB.

Answer: 9 KB.

Common misconception. Reporting the unused partition instead of the waste inside used partitions, or allocating the 24 KB partition to the 7 KB request because it is listed first. Best fit is defined by the smallest sufficient partition, not by address order.

Takeaway. Internal fragmentation is paid per placement: sum (partition − request) over the requests that were placed.

OS-U4-Q81MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about compaction in a dynamically partitioned memory are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Compaction removes external fragmentation but cannot remove internal fragmentation.
  2. Compaction requires every process it moves to be relocatable at run time.
  3. A paging system must compact memory after every page fault.
  4. The cost of one compaction grows with the amount of memory that has to be moved.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Compaction is the cure for external fragmentation only: it gathers the free space into one block by sliding the occupied blocks together. It has nothing to say about waste inside a block.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true. After compaction there is one large hole; the unused tail inside a partition or a page is untouched by the move.
  2. (B) is true. A moved process must have all of its addresses adjusted, which is only possible when addresses are translated at run time (base register or paging).
  3. (C) is false. Paging has no external fragmentation to remove: every free frame is usable, so a page fault simply takes any free frame and needs no compaction.
  4. (D) is true. The work is a copy of the occupied regions, so the cost is proportional to the bytes moved — and the system is usually stopped while it happens.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing compaction fixes all fragmentation. It fixes only the fragmentation between blocks; waste inside a block is a property of the block size and survives every move.

Takeaway. Compaction trades processor time for contiguity, and it needs relocation to be legal.

OS-U4-Q82MCQmedium

A long-running first-fit system has a free list of many small holes. An engineer proposes switching to best fit. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. Best fit leaves the smallest possible remainder each time, so it can create even more holes that are too small to be used.
  2. Best fit removes every hole, because it always takes the smallest hole that is large enough.
  3. Best fit and first fit always finish with the same layout, so the change is cosmetic.
  4. Best fit removes external fragmentation and replaces it with internal fragmentation inside the partitions.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Best fit minimises the size of the hole left behind. That sounds like the tightest policy, and it is — for the single request in front of it. Over a long run, minimising each remainder produces a dust of holes that no later request can use.

Step by step.

  1. Best fit scans the whole free list and picks the smallest hole that fits, so the remainder is as small as it can be.
  2. A small remainder is, by definition, unlikely to satisfy any future request; repeated, it accumulates unusable slivers.
  3. Best fit also costs a full scan per request, so it is slower than first fit as well as no better in the long run.
  4. Option (B) is false: a hole is left behind every time, by construction. Option (C) is false: the layouts differ. Option (D) is false: the remainder of a split is still a hole, not internal fragmentation, which belongs to fixed partitions and pages.

Answer: Option (A) — best fit can make external fragmentation worse.

Common misconception. Choosing the policy by the name. Best fit optimises the immediate remainder, not the free-list health; worst fit is the policy that deliberately keeps large holes large.

Takeaway. Greedy tightness per request is not the same as a good long-run layout.

paging-page-table-structures 27
OS-U4-Q08MCQeasy

In a paging system, an entry of a per-process page table normally maps:

  1. a physical frame number to the virtual page that occupies it
  2. a segment number to the base address of that segment
  3. a virtual page number to the physical frame number that holds it
  4. a virtual address to the disk block that holds the page
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each process has its own page table, indexed by virtual page number; the entry at that index holds the frame number where the page currently sits.

Step by step.

  1. The virtual address is split into a page number and an offset.
  2. The page number indexes this process's page table.
  3. The entry read out is the frame number; the offset is copied unchanged into the physical address.

Answer: Option (C)

Common misconception. Thinking the table maps frames back to pages. That is the inverted page table, which is a single system-wide structure indexed by frame number, not the ordinary per-process page table.

OS-U4-Q09MCQeasy

A machine has a 32-bit logical address and a page size of 4 KB. How many pages can a single process address?

  1. 2²⁰
  2. 2¹²
  3. 2¹⁰
  4. 2³²
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The page size fixes the number of offset bits; the remaining bits of the logical address are the page number.

Step by step.

  1. 4 KB = 2¹² bytes, so the offset needs 12 bits.
  2. The page number therefore has 32 − 12 = 20 bits.
  3. The number of distinct pages is 2²⁰ = 1 048 576.

Answer: Option (A)

Common misconception. Reporting 2¹², which is the number of bytes in a page, or 2³², which is the number of bytes addressable, not the number of pages.

OS-U4-Q10MCQmedium

A TLB is searched in 10 ns, a main-memory access costs 100 ns, and the system uses a single-level page table. The TLB hit ratio is 0.9. What is the effective memory access time?

  1. 110 ns
  2. 120 ns
  3. 130 ns
  4. 210 ns
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With a single-level page table a TLB hit costs one memory access, while a TLB miss costs two: one to read the page-table entry and one to read the data.

Step by step.

  1. Hit: 10 + 100 = 110 ns, and this happens 90% of the time.
  2. Miss: 10 + 100 + 100 = 210 ns, and this happens 10% of the time.
  3. EAT = 0.9 × 110 + 0.1 × 210 = 99 + 21 = 120 ns.

Answer: Option (B)

Common misconception. Charging a miss only one memory access (the data access) and forgetting the page-table read, which gives 0.9 × 110 + 0.1 × 110 = 110 ns.

OS-U4-Q11MCQhard

A system uses a two-level page table, a TLB search of 1 ns and a main-memory access of 100 ns. The measured effective memory access time is 141 ns. What is the TLB hit ratio?

  1. 0.70
  2. 0.75
  3. 0.80
  4. 0.90
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A two-level page table needs two page-table memory reads on a TLB miss, plus the data access; a TLB hit needs only the data access.

Step by step.

  1. Hit: 1 + 100 = 101 ns.
  2. Miss: 1 + 100 + 100 + 100 = 301 ns.
  3. EAT = 101h + 301(1 − h) = 301 − 200h.
  4. Setting 301 − 200h = 141 gives 200h = 160, so h = 0.8.

Answer: Option (C)

Common misconception. Using the single-level miss cost of 201 ns, which gives h = 0.6, a value not even among the options. Count one memory read per level of the page table.

OS-U4-Q12MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about paging and the TLB are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A larger page size makes the page table smaller but increases internal fragmentation.
  2. Two processes can share one physical frame by mapping different virtual pages to it.
  3. Every TLB miss causes a page fault.
  4. The page table is kept in main memory, and the TLB caches recently used entries of it.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Page size trades table size against internal fragmentation; the TLB is only a cache of page-table entries, not a record of which pages are resident.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: fewer, larger pages mean fewer page-table entries, but the unused tail of the last page is larger on average.
  2. (B) is true: give both processes a page-table entry pointing at the same frame, and the code or data is physically shared.
  3. (C) is false: a miss means only that the mapping is not cached; the page-table entry may be present and valid, and the walk succeeds.
  4. (D) is true: the page table lives in memory and the TLB holds a small number of its entries.

Answer: Options (A), (B), (D)

Common misconception. Confusing a TLB miss with a page fault. A page fault means the valid bit is clear and the page must be brought in from secondary storage.

OS-U4-Q13NATeasy

A system uses pages of 8 KB and a 32-bit logical address. How many bits of the logical address specify the page number?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 19

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Logical address = page number bits followed by offset bits, and the offset must be able to address every byte inside one page.

Step by step.

  1. 8 KB = 8 × 1024 = 8192 = 2¹³ bytes, so the offset takes 13 bits.
  2. The page-number field takes the rest: 32 − 13 = 19 bits.

Answer: 19

Common misconception. Answering 13, the offset width, or 8, the power of two in "8 KB". The question asks for the page-number field.

OS-U4-S2-Q07MCQeasy

A machine has 48-bit virtual addresses and 8 KB pages. How many entries does a single-level page table for one process have?

  1. 2³⁵
  2. 2³⁶
  3. 2¹³
  4. 2⁴⁸
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A single-level page table has one entry per virtual page, so the entry count is the size of the address space divided by the page size, i.e. 2(address bits − offset bits).

Step by step.

  1. 8 KB = 2³ × 2¹⁰ = 2¹³ bytes, so the offset field is 13 bits.
  2. The page number field is therefore 48 − 13 = 35 bits.
  3. That gives 2³⁵ distinct virtual pages, and hence 2³⁵ page-table entries.

Option (A)

Common misconception. Answering 2⁴⁸, the number of addressable bytes, or 2¹³, the number of bytes in a page. The table is indexed by page, not by byte.

OS-U4-S2-Q08NATeasy

A machine has 40-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages. How many bits does the page-number field of the virtual address contain?

Show answer & solution

Answer: Answer: 28

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The virtual address is split into a page number and an offset, and the offset must be able to name every byte inside one page.

Step by step.

  1. 4 KB = 2¹² bytes, so the offset needs 12 bits.
  2. The page number takes the remaining bits: 40 − 12 = 28.

Answer: 28

Common misconception. Reporting 12, which is the offset width, or 40, which is the whole address. The question asks for the page-number field only.

OS-U4-S2-Q09MCQeasy

A process has a virtual address space of 2 GB and the system uses 4 KB pages. Assuming the whole space is mapped, how many page-table entries does the process need?

  1. 2¹⁸ = 262144
  2. 2²¹ = 2097152
  3. 2³¹ = 2147483648
  4. 2¹⁹ = 524288
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. One page-table entry covers exactly one page, so the entry count is the address-space size divided by the page size.

Step by step.

  1. 2 GB = 2 × 2³⁰ = 2³¹ bytes.
  2. 4 KB = 2¹² bytes.
  3. Entries = 2³¹ ÷ 2¹² = 2¹⁹ = 524 288.

Option (D)

Common misconception. Dividing by 1024 twice instead of by 2¹² once, or answering the number of bytes in the address space. 2³¹ counts bytes, not pages.

OS-U4-S2-Q10NATmedium

A TLB access takes 5 ns and a main-memory access takes 100 ns. The system uses a single-level page table. The measured effective access time is 125 ns. What is the TLB hit ratio, in percent?

Show answer & solution

Answer: Answer: 80

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With one level of paging a TLB hit costs the TLB probe plus the data access; a TLB miss costs the probe, the page-table read and then the data access.

Step by step.

  1. Hit path: 5 + 100 = 105 ns.
  2. Miss path: 5 + 100 + 100 = 205 ns.
  3. EAT = 105h + 205(1 − h) = 205 − 100h.
  4. Setting 205 − 100h = 125 gives 100h = 80, so h = 0.80, that is 80%.

Answer: 80

Common misconception. Charging a miss only one memory access (105 ns on both paths), which forces an EAT of 105 ns and makes the given 125 ns impossible. A miss reads the page-table entry and the data.

OS-U4-S2-Q11MCQmedium

A 32-bit virtual address is split for two-level paging into a 10-bit outer index, a 10-bit inner index and a 12-bit offset. How many entries does each second-level page table hold?

  1. 1024
  2. 4096
  3. 256
  4. 2²⁰ = 1048576
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each level is indexed by its own field, so the number of entries in a level is 2 raised to that field's width.

Step by step.

  1. The outer index is 10 bits, so the outer page table has 2¹⁰ = 1024 entries, each pointing at one second-level table.
  2. The inner index is also 10 bits, so each second-level table has 2¹⁰ = 1024 entries.
  3. The 12-bit offset then selects a byte inside the 4 KB page. Check: 10 + 10 + 12 = 32 bits.

Option (A)

Common misconception. Answering 4096, the page size in bytes, or 2²⁰, the total number of pages. Each level is sized by its own index field, not by the address space.

OS-U4-S2-Q12MSQhard

Which of the following statements about page-table structures are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. An inverted page table grows with the size of the virtual address space.
  2. A multi-level page table can avoid allocating table pages for unused regions of the address space.
  3. With single-level paging the table is an array indexed by page number, so it must occupy contiguous physical memory.
  4. With 4 KB pages a 32-bit logical address splits into a 20-bit page number and a 12-bit offset.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (B), (C), (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The shape of a page table is dictated by what indexes it. A single-level table is indexed by page number; a multi-level table adds an index over table pages; an inverted table is indexed by frame.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is false: an inverted table has one entry per frame, so it grows with physical memory, not with the virtual address space.
  2. (B) is true: only the second-level tables that are actually referenced need to exist, so sparse address spaces cost little.
  3. (C) is true: entry i sits at a fixed offset from the base, which requires the array to be contiguous.
  4. (D) is true: 4 KB = 2¹², so the offset is 12 bits and 32 − 12 = 20 bits remain for the page number.

Options (B), (C) and (D)

Common misconception. Believing multi-level paging saves memory always. It costs more memory for a fully used address space (extra levels to walk) and saves memory only when the space is sparse.

OS-U4-S2-Q13MCQmedium

A 32-bit address space is paged with 4 KB pages and a two-level scheme whose outer index is 10 bits. Each page-table entry is 4 bytes. How much memory does the outer page table occupy?

  1. 1 MB
  2. 4 KB
  3. 8 KB
  4. 2 MB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The outer page table has one entry per value of the outer index, and every entry is one page-table entry wide.

Step by step.

  1. Outer index = 10 bits, so the table has 2¹⁰ = 1024 entries.
  2. 1024 × 4 bytes = 4096 bytes = 4 KB.

Option (B)

Common misconception. Sizing the table from the whole 32-bit address space (2³² × 4 bytes) instead of from the outer index. Each level is sized only by its own field.

OS-U4-Q57MCQeasy

A system uses single-level paging with the page table held in main memory and has no TLB. How many main-memory accesses does one ordinary load or store take?

  1. Two: one to read the page-table entry and one to reach the data
  2. One: the page table is consulted by dedicated hardware that does not touch memory
  3. Three: the page table, a segment table and then the data
  4. One extra access for every level of the page table, and none for the data
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With the page table in memory, the page number must be translated into a frame number before the data can be addressed, and that translation is itself a memory read.

Step by step.

  1. The CPU forms a virtual address; its page number indexes the page table.
  2. Access 1: read the page-table entry at PTBR + page × entry size. This yields the frame number and the valid and protection bits.
  3. Access 2: form frame × page size + offset and read or write the data.
  4. So a reference costs two memory accesses, which is why the effective access time roughly doubles and why a TLB is worth its cost.

Answer: Option (A) — two accesses.

Common misconception. Assuming the page table lives in fast registers or in a cache the hardware consults for free. Only the page-table base register is a register; the table itself is in memory, and with two levels of paging a reference without a TLB costs three accesses.

OS-U4-Q58MCQeasy

A TLB has 128 entries and the page size is 8 KB. Assuming perfect replacement, what is the TLB reach — the amount of memory that can be mapped without a page-table walk?

  1. 128 KB
  2. 512 KB
  3. 1 MB
  4. 8 MB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The TLB reach is the number of TLB entries multiplied by the page size: it is the working set that the TLB can cover at once.

Step by step.

  1. Entries = 128 = 2⁷.
  2. Page size = 8 KB = 2¹³ bytes.
  3. Reach = 2⁷ × 2¹³ = 2²⁰ = 1 MB.
  4. The practical consequence: with 8 KB pages, 128 entries cover 1 MB, so a program whose hot working set exceeds 1 MB will thrash the TLB unless the page size or the number of entries is increased.

Answer: Option (C) — 1 MB.

Common misconception. Multiplying by the frame number width or by the entry size. The reach counts bytes of address space covered, so it is entries × page size; entry size affects the cost of the TLB, not its coverage.

OS-U4-Q59MCQeasy

A single-level page table has 2¹⁹ entries and each entry is 8 bytes wide. How much main memory does the table itself occupy?

  1. 2 MB
  2. 4 MB
  3. 8 MB
  4. 512 KB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A page table is an array: its size is the number of entries times the width of one entry. The entries are needed for the whole virtual page range of the process, whether or not the pages are in use.

Step by step.

  1. Entries = 2¹⁹ = 524288.
  2. Size = 2¹⁹ × 8 = 2¹⁹ × 2³ = 2²² = 4194304 bytes.
  3. 2²² bytes = 4 MB.
  4. This is exactly the pressure that motivates two-level and inverted tables: a 4 MB array per process, most of it empty, is wasteful when the process touches a few megabytes.

Answer: Option (B) — 4 MB.

Common misconception. Confusing the number of entries with the number of bytes, or using 2¹⁹ entries as if it were 2²⁰. Keep the two powers of two separate: the entry count and the entry width multiply.

OS-U4-Q60NATmedium

A TLB search costs 20 ns and a main-memory access costs 100 ns. The system uses a single-level page table in memory. The effective access time is 20 + 100 + (1 − h) × 100 ns, where h is the TLB hit ratio. What is the smallest hit ratio, in per cent, that keeps the effective access time at or below 130 ns?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 90

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Every reference pays the TLB search and the data access. A hit adds nothing more; a miss adds one extra memory access for the page-table entry.

Step by step.

  1. Hit path: 20 + 100 = 120 ns.
  2. Miss path: 20 + 100 + 100 = 220 ns.
  3. Expected time: h × 120 + (1 − h) × 220 = 220 − 100h, which is the same as 120 + 100(1 − h).
  4. Require 120 + 100(1 − h) ≤ 130, so 100(1 − h) ≤ 10 and 1 − h ≤ 0.1.
  5. Hence h ≥ 0.9, that is 90 per cent. At exactly 90 per cent the effective time is 130 ns, which meets the bound.

Answer: 90 (per cent).

Common misconception. Charging the TLB search only on a hit. The TLB is looked up on every reference, so its 20 ns is paid unconditionally; only the extra 100 ns is probabilistic.

OS-U4-Q61MCQmedium

On a machine with 64-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages, a single-level page table would need 2⁵² entries. The main reason two-level paging helps is that it:

  1. halves the width of each page-table entry
  2. reduces the number of page faults
  3. lets the system allocate page tables only for the parts of the address space a process actually uses
  4. removes the need for a TLB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A single-level table must be contiguous and must cover the whole virtual range, so its size is set by the address width, not by what the process touches. Splitting the page number into an outer and an inner index lets the outer table point at inner tables that are created only when the corresponding region is used.

Step by step.

  1. Single level: one array of 2⁵² entries — petabytes of table for a process that may touch a few megabytes.
  2. Two levels: an outer table of 2²⁹ entries (for an 18/18/12 split) whose entries point at inner tables of 2¹⁸ entries each. An inner table exists only if some page in that region is mapped.
  3. Total table memory therefore grows with the used address space, which is the saving.
  4. The costs are an extra memory access per miss and a worse locality pattern; the entry width and the page-fault rate are unchanged.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Believing a multi-level table is smaller per entry or cheaper per reference. It is neither — it is exactly the opposite per reference. The gain is purely that unused regions cost nothing.

OS-U4-Q62MSQhard

Which of the following statements about the choice of page size are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Increasing the page size reduces the number of page-table entries and increases the TLB reach.
  2. Increasing the page size increases internal fragmentation, because the last page of an object is partly unused.
  3. Increasing the page size increases the number of page faults for a program that scans memory sequentially.
  4. Decreasing the page size reduces the number of bytes transferred per page fault but increases the size of the page tables.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Page size trades three quantities against one another: table size, TLB coverage and internal fragmentation, with fault granularity riding on the same choice.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Doubling the page size removes one bit from the page number, so the number of entries halves; the TLB reach, entries × page size, grows.
  2. (B) True. Allocation is in whole pages, so on average half a page is wasted per object. A larger page wastes more per object.
  3. (C) False. Sequential scanning touches every byte, so the number of pages covered — and hence the number of faults — falls as the page size grows. Larger pages mean fewer, larger transfers.
  4. (D) True. Smaller pages mean more pages, hence more entries, hence larger tables and a smaller TLB reach; the benefit is that each fault brings in less data and internal fragmentation falls.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Reading (C) as "larger pages cause more faults" because each fault costs more. The number of faults falls with larger pages; what rises is the bytes moved per fault and the internal fragmentation.

OS-U4-Q63NAThard

A machine has 48-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages. Paging is two-level, with the page number split into an 18-bit outer index and an 18-bit inner index, and each page-table entry is 8 bytes. What is the size of one second-level page table, in KB?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 2048

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A second-level table is indexed by the inner index, so it has 2¹⁸ entries, each of the stated width. Its size is the product, whatever the outer table does.

Step by step.

  1. Check the split: 4 KB pages give log₂4096 = 12 offset bits; 18 + 18 + 12 = 48, so the whole address is accounted for.
  2. Entries in a second-level table = 2¹⁸ = 262144.
  3. Size = 262144 × 8 = 2097152 bytes = 2 MB.
  4. 2 MB = 2048 KB.

Answer: 2048 KB (2 MB).

Common misconception. Using all 36 index bits for one table. Each level is indexed by its own field only; using 36 bits gives 2³⁶ entries, a table 262144 times too large.

OS-U4-Q83MCQeasy

A page-table entry carries a valid bit and a present bit. What does a cleared valid bit mean?

  1. The page is currently on disk and will be brought in by a page fault.
  2. The virtual page is not part of this process's address space, so the reference is a trap rather than a fault to be serviced.
  3. The frame holding the page has been freed by the replacement policy.
  4. The TLB entry for the page has been flushed and must be reloaded.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The two bits answer two different questions. The valid bit says whether the page number is legal for this process at all; the present bit says whether a legal page is currently in a frame.

Step by step.

  1. A process's page table may be sized for the whole address space while only part of it is used. Entries for the unused part are marked invalid.
  2. A reference to an invalid entry is a programming error — a segmentation-type trap — because the address was never part of the process.
  3. A reference to a valid but not-present entry is the ordinary case in demand paging: the operating system fetches the page from disk and restarts the instruction.
  4. Option (A) therefore describes the present bit, not the valid bit. Options (C) and (D) describe cache and TLB bookkeeping, neither of which is what the valid bit records.

Answer: Option (B) — invalid means the address is not the process's to use.

Common misconception. Treating invalid and not-present as the same condition. One is an error to be reported to the process; the other is a normal event that the operating system fixes silently.

Takeaway. Valid = may this process use the page; present = is it in memory right now.

OS-U4-Q84MCQeasy

A system uses three-level paging with no TLB. How many main-memory accesses does one load instruction need, counting the access that fetches the operand?

  1. 2
  2. 3
  3. 4
  4. 5
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Without a TLB every level of the page table is itself in memory, so each level costs one access before the data can be reached.

Step by step.

  1. Access 1 reads the outermost page-table page and yields the base of the next-level table.
  2. Access 2 reads the middle-level table and yields the base of the innermost table.
  3. Access 3 reads the innermost table and yields the frame number.
  4. Access 4 reads the operand itself.
  5. Total 3 + 1 = 4 main-memory accesses, so the effective access time is four times one memory cycle — which is exactly why a TLB exists.

Answer: Option (C) — 4 accesses.

Common misconception. Counting the table levels only and forgetting the data access, or counting the fetch of the instruction separately. The question asks for one load, so the instruction fetch is not part of it.

Takeaway. Levels + 1 accesses per reference without a TLB.

OS-U4-Q85NATmedium

In a two-level paging scheme the page size is 4 KB and each page-table entry is 4 bytes wide. Each second-level page table is exactly one page long. How many entries does one second-level page table hold?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 1024

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The size of a page table is chosen so that it occupies a whole number of pages; the number of entries then follows from the page size and the entry width.

Step by step.

  1. One second-level table fills one page: 4096 bytes.
  2. Each entry is 4 bytes, so the table holds 4096 / 4 = 1024 entries.
  3. Equivalently, the second-level index is log₂1024 = 10 bits wide, which is the familiar 10-10-12 split of a 32-bit address with 4 KB pages.
  4. The answer is exact: 1024 entries of 4 bytes are 4096 bytes, with no slack.

Answer: 1024 entries.

Common misconception. Dividing by the page size instead of the entry size, or assuming an entry is 8 bytes. The entry width is what converts bytes into entries.

Takeaway. Entries per table page = page size / entry size, and that number sets the index width.

OS-U4-Q86MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about multi-level page tables are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A two-level page table always occupies less memory than a single-level table, whatever the process's access pattern.
  2. The saving comes from leaving second-level tables unallocated for the regions of the address space the process never touches.
  3. Every level that a reference has to walk adds one main-memory access when the TLB misses.
  4. The number of index bits at a level follows from how many entries fit into one table page.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Multi-level paging is a sparse structure: the outer table has one entry per second-level table, and a second-level table exists only if some page in its range is mapped.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is false. A process that touches every page needs every second-level table, and the outer table is extra on top — the multi-level scheme can then cost more than a single-level one.
  2. (B) is true and is the whole point: a process using a few megabytes of a 64-bit space maps a handful of second-level tables and leaves the rest of the outer table empty.
  3. (C) is true: each level is a memory access on a TLB miss, so a three-level table costs four accesses per reference (three walks plus the data).
  4. (D) is true: a table page holds page size / entry size entries, so the index at that level is exactly that many bits wide.

Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming more levels always means less memory. The saving is a property of sparsity, not of depth; a dense address space pays for every level.

Takeaway. Multi-level tables buy memory with accesses, and only where the address space is sparse.

OS-U4-Q87MCQhard

Why must a TLB normally be flushed on a context switch, and what does an address-space identifier (ASID) change?

  1. Because TLB entries hold physical addresses that change when the new process is scheduled; an ASID lets the old physical addresses stay valid.
  2. Because the TLB is smaller than the page table; an ASID enlarges it for the new process.
  3. Because the page-table base register is reloaded; an ASID removes the need for that register.
  4. Because a TLB entry names a virtual page that is only meaningful inside one address space, so entries of the old process must not be used; an ASID tags each entry with its address space, so entries belonging to other processes can stay.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A TLB maps virtual page numbers to frames, and the same virtual page number means different things in different processes. Entries are therefore only valid together with the address space that created them.

Step by step.

  1. Process P is switched out and Q runs. If Q references virtual page 5, a stale entry left by P would translate it to P's frame 5 — a silent read of another process's memory.
  2. The simple fix is to invalidate the whole TLB on every switch, which is correct but throws away useful translations and costs a burst of misses.
  3. An ASID is a small tag, written into each entry, that names the address space the entry belongs to. A lookup compares the tag as well as the page number, so entries of other processes simply never match.
  4. With tags, the TLB need only be flushed when an ASID is reused, so the entries of a returning process can still be there. Option (A) is wrong because entries cache translations, not physical addresses that change with scheduling; (C) is wrong because the base register is still reloaded — the ASID only replaces the flush.

Answer: Option (D) — the tag replaces the flush.

Common misconception. Thinking an ASID removes the need to reload the page-table base. Both are still needed: the base locates the table, the ASID says which address space a cached translation belongs to.

Takeaway. Flush or tag: either way, a translation must never be used outside the address space that produced it.

OS-U4-Q88NAThard

A TLB search costs 10 ns and a main-memory access costs 100 ns. Paging is two-level, the TLB is searched first, and a hit still needs one memory access for the data. The hit ratio is 0.96. What is the effective access time, in ns?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 118

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The effective access time is the probability-weighted mean of the two paths. A hit costs the TLB search plus the data access; a miss costs the TLB search plus one memory access per page-table level plus the data access.

Step by step.

  1. Hit path: 10 + 100 = 110 ns.
  2. Miss path: 10 ns for the TLB search, 100 ns for the outer table, 100 ns for the inner table, 100 ns for the data = 310 ns.
  3. Weighted mean: 0.96 × 110 + 0.04 × 310 = 105.6 + 12.4 = 118 ns.
  4. Check the arithmetic the other way: 110 + 0.04 × (310 − 110) = 110 + 8 = 118 ns, which is the same figure.

Answer: 118 ns.

Common misconception. Charging two memory accesses on a miss, as if paging were single-level, or omitting the TLB search from the hit path. With two levels a miss is three memory accesses plus the search; a hit is one access plus the search.

Takeaway. Write the two paths out in full, then weight them; the levels decide the miss path, the hit ratio only sets the weights.

OS-U4-Q89MSQeasy

Which of the following statements about the page-table base register and the page-table length register are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. The page-table base register holds the physical address of the current process's page table.
  2. The page-table base register holds the virtual address of the page table, which is then translated like any other page.
  3. The page-table length register bounds the page number, so a page number beyond the table traps instead of reading unrelated memory.
  4. Both registers are reloaded as part of a context switch.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The page table is located by a physical address held in a register, because the table cannot be translated through itself. A length register closes the other half of the problem: a page number larger than the table must be rejected, not used as an offset.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: the memory unit uses the base register directly, adding the page number times the entry size, with no translation of that address.
  2. (B) is false: a virtual address for the table would have to be translated, which requires the table — a circular dependency.
  3. (C) is true: without a bound, a bogus page number would index past the end of the table into whatever follows it in memory.
  4. (D) is true: the table belongs to a process, so both registers change with the process.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming the page table is reached through the virtual memory system like any other object. The root of the translation structure must be a physical address, or the machine would need a translation to find the translator.

Takeaway. Base register locates the table physically; length register stops the index at its end.

inverted-page-tables 24
OS-U4-Q14MCQeasy

An inverted page table contains exactly one entry per:

  1. virtual page of every running process
  2. segment of every process
  3. process in the system
  4. physical frame of main memory
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The inverted page table is indexed by frame number, so it has one entry for each frame of physical memory, whatever the number of processes or the size of the virtual address space.

Step by step.

  1. Index = physical frame number.
  2. Entry = the (process id, virtual page number) currently held in that frame.
  3. Number of entries = number of frames = physical memory size ÷ page size.

Answer: Option (D)

Common misconception. Expecting one entry per virtual page. That is the ordinary per-process page table, whose size grows with the virtual address space.

OS-U4-Q15MCQeasy

The main advantage of an inverted page table is that:

  1. it removes the need for a TLB
  2. its size depends on the size of physical memory, not on the size of the virtual address space
  3. it makes page sharing between processes automatic
  4. it stores the replacement policy in the TLB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A per-process page table can be enormous when the virtual address space is sparse; an inverted table is one array with one slot per frame.

Step by step.

  1. With 2ⁿ frames the table has 2ⁿ entries, independent of how large each process's address space is.
  2. So the memory spent on translation is bounded by physical memory, not by the virtual size.

Answer: Option (B)

Common misconception. Believing the TLB becomes unnecessary. Translation on an inverted table is a search, so a TLB is more important there, not less.

OS-U4-Q16MCQmedium

The main cost of an inverted page table is that:

  1. each page entry must be duplicated for every process
  2. page faults can no longer be detected
  3. a TLB miss requires searching the table for the entry whose (process id, virtual page) pair matches
  4. every byte read needs one extra memory access
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The inverted table is keyed by frame, but translation needs the reverse direction: given (pid, page) find the frame. That is a search, usually over a hash table.

Step by step.

  1. A TLB hit is unaffected: the frame number comes straight from the TLB.
  2. On a miss the hardware must locate the entry that records this process and this virtual page.
  3. With linear search that costs time proportional to the number of frames; a hash table on (pid, page) reduces it to a few probes, at the cost of handling collisions.

Answer: Option (C)

Common misconception. Thinking the table stores the frame directly at the index of the virtual page. It cannot: the index is the frame, and the virtual page is stored inside the entry.

OS-U4-Q17MCQhard

A machine has 1 GB of physical memory, a page size of 4 KB and an inverted page table with 8-byte entries. What is the total size of the inverted page table?

  1. 2 MB
  2. 4 MB
  3. 8 MB
  4. 512 KB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Table size = (physical memory ÷ page size) × entry size, because there is one entry per frame.

Step by step.

  1. 1 GB ÷ 4 KB = 2³⁰ ÷ 2¹² = 2¹⁸ = 262 144 frames.
  2. 262 144 × 8 bytes = 2 097 152 bytes.
  3. 2 097 152 bytes = 2 MB.

Answer: Option (A)

Common misconception. Multiplying by the virtual address space, or forgetting that the entry count follows frames. A 64-bit virtual space would not change this answer at all.

OS-U4-Q18MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about inverted page tables are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. An inverted page table needs one entry per physical frame, so its size is fixed by the amount of physical memory.
  2. Sharing a frame between two processes is awkward, because a frame records only one (process, page) pair.
  3. A linear search of the table on a TLB miss costs time proportional to the number of frames in the worst case.
  4. An inverted page table removes the need for a TLB, because the table is small.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. One slot per frame saves memory but makes translation a search, and a frame belongs to exactly one recorded (process, page) pair.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: frames determine the entry count.
  2. (B) is true: a shared frame can only record one owner, so sharing needs extra machinery such as a separate alias record or a chain of sharers.
  3. (C) is true for a linear scan; hashing reduces the expected cost but not the worst case.
  4. (D) is false: the search cost makes a TLB essential to acceptable performance.

Answer: Options (A), (B), (C)

Common misconception. Assuming a small table means fast translation. Size and lookup cost are separate properties, and here the small table is the slow one.

OS-U4-Q19NATmedium

A machine has 64 MB of physical memory and pages of 4 KB. Its inverted page table has one 8-byte entry per frame. What is the size of the table, in KB?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 128

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Frames = physical memory ÷ page size; table size = frames × entry size.

Step by step.

  1. 64 MB = 2²⁶ bytes and 4 KB = 2¹² bytes, so there are 2¹⁴ = 16 384 frames.
  2. 16 384 × 8 = 131 072 bytes.
  3. 131 072 ÷ 1024 = 128 KB.

Answer: 128

Common misconception. Dividing by 1024 twice, or multiplying the number of pages of one process by the entry size instead of the number of frames.

OS-U4-S2-Q14MCQeasy

Physical memory is 4 GB and the page size is 8 KB. How many entries does an inverted page table have?

  1. 2¹³ = 8192
  2. 2¹⁹ = 524288
  3. 2³²
  4. 2²⁹
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An inverted page table is indexed by frame number, so it has exactly one entry per frame of physical memory, whatever the number of processes.

Step by step.

  1. 4 GB = 2³² bytes.
  2. 8 KB = 2¹³ bytes per frame.
  3. Frames = 2³² ÷ 2¹³ = 2¹⁹ = 524 288, so the table has 2¹⁹ entries.

Option (B)

Common misconception. Multiplying by the number of processes. That is the cost of ordinary per-process page tables; the inverted table is a single system-wide array sized by physical memory.

OS-U4-S2-Q15MCQeasy

An entry of an inverted page table records which of the following?

  1. the frame number that holds a given virtual page
  2. the virtual page number and the process identifier whose page currently occupies this frame
  3. the physical address of the next page-table page
  4. the segment base and limit of the process
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The table is indexed by frame, so the frame number is implicit in the position of the entry; what the entry must store is the owner of that frame.

Step by step.

  1. Index = frame number.
  2. Entry = (process id, virtual page number) of the page currently resident in that frame.
  3. Translation therefore runs backwards: given (pid, page) the hardware must find the frame.

Option (B)

Common misconception. Choosing (A), which describes an ordinary page table. An inverted table cannot store the frame at an index given by the virtual page number, because the index is the frame.

OS-U4-S2-Q16MCQmedium

A system uses one inverted page table keyed by frame number, plus a hash table on (pid, page). Which statement about a TLB miss is TRUE?

  1. The frame number follows directly from the virtual page number, so no search is needed.
  2. The entry must be located by a search, because the table is indexed by frame while translation needs the reverse direction.
  3. A TLB becomes unnecessary because the inverted table is small.
  4. Each process keeps its own inverted page table, so the lookup is per-process.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Translation asks "which frame holds (pid, page)?"; an inverted table answers "which (pid, page) is in this frame?". The direction is reversed, so a lookup cannot be an index.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is wrong: the virtual page number is not the index of an inverted table.
  2. (B) is right: the hash table on (pid, page) is what makes the reversed lookup fast, and without it the hardware would have to scan every entry.
  3. (C) is wrong: the table is small but slow to search, which makes a TLB more valuable, not less.
  4. (D) is wrong: the whole point is one shared table, one entry per frame.

Option (B)

Common misconception. Concluding that a small table means cheap translation. Size and lookup cost are independent: the inverted table is the small one and the slow one.

OS-U4-S2-Q17MSQmedium

An operating system replaces the per-process page tables of every running process with one inverted page table. Which statements about the resulting system are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. The table has exactly one entry per physical frame.
  2. It removes the need for a TLB.
  3. Its size is independent of the number of processes and of the size of each virtual address space.
  4. Each process keeps its own inverted page table.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The inverted table is a single array with one slot per frame, so its size is fixed by physical memory alone.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true by construction: the index is the frame number.
  2. (B) is false: translation becomes a search, which is exactly why a TLB is needed.
  3. (C) is true: adding processes or enlarging virtual address spaces does not add frames.
  4. (D) is false: one table is shared by all processes, which is the source of both its small size and its sharing problem.

Options (A) and (C)

Common misconception. Assuming the table must grow with the address space, as ordinary page tables do. Its independence from the virtual address space is the whole reason it exists.

OS-U4-S2-Q18MCQhard

A system has 256 MB of physical memory, 4 KB pages and an inverted page table whose entries are 16 bytes each. How much memory does the table occupy?

  1. 1 MB
  2. 2 MB
  3. 512 KB
  4. 4 MB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Table size = number of frames × entry size, and the frame count is physical memory divided by page size.

Step by step.

  1. 256 MB = 2²⁸ bytes, and 4 KB = 2¹² bytes, so there are 2²⁸ ÷ 2¹² = 2¹⁶ = 65 536 frames.
  2. 65 536 × 16 bytes = 1 048 576 bytes = 1 MB.

Option (A)

Common misconception. Sizing the table from a 64-bit virtual address space, which would be astronomically larger. The inverted table knows nothing about virtual addresses.

OS-U4-S2-Q19MSQeasy

Which of the following statements about an inverted page table are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Its size depends on physical memory rather than on the virtual address space.
  2. One table is shared by all processes.
  3. Translation on a TLB miss requires a search or a hash lookup.
  4. It eliminates the page-table walk on a TLB miss.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B), (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Three properties follow directly from the index being the frame number: the size, the sharing and the need to search.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: one entry per frame, so physical memory fixes the size.
  2. (B) is true: a single system-wide table describes every frame.
  3. (C) is true: given (pid, page) the hardware must find the matching entry, which a hash table makes fast but does not make free.
  4. (D) is false: it adds work on a miss, since the entry must be searched for rather than indexed.

Options (A), (B) and (C)

Common misconception. Reading "small table" as "fast translation". The inverted table trades size for lookup cost.

OS-U4-Q64MCQeasy

Which one of the following is a direct consequence of keying an inverted page table by frame rather than by virtual page?

  1. The table has one entry per physical frame, so its size is fixed by physical memory and not by the size of any address space.
  2. The table has one entry per virtual page of each process, so its size grows with the number of processes.
  3. The table has one entry per segment, so its size grows with the segment count.
  4. The table has one entry per page-table entry of each process, so it is the same size as the sum of all per-process tables.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An inverted page table stores exactly one entry for each physical frame. The frame number is the index, and the entry records which process and which virtual page currently occupy that frame.

Step by step.

  1. The number of frames is physical memory ÷ page size, a property of the machine.
  2. So the table size is one system-wide array of that many entries — no per-process tables at all.
  3. The saving is large: 64-bit address spaces can be supported with a table of a few million entries instead of 2⁵² entries per process.
  4. The cost is that the table is no longer indexed by what the hardware supplies (the page number), so a lookup needs a search or a hash.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Assuming the table is per process. There is exactly one inverted table for the whole system, which is why an entry must carry a process identifier.

OS-U4-Q65MCQeasy

Which field must an inverted page-table entry contain that a per-process page table does not need?

  1. A frame number
  2. A valid bit
  3. A reference bit
  4. A process identifier
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. In a per-process page table the owner of the table is implicit: the table belongs to one process, so the page number alone identifies the mapping. A single system-wide inverted table holds mappings of every process, and page 5 of one process has nothing to do with page 5 of another.

Step by step.

  1. The index of an inverted entry is the frame number, so the frame number itself need not be stored as a lookup key — that rules out (A).
  2. Valid and reference bits are ordinary control bits that per-process tables carry as well — that rules out (B) and (C).
  3. What is genuinely new is ownership: the entry must say whose page this frame holds, otherwise two processes mapping the same virtual page number would be indistinguishable.
  4. Hence the entry is a triple (pid, page, control bits) for each frame.

Answer: Option (D) — a process identifier (or address-space identifier).

Common misconception. Thinking the frame number must be stored because the table is "about frames". The frame number is the array index; storing it would duplicate the index.

OS-U4-Q66NATeasy

A machine has 512 MB of physical memory and 4 KB pages. Its inverted page table has one 8-byte entry per frame. What is the size of the table, in KB?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 1024

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The number of inverted entries equals the number of frames, and each entry costs its stated width.

Step by step.

  1. Frames = 512 MB ÷ 4 KB = 2²⁹ ÷ 2¹² = 2¹⁷ = 131072.
  2. Table size = 131072 × 8 = 1048576 bytes.
  3. 1048576 bytes = 1 MB = 1024 KB.
  4. Compare that with a per-process single-level table for a 48-bit address space, which would need 2³⁶ entries — the inverted table is smaller by many orders of magnitude.

Answer: 1024 KB (1 MB).

Common misconception. Using the virtual address width to size the table. Only physical memory and the page size matter; the virtual address width plays no part.

OS-U4-Q67MCQhard

Two processes share one physical frame that holds a read-only library page. Why is this awkward in a system with a single inverted page table?

  1. Because the frame number of a shared page would have to change for each process
  2. Because the TLB can hold only one entry per frame and would keep evicting the shared page
  3. Because each frame has exactly one entry, so the frame can name only one (process, virtual page) mapping; sharing needs extra entries or an auxiliary structure
  4. Because sharing requires both processes to place the page at the same virtual page number
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An inverted table is a function frame → (process, page). It is one-to-one by construction. Sharing needs the inverse: two distinct virtual pages must map to the same frame, which is two domain elements with one image.

Step by step.

  1. Per-process page tables express sharing trivially: both tables point their own entries at the same frame number.
  2. In an inverted table there is one slot per frame, and that slot can record only one owner. A second process mapping the same frame has nowhere to be recorded.
  3. The usual fixes are to allow chains of mappings in one entry, or to keep a small side table of shared mappings — both add work to every miss.
  4. The frame number is a property of the frame and does not vary per process, so (A) is wrong; the TLB is not limited to one entry per frame, so (B) is wrong; virtual addresses need not agree, so (D) is wrong.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Assuming sharing works as it does with per-process tables. The direction of the mapping is reversed, and that is precisely what makes sharing the standard objection to inverted tables.

OS-U4-Q68MSQmedium

Consider a machine whose only translation structure is one system-wide inverted page table. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. There is one entry per physical frame, so the table size is independent of the virtual address width.
  2. A translation that misses the TLB may require a hash-table search on the (process, page) pair, because the table is not indexed by the page number.
  3. The table is system-wide rather than per process, so a context switch does not have to change the table base register to a different table.
  4. Sharing a frame between two processes is easier than with per-process page tables, because the frame has a single entry.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The inverted table is one array indexed by frame. Everything that follows — its size, its lookup cost, its sharing behaviour — follows from that one decision.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Entries = frames = physical memory ÷ page size. A 64-bit address space costs nothing extra.
  2. (B) True. The hardware supplies a page number, but the table is keyed by frame, so the entry must be found by a search. Real systems hash on (pid, page) and chain collisions.
  3. (C) True. One table serves every process, so switching processes does not switch tables; only the entries' ownership changes meaning.
  4. (D) False. One entry per frame means one (process, page) mapping per frame, so a shared frame cannot be named by both processes. Sharing is the weak point of this design.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Reading (D) as a benefit of the single entry. The single entry is exactly the obstruction: sharing requires two mappings into one frame.

OS-U4-Q69NATmedium

A machine has 16 GB of physical memory and 8 KB pages. How many entries does its inverted page table contain?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 2097152

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. One entry per frame: the count is physical memory divided by the page size, with both quantities in the same unit.

Step by step.

  1. 16 GB = 2⁴ × 2³⁰ = 2³⁴ bytes.
  2. 8 KB = 2³ × 2¹⁰ = 2¹³ bytes.
  3. Entries = 2³⁴ ÷ 2¹³ = 2²¹ = 2097152.
  4. With 16-byte entries the table would occupy 32 MB — a fixed cost, whatever the processes' virtual address spaces look like.

Answer: 2097152 entries.

Common misconception. Mixing GB and KB by treating 16 GB as 16 × 10⁶ KB. Work in powers of two: the quotient is exact only when both sides use the same base.

OS-U4-Q90MCQeasy

How many inverted page tables does a system keep?

  1. One for the whole system, with one entry per physical frame.
  2. One per process, with one entry per virtual page of that process.
  3. One per segment, with one entry per segment of the process.
  4. One per frame, so the number of tables equals the number of frames.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An inverted page table turns the usual structure inside out: instead of one entry per virtual page, it has one entry per physical frame, and the table is shared by the whole system.

Step by step.

  1. Physical memory is finite, so the number of frames is a fixed, modest number; one entry per frame is a fixed cost regardless of how many processes run.
  2. Because a frame belongs to at most one process at a time, one table can describe every frame in the machine.
  3. Each entry records which process and which virtual page currently occupy that frame, which is what makes a single shared table possible.
  4. Option (D) misreads the phrase “one per frame”: it means one entry per frame, not one table per frame.

Answer: Option (A) — a single system-wide table, indexed by frame.

Common misconception. Reading the name as “one table per process, inverted”. The inversion is of the index: frame in, (process, page) out.

Takeaway. Per-process tables scale with virtual space; one inverted table scales with physical frames.

OS-U4-Q91MCQmedium

A process declares a sparse 2⁴⁸-byte virtual address space on a machine with 1 GB of physical memory whose only translation structure is an inverted page table. What is the effect on the size of that structure?

  1. It must hold 2⁴⁸ entries, so it cannot be kept in memory at all.
  2. Its size is fixed by the number of physical frames, so the enormous virtual space costs the table nothing.
  3. It shrinks, because sparse pages need no entries of their own.
  4. It grows in proportion to the number of page faults the process takes.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The size of an inverted page table is physical memory / page size. The width of the virtual address never enters the formula.

Step by step.

  1. With 1 GB of physical memory and 4 KB pages there are 2³⁰/2¹² = 2¹⁸ frames, hence 262 144 entries.
  2. Whether the process asks for 4 GB or 256 TB of virtual space changes nothing: only frames that actually hold a page get an entry.
  3. This is the property that makes the scheme attractive on 64-bit machines, where a per-process table sized for the virtual space would be impossible.
  4. Option (A) describes the per-process table this scheme replaces. Option (C) inverts the logic: sparseness does not shrink the table, it simply never enlarges it. Option (D) confuses a running statistic with the size of a static structure.

Answer: Option (B) — the table is bounded by physical memory, not by the virtual space.

Common misconception. Assuming a huge virtual address space must produce a huge translation structure. With an inverted table the structure is sized by what is resident, which is exactly the resource that is limited.

Takeaway. Inverted table size = frames, full stop.

OS-U4-Q92MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about an inverted page table are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Its size is set by the number of physical frames, not by the width of the virtual address.
  2. One inverted page table is kept per process, so that each process can be paged independently.
  3. A virtual-to-physical lookup needs a search unless a hash table on (pid, page) is added.
  4. Because it has one entry per frame, it can hold a full per-process page table inside each entry.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. One entry per frame is a small, fixed structure, but it is indexed the wrong way round for the hardware: the CPU knows (pid, virtual page) and needs a frame number.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: entries = physical memory / page size, whatever the virtual address width.
  2. (B) is false: the table is system-wide. Per-process tables are exactly what it replaces.
  3. (C) is true: without an index on (pid, page) the hardware would have to scan every entry, so a hash anchor table narrows the search to one bucket and chaining resolves collisions.
  4. (D) is false: an entry holds a (pid, page) pair plus control bits — a handful of bytes, not a table.

Answer: Options (A) and (C).

Common misconception. Believing the inverted table is simply a smaller page table. It is a different index: cheap in space, expensive in lookup unless a hash is added.

Takeaway. Inverted = frame-indexed: space bounded by frames, lookup needs hashing.

OS-U4-Q93MCQhard

Two processes map the same read-only library frame at different virtual addresses on a machine whose only translation structure is one inverted page table keyed by frame number. Why is this awkward, and what is the standard remedy?

  1. It is impossible in principle, because a frame can hold the page of only one process.
  2. The frame number is not unique, so the table cannot be indexed by it at all.
  3. Each entry records a single (process, virtual page) pair for its frame, so a shared frame needs a chain of pairs or a separate reverse map; the remedy is a chained entry or per-process shadow tables.
  4. Sharing is handled entirely by the TLB, so the inverted table never needs to know about it.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The inverted table stores, per frame, the one virtual page that currently maps it. Sharing breaks the “one”: a single frame may be the target of several (pid, page) pairs.

Step by step.

  1. Frame F holds the library page. Process P reaches it as virtual page 3 and process Q as virtual page 40.
  2. A single entry can name only one of those pairs, so one of the two processes would translate incorrectly.
  3. The fixes are structural: let an entry carry a chain (or list) of the pairs that map the frame, or keep a small per-process shadow table that records the extra mappings.
  4. Option (A) is false — sharing one physical page among processes is ordinary; it is the table's shape that resists it. Option (B) is false: frame numbers are unique identifiers. Option (D) is false: the TLB is a cache in front of the table, so a miss must still be resolved by the table.

Answer: Option (C) — one frame, several (pid, page) pairs, so the entry has to become a list.

Common misconception. Assuming that sharing works the same way as in per-process tables, where each process simply writes the same frame number into its own entry. The inverted table has only one place to write it.

Takeaway. Inverting the index saves space and makes many-to-one mappings the hard case.

OS-U4-Q94NATeasy

An inverted page table has 8192 entries and each entry is 16 bytes wide. How much memory does the table itself occupy, in KB?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 128

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The table is a flat array of entries, so its size is entries × entry size, converted to the unit asked for.

Step by step.

  1. 8192 × 16 = 131 072 bytes.
  2. 131 072 / 1024 = 128 KB.
  3. As a check: 8192 entries means 8192 frames, which at 4 KB per frame would be 32 MB of physical memory — and 128 KB of table for 32 MB of memory is a plausible overhead of 0.4 %.

Answer: 128 KB.

Common misconception. Dividing by 1000, or multiplying the number of entries by the page size instead of the entry size.

Takeaway. Table bytes = entries × entry width; the page size plays no part in this multiplication.

OS-U4-Q95MCQmedium

Why does a system that uses an inverted page table normally keep a hash anchor table on (pid, virtual page number)?

  1. To hold the contents of each frame, so that a hit needs no second memory access.
  2. To record which pages are dirty and must be written back to disk.
  3. To replace the TLB, which cannot be used with an inverted table.
  4. Because the inverted table is indexed by frame, so finding the frame that holds a given page would otherwise mean scanning every entry; the hash narrows the search to one bucket, and collisions are resolved by chaining.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The hardware supplies (pid, virtual page) and needs a frame number, but the inverted table is keyed the other way. A hash on the supplied pair supplies the missing index.

Step by step.

  1. Indexing by frame answers “who is in frame f?”, which is the question the replacement policy asks.
  2. The translation question is “which frame holds page p of process q?”, and nothing in the table is ordered to answer it directly.
  3. A linear scan of all frames per reference would be hopeless, so a hash of (pid, page) selects a bucket; the bucket's chain is short, and each entry is checked for a full match.
  4. Options (A), (B) and (C) each assign the hash a job that belongs to the frame contents, the dirty bit or the TLB.

Answer: Option (D) — the hash supplies the index the table does not have.

Common misconception. Believing the hash table stores translations. It stores pointers into the inverted table; the entries themselves remain frame-indexed.

Takeaway. Inverted table + hash = space proportional to frames, lookup cost proportional to bucket length.

segmentation-paged-segmentation 23
OS-U4-Q20MCQeasy

In a segmented memory system, a logical address consists of:

  1. a single linear offset from the start of physical memory
  2. a page number and a frame number
  3. a frame number and an offset within that frame
  4. a segment number and an offset within that segment
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Segmentation is a variable-sized, logical division of the address space, so a reference names the segment and then a position inside it.

Step by step.

  1. The segment number indexes the segment table.
  2. The entry supplies the base and the limit of that segment.
  3. The offset is checked against the limit and then added to the base.

Answer: Option (D)

Common misconception. Confusing the segment number with a page number. Pages are fixed-size and invisible to the programmer; segments are variable-sized and usually correspond to code, data and stack.

OS-U4-Q21MCQmedium

A segment table entry holds base 8000 and limit 900. A program refers to offset 950 within that segment. What happens?

  1. a trap is raised, because the offset exceeds the segment limit
  2. the reference is translated to physical address 8950
  3. the reference is translated to physical address 8000
  4. the segment is extended automatically to 950 bytes
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The limit is the length of the segment. A valid offset satisfies 0 ≤ offset < limit; anything else is an addressing error caught by the hardware.

Step by step.

  1. The limit is 900, so valid offsets are 0 to 899.
  2. The offset 950 is outside that range, so the check fails before any address is formed.
  3. The hardware raises a trap; no physical address is produced.

Answer: Option (A)

Common misconception. Adding base and offset anyway to get 8950. Without the limit check, an out-of-range offset would silently read another segment's memory — the very protection segmentation exists to provide.

OS-U4-Q22MCQeasy

A pure segmentation system, with no paging underneath, suffers from:

  1. internal fragmentation only
  2. neither internal nor external fragmentation
  3. internal fragmentation in the last segment only
  4. external fragmentation
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Segments are variable-sized, so a segment is allocated as one contiguous run and no space inside it is wasted.

Step by step.

  1. Each segment gets exactly the space it needs, so there is no internal fragmentation.
  2. As segments of different sizes come and go, the free memory breaks into holes of assorted sizes.
  3. Those holes may be too small for a new segment even when their total is large: external fragmentation.

Answer: Option (D)

Common misconception. Thinking variable-sized units avoid fragmentation altogether. They avoid internal fragmentation and pay for it with external fragmentation, which is exactly why paged segmentation exists.

OS-U4-Q23MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about segmentation and paged segmentation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Segmentation makes the limit check unnecessary, because the offset field is wide enough for any segment.
  2. Segmentation matches the programmer's view of a program as code, data and stack.
  3. Two processes can share a segment by pointing their segment-table entries at the same base.
  4. In paged segmentation a segment-table entry points to a page table, and the segment offset is split into a page number and a page offset.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Segmentation is a logical division with a base and a limit per segment; paged segmentation keeps that structure but pages each segment so that physical allocation is in fixed frames.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is false: the limit check is what enforces the segment boundary; a wide offset field would still allow an out-of-range value.
  2. (B) is true: segments correspond to the program's own modules, which is what makes protection and sharing natural.
  3. (C) is true: identical base and limit in two segment tables gives shared memory.
  4. (D) is true: the segment is paged, so its offset addresses a page of that segment and then a byte within the page.

Answer: Options (B), (C), (D)

Common misconception. Believing paging makes segmentation redundant. Paged segmentation keeps the logical segment structure and adds paging only to remove external fragmentation.

OS-U4-Q24NAThard

In a paged segmentation scheme a logical address is (8-bit segment number, 24-bit offset), pages are 4 KB, and each page-table entry is 4 bytes. What is the size, in KB, of the page table of one segment?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 16

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each segment has its own page table with one entry per page of that segment, so the table size follows the maximum number of pages a segment can contain.

Step by step.

  1. A 24-bit offset addresses 2²⁴ bytes within a segment.
  2. With 4 KB = 2¹² pages, a segment holds at most 2²⁴ ÷ 2¹² = 2¹² = 4096 pages.
  3. 4096 entries × 4 bytes = 16 384 bytes = 16 KB.

Answer: 16

Common misconception. Multiplying by the number of segments (256). The question asks for one segment's page table; the segment number only selects which table to use.

OS-U4-Q25NATeasy

A segment table entry holds base 3000 and limit 500. A reference to offset 400 within that segment is valid. What physical address does it produce?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 3400

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. After the limit check succeeds, the physical address is the segment base plus the offset.

Step by step.

  1. The offset 400 is below the limit 500, so the reference is legal.
  2. Physical address = 3000 + 400 = 3400.

Answer: 3400

Common misconception. Adding the limit as well, or treating the base as a byte count to be divided. The base is the starting physical address of the segment.

OS-U4-S2-Q20MCQeasy

A segment table entry holds base 8000 and limit 1200. A reference to offset 500 of that segment produces which physical address?

  1. 9200
  2. 7500
  3. 8000
  4. 8500
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The limit is a bound on the offset, not part of the address; once the offset passes the bound check the physical address is simply base + offset.

Step by step.

  1. Check the bound: 500 < 1200, so the reference is legal.
  2. Physical address = 8000 + 500 = 8500.

Option (D)

Common misconception. Adding the limit as well (8000 + 1200 + 500 = 9700), or subtracting the offset. The limit only decides whether the reference is allowed.

OS-U4-S2-Q21MCQeasy

A segment table entry holds base 8000 and limit 1200. A reference to offset 1500 of that segment causes which outcome?

  1. physical address 9500
  2. physical address 8000
  3. an addressing trap, because the offset is not less than the limit
  4. the offset is reduced modulo the limit, giving physical address 8300
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The limit is the length of the segment. A legal offset satisfies 0 ≤ offset < limit; anything else is an addressing error detected by the hardware before any address is formed.

Step by step.

  1. Valid offsets for this segment are 0 to 1199.
  2. 1500 is outside that range, so the comparison fails.
  3. The hardware raises a trap (an addressing or segmentation fault) and no physical address is produced.

Option (C)

Common misconception. Computing 8000 + 1500 = 9500 anyway. Without the bound check the reference would silently read memory belonging to another segment — the protection that segmentation exists to provide.

OS-U4-S2-Q22MCQmedium

A process has this segment table: segment 0 base 219 limit 600; segment 1 base 2300 limit 14; segment 2 base 90 limit 100. Which logical address causes a trap?

  1. (0, 430)
  2. (1, 10)
  3. (1, 20)
  4. (2, 99)
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each segment has its own bound. A reference is legal exactly when its offset is less than that segment's limit.

Step by step.

  1. (0, 430): 430 < 600, legal, physical 219 + 430 = 649.
  2. (1, 10): 10 < 14, legal, physical 2300 + 10 = 2310.
  3. (1, 20): 20 is not less than the limit 14, so this reference traps.
  4. (2, 99): 99 < 100, legal, physical 90 + 99 = 189.

Option (C)

Common misconception. Checking the offset against the wrong segment's limit, or against the base. Every segment carries its own limit, and segment 1 is tiny (14 bytes).

OS-U4-S2-Q23MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about segmentation and paging are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Segmentation has no internal fragmentation, because a segment is exactly as large as the logical unit it holds.
  2. Segmentation can suffer external fragmentation as segments of different sizes come and go.
  3. The segment size is fixed by the hardware at 4 KB.
  4. Paging avoids external fragmentation because every frame has the same size.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B), (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Segmentation allocates variable-sized logical units; paging allocates fixed-size frames. That single difference decides which fragmentation each one suffers.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: the block handed to a segment is exactly the segment length, so nothing inside it is wasted.
  2. (B) is true: freeing segments of assorted sizes leaves holes that may be too small for the next segment.
  3. (C) is false: segment sizes are set by the program's logical structure and the hardware allows them to vary; 4 KB is a page size.
  4. (D) is true: any free frame can hold any page, so no usable free space is left between allocations.

Options (A), (B) and (D)

Common misconception. Mixing up the two kinds of fragmentation: segmentation trades internal for external, paging trades external for internal.

OS-U4-S2-Q24NAThard
