Concept. PFF control is a two-sided controller. Above the upper bound the process needs more memory; below the lower bound it is holding more memory than it needs, and those frames are better given to someone else.

Step by step.

  1. Measure the process's fault rate over an interval.
  2. Rate above the upper bound → increase its frame allocation.
  3. Rate below the lower bound → decrease its frame allocation; the freed frames go to processes that are short.
  4. Rate inside the band → leave the allocation alone.

Answer: Option (B) — take frames away.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the response to a rate above the upper bound.
  • (C) is the response to a process that cannot be given enough frames to leave the thrashing region.
  • (D) changes scheduling, not memory allocation, and cannot fix a fault rate.

Common misconception. Reading "low fault rate" as "give it more memory, it is working well". A very low rate means the allocation is over-generous.

Takeaway. Too high → add frames; too low → remove frames; in band → leave it.

OS-U5-Q72MSQeasy

Which of the following statements about local and global replacement are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Under global replacement a process can take a frame from another process, so one process's poor locality can degrade everyone's fault rate.
  2. Under local replacement a process chooses its victims only among its own frames, so a thrashing process mainly harms itself.
  3. Global replacement makes it impossible for the system as a whole to thrash.
  4. Under local replacement the number of frames a process holds does not change when another process faults.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The choice of victim pool decides who pays for a bad locality. Global replacement lets a process compete for every frame in the system; local replacement confines its victims to its own allocation.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. With a system-wide pool a process that faults often simply evicts other processes' pages, raising their fault rates too.
  2. (B) False. Local replacement confines the victims, but a process whose working set exceeds its own allocation still thrashes; the harm is limited, not eliminated.
  3. (C) False. Global replacement makes thrashing easier to spread, not impossible.
  4. (D) True. Another process's fault cannot change this process's frame count under a local policy.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing local replacement prevents thrashing. It prevents the spread of thrashing; the badly allocated process still thrashes on its own.

Takeaway. Global replacement → better utilisation, contagious faults; local replacement → stable allocations, contained damage.

OS-U5-Q73MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about thrashing and the working-set model are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Thrashing shows up as high paging-disk utilisation together with low CPU utilisation.
  2. Under working-set control a process is admitted only if the sum of the working-set sizes of the resident processes stays within the frames available.
  3. The working set W(t, Δ) is the set of distinct pages referenced in the last Δ references.
  4. Raising the degree of multiprogramming always raises CPU utilisation.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Thrashing is a positive-feedback failure: too few frames per process raises the fault rate, the processes queue on the paging device, CPU utilisation collapses, and the scheduler may respond by admitting yet more processes.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. The disk is saturated with page transfers while the CPU idles waiting for them — the diagnostic signature.
  2. (B) True. Working-set control computes D = Σ WSSi and refuses admission while D would exceed the frame count.
  3. (C) True, by definition, with the window ending at the current reference.
  4. (D) False. Utilisation rises, peaks, and then falls as memory is over-committed; beyond the knee, more processes mean less work done.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Reading high disk activity as "the disk is the bottleneck, buy a faster disk". If the paging disk is saturated while the CPU is idle, the shortage is memory, not disk bandwidth.

Takeaway. Thrashing = memory shortage; the cure is fewer resident processes or more frames, not a faster disk.

OS-U5-Q74MCQhard

A process faults 18 times per 1000 references with 4 frames, 9 times per 1000 with 6 frames, and 3 times per 1000 with 8 frames. PFF control sets the upper bound at 10 faults per 1000 references and the lower bound at 2 per 1000. Starting from 4 frames, how many frames will the process hold once the controller settles?

  1. 4 frames
  2. 6 frames
  3. 8 frames
  4. 10 frames
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. PFF control moves the allocation until the measured rate lies inside the band. It stops at the first allocation whose rate is acceptable — it does not jump to the best allocation available.

Step by step.

  1. At 4 frames the rate is 18 per 1000, above the upper bound of 10 → add frames.
  2. At 6 frames the rate is 9 per 1000, which is inside [2, 10] → the controller stops.
  3. At 8 frames the rate would be 3 per 1000, also inside the band, but the controller has no reason to go there.
  4. So the settled allocation is 6 frames.

Answer: Option (B) — 6 frames.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) leaves the rate above the upper bound; the process would still be thrashing.
  • (C) overshoots: 3 is inside the band, but nothing drives the allocation that far.
  • (D) is past the point where the rate stops falling, and would only be reached if the lower bound were breached and frames were being reclaimed in the other direction.

Common misconception. Choosing the allocation with the lowest fault rate. PFF control is a band controller, not an optimiser: it stops as soon as the process is healthy, leaving the spare frames to other processes.

Takeaway. Walk the allocations upward until the rate enters the band: 18 → 9, so 6 frames.

OS-U5-Q75NAThard

A process makes 2 × 106 memory references per second and its page-fault rate is 1.5 × 10−5. Each page fault takes 6 ms of paging-disk time. What percentage of the disk's time is spent servicing this process's faults?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 18

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Disk utilisation is the product of the arrival rate of faults and the service time of one fault: faults per second times seconds per fault gives the fraction of each second the disk is busy.

Step by step.

  1. Faults per second = 2 × 106 × 1.5 × 10−5 = 30.
  2. Seconds of disk time per second = 30 × 6 × 10−3 = 0.18 s.
  3. As a percentage: 0.18 × 100 = 18 %.
  4. For contrast, at a fault rate of 10−4 the same process would need 2 × 106 × 10−4 × 6 ms = 1,200 % of the disk — a saturated disk and a thrashing system.

Answer: 18 % of the disk's time.

Common misconception. Multiplying the reference rate by the service time and forgetting the fault rate, or leaving the service time in milliseconds and reporting 0.018 %. The unit of the answer is a fraction of a second per second.

Takeaway. Disk load = fault rate × reference rate × service time; 30 faults/s × 6 ms = 18 %.

OS-U5-Q95MCQeasy

The working-set window Δ of a process is set much smaller than the size of its locality. Which one of the following is the consequence?

  1. The working set overcounts what the process needs, so frames are wasted.
  2. Δ does not affect the frame allocation; only the page-fault rate matters.
  3. The page-fault rate falls, because fewer pages are counted inside the window.
  4. The working set undercounts what the process needs, so the process is given too few frames and its fault rate rises.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The working set is the set of pages referenced in the last Δ references. It is an estimate of the locality, and the estimate is only as good as the window: too small and the estimate is a fraction of the real locality.

Step by step.

  1. Suppose the locality is 8 pages and Δ is 4 references.
  2. Only the last four references can be inside the window, so |WS| ≤ 4.
  3. The operating system allocates frames on that estimate and hands the process four frames instead of eight.
  4. The process faults on the pages it needs but does not have, and the fault rate rises — the classic route into thrashing.

Answer: Option (D).

Common misconception. Assuming a smaller window is always safer because it asks for fewer frames. Asking for fewer frames than the locality needs is precisely how a system thrashes.

OS-U5-Q96MCQeasy

A process has made the references 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 2, the last one being the most recent. With a working-set window Δ = 4, what is |WS(t, Δ)| at the end of this string?

  1. 2
  2. 3
  3. 4
  4. 5
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. WS(t, Δ) is the set of distinct pages referenced in the last Δ references. Repetitions inside the window collapse to one element.

Step by step.

  1. The last four references are 1, 2, 1, 2 (positions 7 to 10 of the string).
  2. Taking the set of those references gives {1, 2}.
  3. |WS| = 2, not 4: the window length and the working-set size are different quantities.

Answer: Option (A) — 2.

Common misconception. Answering Δ = 4. The window bounds the number of references examined; the size of the set is at most Δ and is usually smaller.

OS-U5-Q97MSQmedium

A system is thrashing. Which of the following actions can relieve it? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Enlarging the working-set window Δ, so that each process is judged to need fewer frames.
  2. Suspending one or more processes, lowering the degree of multiprogramming.
  3. Switching from global to local replacement, so that a process cannot take another process’s frames.
  4. Adding physical memory, so that more frames are available to the working sets.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Thrashing is a supply-and-demand problem: the sum of the working sets exceeds the frames available, so every process spends its time waiting for its own pages. Any action that raises supply or lowers demand helps; anything that raises the estimated demand makes it worse.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is false. A larger window covers more references, so |WS| grows and each process is judged to need more frames, not fewer.
  2. (B) is true. Suspending a process returns its frames to the free pool, so the remaining processes can hold their working sets.
  3. (C) is true. Under global replacement one process can evict another’s pages, so a fault in one process causes faults in another; local replacement breaks that cascade, at the cost of leaving some frames idle.
  4. (D) is true. More physical memory means more frames for the same demand.

Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Reaching for the working-set window first. Changing Δ changes the measurement, not the memory; only suspending work or adding memory changes the balance.

OS-U5-Q98MSQmedium

An operating system approximates the working set with the hardware reference bit, sampling it every I references and keeping the last k samples. Which of the following statements about this approximation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. The reference bit lets the kernel judge recency without taking a software timestamp on every memory reference.
  2. The window actually covered is about k · I references.
  3. The approximation can only overestimate a process’s working set, never underestimate it.
  4. A page whose reference bit is clear in all k retained samples is a candidate for eviction.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Exact working-set tracking would need a timestamp or a counter updated on every reference, which no ordinary hardware provides. The reference bit gives a one-bit summary per page per period, and the kernel reads it at intervals.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true. The bit is set by the MMU on any access, so the kernel learns only “was this page touched since I last looked”, which is enough for a sampled estimate.
  2. (B) is true. Sampling every I references and keeping k samples looks back over roughly k · I references, so Δ ≈ k · I.
  3. (C) is false. A page touched once between two samples and then evicted has its bit cleared before the next read, so the estimate can miss pages the process is still using — it can underestimate.
  4. (D) is true. k clear samples mean the page has not been touched for the whole window, which is exactly the eviction criterion the model wants.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing a sampled estimate is conservative. Sampling loses information in both directions, and the choice of I is a real trade-off: a long interval misses short bursts of use, a short interval costs more kernel work.

OS-U5-Q99MCQeasy

A system has F frames and the sum of the working-set sizes of the running processes is exactly F. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. The system is already thrashing.
  2. Each process can be given its working set only while no further process is admitted; admitting one more will start thrashing.
  3. Since D = F, every process’s page-fault rate must be zero.
  4. The working-set model cannot be used when D equals the number of frames.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The working-set model admits a process only while D + WSS(new) ≤ F. Equality is the boundary: the current set fits exactly, and there is no spare frame for anyone else.

Step by step.

  1. With D = F every running process can hold its whole working set, so the fault rate is that of a well-behaved system, not zero: compulsory and replacement faults still occur.
  2. Admitting one more process raises D above F, so some process must lose a page it needs.
  3. That process faults, and its replacement may take a page from another process, so faults spread.
  4. The system enters thrashing. Hence the boundary statement in (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Reading D = F as a fault-free state, or as a thrashing state. It is the point of maximum occupancy at which the system still works.

OS-U5-Q100NAThard

A machine has 400 frames. Each process needs a working set of 48 pages, and the operating system keeps 10% of the frames in reserve for its own use. What is the largest number of processes that can run without thrashing?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 7

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The working-set model admits processes while the total demand fits in the frames available to user processes. Frames reserved by the kernel are not available, so the reserve must be subtracted before the division.

Step by step.

  1. Reserve = 10% × 400 = 40 frames; usable = 360.
  2. 360 / 48 = 7.5.
  3. Seven processes need 7 × 48 = 336 ≤ 360, so they fit.
  4. Eight would need 8 × 48 = 384 > 360, so the eighth must be refused.

Answer: 7 processes

Common misconception. Dividing 400 by 48 and rounding 8.33 down to 8, which ignores both the reserve and the fact that a process cannot be given a fraction of its working set.

Unit 6 — File Systems & Disk Scheduling · 100 solved questions (2026-10-29)
file-allocation-methods-indexed-linked 32
OS-U6-Q01MCQeasy

In linked allocation a file is a linked list of disk blocks, and the blocks may be scattered anywhere on the disk. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. Any block of the file is reached in one disk read, because its address is computed from the first block.
  2. It suffers no external fragmentation, but every block gives up space for a pointer, and reaching the k-th block costs k disk reads.
  3. It requires the blocks of a file to be contiguous, so it suffers from external fragmentation.
  4. If one pointer is damaged, only the block it points to is lost and the rest of the file is still reachable.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Linked allocation stores each block with a pointer to the next block of the same file, so the file is a chain that can be built from any free blocks. Two consequences follow at once: no free space is left unusable between files, and no block can be located without walking the chain.

Step by step.

  1. Because blocks are taken from anywhere, there is no external fragmentation — any free block will do.
  2. Each block must carry the pointer, so a block of size B with a pointer of p bytes holds only B − p bytes of data. That is a cost paid on every block.
  3. To read logical block k, the system must start at the first block and follow k pointers, so direct access is lost.
  4. If a pointer is corrupted, the rest of the chain is unreachable — the file loses everything from that point on, not merely one block.

Answer: Option (B) — no external fragmentation, but a pointer per block and no direct access.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) describes contiguous allocation, where the address is start + k.
  • (C) reverses the point of linking: blocks are deliberately scattered.
  • (D) understates the damage. Losing a pointer orphans the whole remainder of the chain.

Common misconception. Reading “linked list” as “cheap”. The chain is cheap in space management and expensive in access: sequential access is fine, random access is not.

Takeaway. Linked allocation trades direct access for the elimination of external fragmentation and for trivial file growth.

OS-U6-Q05MCQeasy

Which one of the following is the advantage that contiguous allocation has over linked allocation?

  1. A file never suffers external fragmentation.
  2. The address of the k-th block is start + k, so that block is reached with a single disk access.
  3. A file can grow without moving any of its blocks.
  4. A file never wastes space in its last block.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Contiguous allocation gives a file one run of consecutive blocks. That single decision buys the best possible access behaviour and costs flexibility in growth.

Step by step.

  1. Because the blocks are consecutive, block k of the file lives at block start + k: one arithmetic step, one disk access.
  2. The same contiguity makes sequential access fast, because consecutive logical blocks are physically adjacent and the head hardly moves.
  3. Growth is the price. To extend a file the blocks immediately after it must be free, otherwise the file must be copied elsewhere.
  4. Free space becomes a set of holes between surviving files, which is external fragmentation.

Answer: Option (B) — computed block addresses give direct access.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Contiguous allocation is the scheme that suffers external fragmentation most visibly.
  • (C) Growth is precisely its weakness.
  • (D) The last block of a file is partly empty in every block-based scheme; only the amount differs.

Common misconception. Crediting contiguous allocation with the absence of fragmentation. It has no internal fragmentation in the paging sense, but external fragmentation is its signature defect.

Takeaway. Contiguous: fastest access, worst growth. Linked: any growth, no direct access.

OS-U6-Q09NATeasy

A file system uses indexed allocation in which each file has exactly one index block, and the index block holds 256 block pointers. The block size is 1 KB. What is the largest file, in KB, that this scheme can represent?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 256

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With one index block, the file can point at exactly as many data blocks as the index block has entries. Maximum file size = entries × block size.

Step by step.

  1. The index block holds 256 pointers.
  2. Each pointer addresses one 1 KB data block.
  3. Maximum size = 256 × 1 KB = 256 KB.

Answer: 256 KB.

Common misconception. Adding the index block itself (257 KB) or subtracting it. The index block holds metadata, not file data, so it does not count towards the file's size.

Takeaway. Single-level indexing caps a file at (pointers per block) × (block size); to go beyond it, a second level is needed.

OS-U6-Q13MCQmedium

An inode holds 12 direct pointers, one single-indirect pointer and one double-indirect pointer. The block size is 4 KB and a block pointer is 4 bytes. Counting logical blocks from 0, which pointer chain is used to reach logical block 5000?

  1. A direct pointer
  2. The single-indirect pointer
  3. The double-indirect pointer
  4. No chain — a file of this size cannot be represented
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Multi-level indexing partitions the logical block numbers into ranges: the direct pointers cover the first few blocks, the single-indirect pointer the next (block size ÷ pointer size) blocks, and the double-indirect pointer everything after that.

Step by step.

  1. Pointers per block = 4096 ÷ 4 = 1024.
  2. Direct pointers cover blocks 0 to 11 — that is 12 blocks.
  3. Single indirect covers 1024 blocks: 12 to 1035.
  4. Double indirect covers 1024² = 1,048,576 blocks: 1036 to 1,049,611.
  5. 5000 lies between 1036 and 1,049,611, so the double-indirect pointer is used: the first-level index gives the second-level index block, and that block gives the data block.

Answer: Option (C) — the double-indirect pointer, with two index blocks traversed.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) a direct pointer reaches only blocks 0 to 11.
  • (B) the single-indirect pointer stops at block 1035.
  • (D) the structure addresses over a million blocks, so 5000 is well within reach.

Common misconception. Forgetting that the 12 direct blocks shift every later range by 12, or computing 1024² = 1,048,576 as if the pointer size were the block size. Keep the three ranges explicit.

Takeaway. Ranges: direct 0–11, single 12–1035, double 1036–1,049,611 for 4 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers.

OS-U6-Q17MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about indexed allocation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. It supports direct access, because the index block gives the address of every data block of the file.
  2. It suffers no external fragmentation, because each data block of a file is allocated on its own.
  3. The index block costs space even for a very small file, and it must be read before any data block can be touched.
  4. A file can be extended without limit in place, because its index block grows with the file.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Indexed allocation gives each file a block of pointers. One level of indirection buys direct access at the price of a fixed-size index.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. The k-th entry of the index block is the address of the k-th data block, so one index read plus one data read reaches any block.
  2. (B) True. Data blocks are taken individually from the free pool, so there are no unusable holes between files.
  3. (C) True. A file of one block still needs a whole index block, and every access begins with a read of the index. Internal fragmentation of the last data block also remains.
  4. (D) False. The index block has a fixed number of entries. Growth beyond it needs a second level of indexing, or an extension mechanism such as a linked chain of index blocks.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C) are true; (D) is false.

Common misconception. Assuming indexed allocation removes every limit and every kind of waste. It removes external fragmentation and the growth restriction of contiguous allocation, but the index block is a fixed-size ceiling and a per-file space cost.

Takeaway. Indexed: direct access and no external fragmentation, at the cost of an index block and a one-block ceiling per level.

OS-U6-Q21MCQmedium

A FAT-based file system manages 2²⁰ blocks. What is the minimum number of bits that each FAT entry must have?

  1. 16
  2. 20
  3. 24
  4. 32
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The file allocation table has one entry per disk block, and the entry holds the number of the next block in the chain. An entry must therefore be wide enough to name any block, and — in practice — to hold a few reserved markers.

Step by step.

  1. Block numbers run from 0 to 2²⁰ − 1, so 2²⁰ distinct values must be representable.
  2. A field of b bits holds 2b values, so 2b ≥ 2²⁰ gives b ≥ 20.
  3. 16 bits would address only 2¹⁶ = 65,536 blocks, far fewer than 2²⁰.
  4. 24 or 32 bits would work but are not the minimum.

Answer: Option (B) — 20 bits is the minimum; real systems use 16, 28 or 32 bits for convenience.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 2¹⁶ blocks is 65,536, which cannot name block 1,048,575.
  • (C) and (D) are sufficient but larger than needed.

Common misconception. Dividing the disk size by the block size and forgetting to take the base-2 logarithm — the entry width depends on the number of blocks, not on their size.

Takeaway. Entry width ≥ log₂(number of blocks). The whole FAT then occupies (blocks × width ÷ 8) bytes, which is why large FAT disks keep it partly on disk.

OS-U6-Q24MSQhard

Which of the following statements comparing file-allocation methods are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Contiguous allocation gives the best sequential and direct access, but a file cannot grow unless the blocks immediately after it are free, so growth often means copying the file.
  2. Linked allocation never needs to move a file in order to grow it, since growth is just linking another block, and the price is the loss of direct access.
  3. Multi-level indexed allocation removes internal fragmentation, because every block of the file is addressed individually.
  4. A file stored with multi-level indexing cannot be sparse, because every block must have a pointer in the index.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A) and (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The three allocation methods sit on a single trade-off: how cheaply a block can be found against how freely the file can grow. Fragmentation and sparse files are separate properties that follow from how blocks are assigned.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Contiguity is what makes start + k work; it is also what makes growth expensive, and it leaves holes behind when files are deleted.
  2. (B) True. A new block can be linked at the tail wherever free space happens to be, so no file ever has to move. Reading block k then costs k pointer chases.
  3. (C) False. Internal fragmentation is the unused tail of the last allocated block, and it is present in every block-based scheme. Multi-level indexing removes external fragmentation, not internal.
  4. (D) False. A sparse file is one whose index entries are absent or marked invalid for blocks never written; reads of those blocks return zeros. Indexing is exactly the structure that makes sparse files practical, because no data block need exist for a hole.

Answer: Options (A) and (B) are true; (C) and (D) are false.

Common misconception. Believing that per-block allocation eliminates all waste. It eliminates the waste between files and keeps the waste inside the last block.

Takeaway. Contiguous: best access, worst growth. Linked: best growth, worst access. Indexed: both good, at the cost of index blocks — and it is the scheme that makes sparse files cheap.

OS-U6-Q26MCQeasy

A FAT file system keeps one entry per disk block in the FAT, and the directory entry of a file stores only its first block number. Which one of the following follows directly from that design?

  1. Caching the FAT in main memory turns every step of the block chain into a table lookup, so the chain is followed at memory speed rather than at one disk read per block.
  2. The directory entry has to be rewritten every time the file grows, because the FAT cannot record where the new block went.
  3. The FAT stores the same block numbers as the directory entries, so the two structures can disagree about where a file starts.
  4. A FAT entry is needed only for blocks that a file actually uses, so the FAT grows with the number of files rather than with the size of the disk.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The FAT is an array indexed by block number; entry i holds the number of the block that follows block i in the file that owns it. The directory entry supplies only the head of the chain, so growth appends a FAT entry and never moves the directory entry.

Step by step.

  1. A file is a chain: directory entry → first block → FAT[first] → FAT[FAT[first]] → … → end-of-file marker.
  2. Following that chain without caching costs one disk read of the FAT per link, which is why plain linked allocation is slow for random access.
  3. The FAT is small enough to be held in memory (one entry per block), so the same traversal becomes a sequence of array accesses.
  4. That is the whole point of FAT: it converts a per-block disk read into a memory lookup, at the cost of keeping the table resident and writing it back on change.

Answer: Option (A) — the FAT converts chain traversal into an in-memory table lookup.

Common misconception. Option (C) is the seductive one: students assume two structures holding block numbers must duplicate each other. The directory entry stores the first block only, so there is nothing to disagree about.

Takeaway. FAT = linked allocation with the links lifted out of the data blocks into one central table.

OS-U6-Q30MCQeasy

A file is stored by linked allocation in 5 disk blocks. The block size is 512 bytes, and 4 bytes of every block are used to hold the pointer to the next block. What is the largest amount of file data those 5 blocks can hold?

  1. 2560 bytes
  2. 2556 bytes
  3. 2540 bytes
  4. 2048 bytes
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. In linked allocation each block spends part of its payload on the link to the next block. Only the remainder is file data, and the last block still carries a pointer (an end-of-file marker) unless the design uses a separate terminator.

Step by step.

  1. Payload per block = block size − pointer size = 512 − 4 = 508 bytes.
  2. Five blocks therefore hold 5 × 508 = 2540 bytes of data.
  3. The pointer overhead across the file is 5 × 4 = 20 bytes, so 2560 − 20 = 2540. ✔
  4. 2540 bytes is the answer; 2560 would be the answer only if the pointers lived outside the blocks.

Answer: Option (C) — 2540 bytes.

Common misconception. Answering 2560 forgets the per-block pointer entirely; answering 2556 subtracts a single pointer instead of one per block.

Takeaway. Linked allocation costs one pointer per block, so usable capacity is (block size − pointer size) × blocks.

OS-U6-Q33MCQmedium

A FAT file system uses 12-bit FAT entries and a cluster (allocation unit) size of 4 KB. What is the largest volume this design can address?

  1. 4 MB
  2. 16 MB
  3. 64 MB
  4. 2 GB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A FAT entry numbers the next cluster, so an n-bit FAT entry can name at most 2n distinct clusters. Volume size is that count multiplied by the cluster size.

Step by step.

  1. 12-bit entries give 212 = 4096 addressable clusters.
  2. Cluster size = 4 KB.
  3. Maximum volume = 4096 × 4 KB = 16 384 KB = 16 MB.
  4. The 4 MB option corresponds to 1024 clusters, i.e. 10-bit entries; 64 MB needs 14 bits.

Answer: Option (B) — 16 MB.

Common misconception. The frequent mistake is to multiply the entry width (12 bits = 1.5 bytes) by the cluster size, or to use 212 bytes instead of 212 clusters.

Takeaway. Volume limit = 2entry bits × cluster size.

OS-U6-Q36NATmedium

An inode holds 12 direct block pointers and one single-indirect pointer. The block size is 2 KB and a block pointer is 4 bytes. What is the largest file, in KB, that this inode can describe?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 1048

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Direct pointers address data blocks one for one; a single-indirect pointer addresses one index block, and every pointer inside that index block addresses one further data block.

Step by step.

  1. Pointers per index block = block size / pointer size = 2048 / 4 = 512.
  2. Blocks reachable = 12 direct + 512 through the single-indirect block = 524 data blocks.
  3. Each data block holds 2 KB of file data.
  4. Maximum file size = 524 × 2 KB = 1048 KB.
  5. Note that the index block itself is metadata, not file data, so it is not counted.

Answer: 1048 KB.

Common misconception. Two errors recur: counting the index block as 513 addressable data blocks, and using 256 pointers because the solver assumes 1 KB blocks.

Takeaway. Capacity = (direct + pointers per indirect block) × block size, for one level of indirection.

OS-U6-Q40MCQmedium

A file of 8 blocks is stored by contiguous allocation. It must grow by one block, but the block immediately after the file already belongs to another file. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. The file system can simply link the new block on, because a contiguous file is always followed by free space.
  2. The new block can be placed anywhere, because the k-th block is still found at start + k.
  3. Only the file's index block has to be updated, since the data blocks never move.
  4. The file must be relocated to a hole large enough to hold 9 blocks, copying all 8 existing blocks, unless the system reserved room for growth in advance.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Contiguous allocation buys one-read direct access by promising that block k of a file lives at start + k. That promise is exactly what makes growth expensive: the file cannot be spliced.

Step by step.

  1. The address of block k is computed as start + k, so the blocks must be physically adjacent.
  2. If the neighbour is taken, there is no free slot at start + 8; the file cannot be extended in place.
  3. The system must find a hole of at least 9 blocks, copy the 8 existing blocks, and free the old extent.
  4. This copying cost, and the external fragmentation it leaves behind, is why systems use extents or reserve slack space when a file is created.

Answer: Option (D) — the file is relocated, or growth must have been reserved in advance.

Common misconception. Option (C) is the standard confusion: “start + k” only works while the blocks stay adjacent. Placing the ninth block elsewhere destroys the addressing rule that is the whole point of contiguous allocation.

Takeaway. Contiguous allocation trades growth cost for address arithmetic.

OS-U6-Q43MCQhard

An inode holds 12 direct pointers, one single-indirect pointer and one double-indirect pointer. The block size is 4 KB and a block pointer is 4 bytes. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. The double-indirect pointer alone can address 1024 × 1024 = 1 048 576 data blocks, that is, 4 GB of file data.
  2. A file of 8 MB is described entirely by the direct pointers and the single-indirect pointer.
  3. The single-indirect block addresses 1024 data blocks, so the first 1024 blocks of every file are reached through it.
  4. Every file needs at least one indirect block, because the inode can hold only 12 direct pointers.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Pointers per block = block size / pointer size = 4096 / 4 = 1024. One level of indirection addresses 1024 data blocks; two levels address 1024 × 1024.

Step by step.

  1. Direct range: logical blocks 0–11, that is 48 KB.
  2. Single-indirect range: 1024 blocks, that is 4 MB, covering logical blocks 12–1035.
  3. Double-indirect range: 1024 × 1024 = 1 048 576 blocks, that is 4 GB, covering logical blocks 1036 onwards.
  4. Check (B): 8 MB = 2048 blocks, and direct plus single-indirect reaches only 12 + 1024 = 1036 blocks, so a double-indirect block is required. False.
  5. Check (C): the first 12 blocks are direct; the single-indirect block starts at block 12. False.
  6. Check (D): a 1 KB file uses one direct pointer and no indirect block at all. False.

Answer: Option (A) — the double-indirect pointer addresses 1 048 576 blocks, i.e. 4 GB.

Common misconception. The common error is to multiply 1024 by the pointer size instead of the block size, or to assume the single-indirect block also serves the first 12 blocks.

Takeaway. One indirection multiplies capacity by 1024; each further level multiplies again.

OS-U6-Q47MSQmedium

A FAT file system uses 4-byte FAT entries and manages 232 blocks. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. The FAT occupies 232 × 4 bytes = 16 GB, so it is read on demand or partially cached rather than held whole in memory on an ordinary machine.
  2. The directory entry of a file needs only its first block number and its length, because the rest of the chain lives in the FAT.
  3. Because each FAT entry is 4 bytes wide, no single file can be larger than 4 GB.
  4. A FAT-based file system can reach the k-th block of a file with a single disk read, just as contiguous allocation can.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A) and (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The FAT is one table with an entry per block, so its size scales with the disk, not with the files. Traversal is a chain walk through that table.

Step by step.

  1. Entries = 232, each 4 bytes, so the table is 234 bytes = 16 GB. That is far beyond a resident table, so it is cached in pieces. (A) is true.
  2. The directory entry stores the first block and the file length; the successor of every block is in the FAT. (B) is true.
  3. (C) confuses the width of one link with the length of the chain. A 4-byte entry can name any of 232 blocks; the file size limit comes from the number of entries available, not from the entry width. False.
  4. (D) is false: reaching block k means following k links, so it costs k table lookups — cheap in memory, but not one disk read in the way contiguous addressing is.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. Option (C) is the popular error: “4-byte entry means 4 GB file”. The entry width bounds the number of blocks addressable, not the size of one file.

Takeaway. FAT size scales with disk capacity; access cost scales with the position of the block in the chain.

OS-U6-Q51MCQeasy

A file system allocates each file as one contiguous run of disk blocks. Which one of the following must the directory entry of the file record?

  1. only the address of the file's first block
  2. the address of the file's first block together with the length of the allocation
  3. the address of the file's index block
  4. nothing beyond the file name, because the blocks are stored next to the directory entry
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Contiguous allocation reserves one run of consecutive blocks per file. To find block k of the file the system needs only the start address and an offset, so the extent (start, length) is the whole of the metadata.

Step by step.

  1. With only the start address, the system cannot tell where the file ends and the next file begins; the length is essential.
  2. With the start and the length, block k is at start + k, so direct access costs one seek and no traversal.
  3. An index block belongs to indexed allocation, not to contiguous allocation.
  4. Blocks of a file are contiguous with each other, not with the directory entry, which usually lives elsewhere on the disk.

Answer: Option (B) — start address plus length.

Common misconception. Reading “contiguous” as “no metadata needed”. The length is what lets the file system distinguish the end of one file from the beginning of the next.

OS-U6-Q52MCQeasy

A file grows so large that its index block can no longer hold a pointer to every block of the file. In the classic Unix inode design, how are the remaining blocks addressed?

  1. the file is split into several files, each with its own inode
  2. the index block is moved to the last block of the file
  3. the inode holds single-, double- and triple-indirect pointers, each pointing to a block that is itself full of pointers
  4. the last entry of the index block points to the first data block, so the blocks are chained
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A multi-level index extends the reach of a single index block: an indirect block contains block addresses, so one pointer in the inode reaches a whole block of pointers, and two levels reach a block of blocks of pointers.

Step by step.

  1. The inode keeps a small number of direct pointers that address the first blocks of the file without any extra read.
  2. One single-indirect pointer addresses a block holding further block numbers; one double-indirect pointer addresses a block of single-indirect blocks; one triple-indirect pointer goes one level deeper.
  3. The number of addressable blocks grows as 1, n, n², n³ with the depth, so a few pointers in the inode cover files of many gigabytes.
  4. Only the blocks that the file actually uses have their indirect blocks allocated, so a small file pays nothing for the depth.

Answer: Option (C) — single-, double- and triple-indirect pointers.

Common misconception. Believing that a large file needs a larger index block. The index block keeps its fixed size; what changes is how many levels of pointer sit between the inode and the data.

OS-U6-Q53MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about a Unix-like inode and the directory entries that name it are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A directory entry maps a file name to an inode number.
  2. Two hard links to the same file share one inode and therefore one set of data blocks.
  3. Deleting one of the two hard links of a file frees the file's data blocks.
  4. A symbolic link stores the path name of its target rather than the target's inode number.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The inode holds everything about a file except its name; the name lives in a directory entry, which is only a pair (name, inode number). Several entries may carry the same inode number, and the inode keeps a link count of them.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true by construction: the directory is a table of names against inode numbers.
  2. (B) is true: a hard link is a second name for the same inode number, so both names reach the same blocks and the same metadata.
  3. (C) is false: removing one name decrements the link count from 2 to 1, and the blocks are freed only when the count reaches 0.
  4. (D) is true: a symbolic link is a small file whose contents are the target's path, so it can even point at a name that does not exist.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming that unlink deletes the file. It deletes a name; the data survives while any other name, or any open file descriptor, still refers to the inode.

OS-U6-Q54MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about the three classic file-allocation methods are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Contiguous allocation gives the fastest direct access of the three methods.
  2. Linked allocation suffers from external fragmentation.
  3. Indexed allocation spends an index block on every file, even a file of a single block.
  4. FAT keeps the block pointers in one central table instead of inside the data blocks.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The three methods trade metadata overhead against access cost: contiguous needs only (start, length), linked stores a pointer in every data block, and indexed adds a dedicated index block per file.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: block k of a contiguous file is at a computed offset, so one seek reaches it.
  2. (B) is false: linked allocation places each block anywhere on the disk and chains them, so it has no external fragmentation at all, only the internal waste of the pointer field in every block.
  3. (C) is true: the index block is allocated with the file, so even a one-block file occupies two blocks.
  4. (D) is true: that is exactly what a File Allocation Table is — the chain of a linked file lifted out of the data blocks into one table indexed by block number.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Attributing external fragmentation to linked allocation. It is the opposite: chaining removes external fragmentation and pays for it with pointer space and with sequential-only access.

OS-U6-Q55NATeasy

An inode holds 12 direct block pointers and one double-indirect pointer. The block size is 1 KB and a block pointer occupies 4 bytes. How many blocks of the file can be addressed in total?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 65548

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A block of 1 KB holding 4-byte pointers holds 1024 / 4 = 256 pointers, and a pointer of depth d therefore reaches 256^d data blocks.

Step by step.

  1. Pointers per block: 1024 / 4 = 256.
  2. Direct pointers address 12 blocks.
  3. The double-indirect pointer addresses a block of 256 pointers, each to a block of 256 data blocks: 256 × 256 = 65536 blocks.
  4. Total = 12 + 65536 = 65548 blocks, about 64 MB at 1 KB per block.

Answer: 65548 blocks.

Common misconception. Counting the double-indirect pointer as 256 blocks instead of 256². The depth matters: one level is a block of pointers, two levels are a block of blocks of pointers.

OS-U6-Q56MCQhard

A file system replaces linked allocation, in which each data block stores the pointer to the next block, with a FAT, in which all the pointers live in one table indexed by block number. Which one of the following is the principal cost of the change?

  1. every file now needs an index block of its own
  2. the table covers the whole volume, so it is large, is normally cached in main memory, and every allocation writes to the same hot region
  3. direct access becomes impossible, because the table has to be searched linearly
  4. a file can no longer grow beyond the number of entries in its first block
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Moving the chain out of the data blocks into a table changes both the space and the locality of the metadata: the table is per volume, not per file, and it is read and written constantly.

Step by step.

  1. A volume of 2²⁰ blocks with 4-byte entries needs a 4 MB table, whatever the number or size of the files on it.
  2. Because every file's chain passes through that table, the table is cached in main memory and a write to it is a write to one small, hot region of the disk.
  3. Direct access actually improves: following the chain is a sequence of table lookups in memory instead of a sequence of disk reads.
  4. An index block belongs to indexed allocation; a FAT file needs none, which is one of its advantages.

Answer: Option (B) — one volume-wide table that must be cached and updated.

Common misconception. Thinking a FAT is “the same as an index block”. An index block belongs to one file; the FAT is shared by every file on the volume, which is why it must be resident in memory and kept consistent.

OS-U6-Q57MCQmedium

An extent is a contiguous run of blocks described by a single (start, length) pair. Modern file systems such as ext4 keep an extent tree instead of a list of individual block pointers. Which one of the following is the reason?

  1. extents remove the need for free-space management
  2. one entry describes a long contiguous run, so the index stays small while access remains direct and the blocks of a file stay together on the disk
  3. extents guarantee that a file never needs more than one run of blocks
  4. extents make a file's blocks unchangeable once the file has been written
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An extent is contiguous allocation applied to pieces of a file: the index records runs rather than blocks, so a file that is mostly sequential costs almost no metadata and still supports direct access inside each run.

Step by step.

  1. A list of individual block pointers costs 4 bytes per block, so a 1 GB file needs 1 MB of index.
  2. The same file as one extent costs one (start, length) pair, and a fragmented file costs one pair per run.
  3. Inside an extent block k is found by arithmetic, so direct access is preserved.
  4. A file may of course be split into many extents; the point is that it usually is not.

Answer: Option (B) — a small index with direct access and good locality.

Common misconception. Confusing an extent with contiguous allocation of the whole file. Extents allow a file to be split into several runs, which is exactly how they avoid the external-fragmentation problem of a single contiguous run.

OS-U6-Q76MCQeasy

A file system allocates every file as one contiguous run of disk blocks. Files of many different sizes are created and deleted over months of use. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. Space is lost only inside the last block of each file, so the loss is bounded by one block per file.
  2. Free space breaks into holes between the files that remain, so a new file can be refused even when the total free space on the disk is large enough.
  3. Deleting a file always merges its blocks with the neighbouring free runs, so no usable space is ever lost.
  4. The directory entry of a file must hold a pointer to every block of the file.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Contiguous allocation gives each file one unbroken run of blocks, so the free space of the disk is whatever is left in the gaps between runs. A gap too small for the next file is unusable even though it is free: that is external fragmentation.

Step by step.

  1. Each file occupies a single run, so free space consists of the gaps between the runs that remain.
  2. A new file needs one gap at least as large as itself, whatever the sum of all the gaps happens to be.
  3. So a 100-block file can be refused on a disk with thousands of free blocks if no single gap holds 100 blocks.
  4. The waste is not bounded by one block per file; that bounded waste would be internal fragmentation, which contiguous allocation does not create.

Answer: Option (B) — external fragmentation can refuse a file although the total free space is sufficient.

Common misconception. Reading the partly filled last block of a file as the only waste. That waste is internal fragmentation, it is bounded by the block size, and it is not what makes contiguous allocation fail on a fragmented disk.

OS-U6-Q91MSQeasy

Which of the following are stored in a Unix inode rather than in the directory entry that names the file? (Select all that apply.)

  1. The file's block pointers.
  2. The file's size and its timestamps.
  3. The file's name.
  4. The file's owner and permission mode.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An inode holds everything about a file except its name; the directory entry holds only the name and the inode number.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Block pointers, direct and indirect, are inode fields. TRUE.
  2. (B) Size, link count and the three timestamps are inode fields. TRUE.
  3. (C) The name lives in the directory entry, which is why renaming a file does not change its inode. FALSE.
  4. (D) Owner, group and the mode bits are inode fields. TRUE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are TRUE; (C) is FALSE.

Common misconception. Placing the name in the inode. Then a file could have only one name, and hard links would be impossible.

OS-U6-Q77MCQeasy

A process calls open() twice on the same file, with no close() in between, and both calls succeed. Which one of the following is TRUE of the two file descriptors?

  1. They share a single file offset, because both refer to the same inode.
  2. Each has its own file offset: the two calls create two entries in the system-wide open-file table, and both entries point at the same inode.
  3. The second call creates a second inode for the same file, so the two descriptors see different data.
  4. The second call fails, because a file cannot be open twice at the same time.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Three tables take part in an open: the per-process descriptor table, the system-wide open-file table and the inode table. The file offset lives in the system-wide entry, so it is shared only by descriptors produced by fork() or dup(), never by two independent opens.

Step by step.

  1. Each open() adds one entry to the system-wide open-file table, holding the offset, the access mode and a pointer to the inode.
  2. The process's descriptor table gains one slot pointing at that entry.
  3. A second open adds a second system-wide entry with its own offset, pointing at the same inode: the data blocks and the inode are shared, the offsets are not.
  4. fork() and dup() behave differently — they copy a descriptor that points at an existing system-wide entry, so those descriptors do share one offset.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Assuming that sharing an inode means sharing an offset, so that a read through one descriptor appears to move the other. It does not, unless the descriptors were duplicated by fork or dup.

OS-U6-Q78MCQeasy

A directory that holds a very large number of entries is implemented as a hash table keyed on the file name instead of as a linear list. Which one of the following does that change?

  1. A lookup by name takes O(1) time on average instead of a linear scan of the directory.
  2. The directory no longer needs to store the file names.
  3. Two different names can no longer hash to the same bucket.
  4. Listing the directory in alphabetical order becomes faster.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A directory is a table mapping names to inode numbers. A linear list searches it entry by entry; a hash table hashes the name to a bucket and searches only that bucket.

Step by step.

  1. A linear list stores (name, inode) pairs and compares the wanted name with each entry in turn: O(n).
  2. A hash table hashes the name to a bucket and compares only the entries chained there: O(1) on average.
  3. Collisions still occur and are resolved by chaining, so option (C) is false.
  4. Hashing destroys the sorted order of the entries, so a sorted listing must sort first: option (D) is not faster.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Thinking a hash directory removes collisions or keeps the names ordered. It removes the scan, nothing else.

OS-U6-Q82MCQeasy

A file is stored by linked allocation and none of its blocks is in the buffer cache. How many disk block reads are needed to reach the k-th block of the file?

  1. 1
  2. k
  3. log₂ k
  4. k²
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. In linked allocation the address of the k-th block is stored inside the (k−1)-th block, so the chain must be walked from the first block: reaching block k costs k reads.

Step by step.

  1. The directory entry holds only the address of the first block.
  2. Block 1 holds the address of block 2, block 2 the address of block 3, and so on.
  3. So blocks 1 … k must each be read — k reads — before the wanted block is in memory.
  4. Random access therefore costs O(k) per block, and a sequential pass over n blocks costs O(n²) without caching.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Assuming a formula such as log k or a single read, by analogy with array indexing. No arithmetic on block numbers is possible here: the addresses exist only inside the preceding blocks.

OS-U6-Q92MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about hard links and symbolic links in a Unix-like file system are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A hard link is a second directory entry for the same inode, so both names share one link count and one set of data blocks.
  2. A symbolic link stores the target's inode number, so it keeps working after the target is deleted.
  3. A hard link cannot cross a file-system boundary, because an inode number is meaningful only inside one file system.
  4. Removing the last hard link to a file frees its data blocks, even if a symbolic link to the old path still exists.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A directory entry is a pair (name, inode number). A hard link adds a second pair with the same number; a symbolic link creates a new inode whose data is the target's path.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Two directory entries carrying the same inode number are two names for one inode, one link count and one set of blocks. TRUE.
  2. (B) A symbolic link stores a path in its own data block, so it dangles once the target is removed. FALSE.
  3. (C) Inode numbers are per file system, so no directory entry can name an inode in another file system; symbolic links, being paths, can cross. TRUE.
  4. (D) When the link count falls to zero the inode and its blocks are freed, and any symbolic link to the old path is left dangling. TRUE.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D) are TRUE; (B) is FALSE.

Common misconception. Reversing the crossing rule, or believing a symbolic link keeps the data alive. Only hard links hold the link count above zero.

OS-U6-Q84MCQmedium

The block size is 4 KB and a block pointer is 4 bytes. A file is described by a single index block that holds nothing but block pointers. What is the largest file the index block can address?

  1. 1 MiB
  2. 4 MiB
  3. 4 GiB
  4. 16 MiB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The reach of one index block is (block size / pointer size) pointers, each pointing at one block of data.

Step by step.

  1. Pointers per index block = 4096 / 4 = 1024.
  2. Each pointer addresses one 4 KB block.
  3. 1024 × 4 KB = 4096 KB = 4 MiB.
  4. A larger file needs a second level of indirection, that is, chained or multi-level index blocks.

Answer: Option (B) — 4 MiB.

Common misconception. Multiplying 1024 pointers by 4 bytes instead of 4 KB, which gives 4 KB, or leaving the answer as 4096 KB without converting to 4 MiB.

OS-U6-Q86MCQmedium

A file grows one block at a time, no block already written may be moved, and the scheme must waste no space outside the file's last block. Which allocation method fits, at the price of making the k-th block cost k block reads?

  1. Contiguous allocation
  2. Linked allocation
  3. Allocation in fixed-size extents decided when the file is created
  4. Allocation from one pre-reserved partition per file
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Linked allocation takes any free block and chains it on the end, so a file grows a block at a time without moving anything and without external fragmentation; the chain is what makes random access linear.

Step by step.

  1. Contiguous allocation cannot grow without moving the file or finding a larger adjacent gap, so it fails the no-move condition.
  2. Fixed extents must be sized at creation, so growth beyond the extent needs a move or a second extent.
  3. Linked allocation appends a block by writing it and updating one pointer: no existing block moves, and only the last block is partly wasted.
  4. The cost is exactly the one the question names: block k is reached only through blocks 1 … k−1.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Choosing indexed allocation for its random access, which the question rules out, or contiguous allocation because it is fastest when the file happens to fit.

OS-U6-Q99NATmedium

A 256 MB partition is divided into 1 KB blocks. Twelve and a half percent of the partition is reserved for the inode table, and each inode occupies 256 bytes. How many inodes can the partition hold?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 131072

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The inode table is a reserved region of the partition, so the number of inodes is the size of that region divided by the size of one inode.

Step by step.

  1. 12.5% of 256 MB is 256/8 = 32 MB reserved for inodes.
  2. 32 MB / 256 B = 131,072 inodes.
  3. The same figure from the block side: 256 MB holds 262,144 blocks of 1 KB, and each 256 B inode is charged to 2 KB of disk, that is one inode per two blocks: 262,144 / 2 = 131,072.

Answer: 131072.

Common misconception. Dividing the whole partition by the inode size, which gives 1,048,576 and ignores the reservation, or dividing by 2 KB instead of by 256 B.

OS-U6-Q88MCQhard

An inode holds 12 direct pointers, one single-indirect pointer, one double-indirect pointer and one triple-indirect pointer. The block size is 4 KB and a block pointer is 4 bytes. No block is cached. Counting the read of the inode itself, how many disk block reads are needed to fetch the data block that holds byte 5,000,000 of the file?

  1. 2
  2. 3
  3. 4
  4. 5
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The number of reads is the depth of the pointer chain — inode, then every indirect block on the path, then the data block — so the first step is to decide which pointer class holds the byte.

Step by step.

  1. Pointers per block = 4096/4 = 1024, so one indirect block addresses 1024 × 4 KB = 4 MiB of data.
  2. The 12 direct pointers cover 12 × 4096 = 49,152 bytes; with the single-indirect pointer the file reaches 49,152 + 4,194,304 = 4,243,456 bytes.
  3. 5,000,000 > 4,243,456, so the byte lies under the double-indirect pointer; its offset in that region is 5,000,000 − 4,243,456 = 756,544 bytes, that is block 184, since 184 × 4096 = 753,664 ≤ 756,544.
  4. 184 is below 1024, so the block hangs from the first entry of the double-indirect block and then entry 184 of that second-level block.
  5. Reads = inode (1) + double-indirect block (1) + second-level block (1) + data block (1) = 4.

Answer: Option (C) — 4 reads.

Common misconception. Forgetting the inode read, or assuming every byte past the direct pointers costs the same three extra reads. The single-indirect region needs only one.

OS-U6-Q100NAThard

An inode holds 12 direct pointers, one single-indirect pointer, one double-indirect pointer and one triple-indirect pointer. The block size is 4 KB and a block pointer is 4 bytes. How many GiB of file data can the triple-indirect pointer alone address?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 4096

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A k-th level indirect pointer addresses (pointers per block)^k blocks of data, and each block holds 4 KB.

Step by step.

  1. Pointers per block = 4096/4 = 1024.
  2. The triple-indirect pointer reaches 1024³ = 2³⁰ data blocks.
  3. 2³⁰ × 4 KB = 2³⁰ × 2¹² bytes = 2⁴² bytes.
  4. 2⁴² / 2³⁰ = 2¹² = 4096 GiB, that is 4 TiB.

Answer: 4096 GiB.

Common misconception. Stopping at 2³⁰ blocks and reporting 1,073,741,824, which is a block count and not a size in GiB, or dropping the third level and answering 4 GiB, the reach of the double-indirect pointer.

free-space-management 22
OS-U6-Q02MCQeasy

A disk has 2²⁴ blocks, and free space is tracked by a bitmap with one bit per block. What is the size of the bitmap?

  1. 256 KB
  2. 1 MB
  3. 2 MB
  4. 16 MB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A bitmap stores one bit per block, so its size in bits equals the number of blocks; converting to bytes divides by 8.

Step by step.

  1. Bits needed = 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 bits.
  2. Bytes = 16,777,216 ÷ 8 = 2,097,152 bytes.
  3. Megabytes = 2,097,152 ÷ 2²⁰ = 2 MB.
  4. Shortcut: 2²⁴ bits = 2²⁴ ÷ 2³ bytes = 2²¹ bytes = 2 × 2²⁰ bytes = 2 MB.

Answer: Option (C) — 2 MB.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 256 KB is what you get by dividing by 8 twice, i.e. treating the answer as 2²⁴ ÷ 64.
  • (B) 1 MB forgets that one byte holds 8 bits.
  • (D) 16 MB is 2²⁴ bytes, i.e. one byte per block.

Common misconception. Losing the factor of 8 in one direction or the other. Write the unit chain explicitly: bits → bytes (÷8) → KB (÷2¹⁰) → MB (÷2²⁰).

Takeaway. Bitmap size in bytes = number of blocks ÷ 8; here 2²⁴ ÷ 8 = 2 MB.

OS-U6-Q06NATeasy

A disk has 1,000,000 blocks and its free-space bitmap uses one bit per block. How many bytes does the bitmap occupy?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 125000

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. One bit per block, so the number of bits equals the number of blocks; dividing by 8 gives bytes.

Step by step.

  1. Bits required = 1,000,000.
  2. Bytes = 1,000,000 ÷ 8.
  3. 1,000,000 ÷ 8 = 125,000 exactly, because 1,000,000 is divisible by 8.

Answer: 125,000 bytes (about 122 KB).

Common misconception. Reporting 1,000,000 bytes by keeping one byte per block, or rounding to 125,001 to “allow a spare bit”. No spare bit is needed: 1,000,000 is an exact multiple of 8.

Takeaway. Bitmap bytes = blocks ÷ 8; only round up when the block count is not a multiple of 8.

OS-U6-Q10MCQmedium

In the counting method of free-space management, each free block stores a count together with a pointer to the next free block. What does the count record?

  1. The number of files that currently share the block.
  2. The number of consecutive free blocks that follow this one, so a run of k free blocks is described by a single entry.
  3. The number of bits in the bitmap that are still unused.
  4. The number of times the block has been written since it was formatted.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The counting method compresses the free list: instead of one entry per free block, one entry describes a whole run of contiguous free blocks.

Step by step.

  1. A free block stores (count, next), where next is the address of the next entry and count is how many contiguous free blocks start at this address.
  2. A disk with large free runs is then represented by a short list, so the list fits in memory more easily.
  3. Allocation takes the first entry with a large enough count and reduces that count.
  4. The count is therefore a length of a run, not a usage statistic.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) sharing is not tracked in the free-space structure at all.
  • (C) the counting method does not use a bitmap.
  • (D) a write counter has no role in allocation.

Common misconception. Confusing counting with grouping. Grouping stores many free-block addresses in one free block; counting stores one address and a run length.

Takeaway. Counting = run-length encoding of the free list.

OS-U6-Q14MCQeasy

Which free-space method makes it cheapest to decide whether the disk holds a run of 8 consecutive free blocks?

  1. A linked free list
  2. The counting method
  3. A bitmap
  4. A grouping list
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The four free-space methods differ in what one entry describes: one block (linked list, bitmap), one run (counting), or many addresses at once (grouping). A question about consecutive blocks is a question about the bitmap's shape.

Step by step.

  1. A bitmap stores the state of block i in bit i, so consecutive blocks occupy consecutive bits. A run of 8 free blocks is simply 8 consecutive zero bits — a word-sized test on a machine whose word is 8 bits or wider.
  2. A linked free list holds only the addresses of free blocks in no particular order, so a run must be detected by sorting or by repeated lookups.
  3. The counting method records runs, but a run of 8 may be split across several entries and its neighbours still have to be checked.
  4. A grouping list is designed for bulk collection of free blocks, not for testing adjacency.

Answer: Option (C) — the bitmap.

Common misconception. Choosing the counting method because it is “about runs”. Counting summarises runs that already exist; the bitmap is what lets you test adjacency directly, which is what the question asks.

Takeaway. Bitmap = positional, so adjacency is free; list methods = address only, so adjacency is not represented.

OS-U6-Q18MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about free-space management are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. If the bitmap is held in memory, finding a free block needs no disk access, but the in-memory copy must eventually be written back to disk.
  2. A linked free list needs one pointer per free block and is easy to keep consistent on disk, but finding a run of consecutive free blocks means walking the list.
  3. Grouping stores the addresses of several free blocks inside the first free block, which reduces the number of disk reads needed to collect a large number of free blocks.
  4. The counting method represents a run of k free blocks with k separate entries.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The four methods are alternative encodings of the same information — which blocks are free. They differ in memory cost, disk cost and the operations they make cheap.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. A memory-resident bitmap answers the question with a bit scan, but it is a cache of on-disk state and must be flushed, which is why a crash can leave it inconsistent unless it is rebuilt at mount time.
  2. (B) True. Each free block stores the address of the next, so consistency needs only one pointer update per allocation; adjacency is not represented, so runs require a walk.
  3. (C) True. Grouping packs n − 1 free-block addresses plus a pointer to the next group into one block, so a single read yields a whole group of addresses.
  4. (D) False. That is the opposite of the counting method, which represents a run of k blocks with one entry.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C) are true; (D) is false.

Common misconception. Mixing up counting and grouping. Counting stores (address, run length); grouping stores many addresses in one block.

Takeaway. Bitmap: cheap test, memory cost. Linked list: cheap update, no adjacency. Counting: run-length. Grouping: bulk collection.

OS-U6-Q22NAThard

A 4 TB disk is divided into 4 KB blocks, and free space is tracked by a bitmap with one bit per block. What is the size of the bitmap, in MB? (Use 1 TB = 2⁴⁰ bytes and 1 MB = 2²⁰ bytes; enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 128

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Bitmap size = number of blocks ÷ 8 bytes. The number of blocks is the disk size divided by the block size, so both quantities should be kept as powers of two.

Step by step.

  1. Disk = 4 TB = 4 × 2⁴⁰ = 2⁴² bytes.
  2. Block = 4 KB = 2¹² bytes.
  3. Blocks = 2⁴² ÷ 2¹² = 2³⁰ = 1,073,741,824.
  4. Bits = 2³⁰, so bytes = 2³⁰ ÷ 2³ = 2²⁷.
  5. MB = 2²⁷ ÷ 2²⁰ = 2⁷ = 128.

Answer: 128 MB.

Common misconception. Losing one power of two by treating 1 KB as 1000 bytes and 1 MB as 10⁶ bytes, which gives about 119 MB, or by forgetting the ÷8 and answering 1024 MB.

Takeaway. Bitmap MB = (disk in MB) ÷ (block in bytes) ÷ 8. Here 4,194,304 MB ÷ 4096 ÷ 8 = 128 MB.

OS-U6-Q27NATeasy

A file system tracks free space with a bitmap holding one bit per disk block. The bitmap is kept entirely in main memory and occupies 64 KB. How many blocks does the disk have?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 524288

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. One bit per block means the number of blocks equals the number of bits in the bitmap. Convert bytes to bits with a factor of 8.

Step by step.

  1. Bitmap size = 64 KB = 64 × 1024 = 65 536 bytes.
  2. Each byte carries 8 bits, so the bitmap holds 65 536 × 8 = 524 288 bits.
  3. One bit per block, therefore 524 288 blocks.
  4. Check the other way: 524 288 blocks need 524 288 bits = 65 536 bytes = 64 KB. ✔

Answer: 524288 blocks (a 64 KB bitmap covers 219 blocks).

Common misconception. The usual slip is to answer 65 536 by forgetting the factor of 8, or to use 1000 instead of 1024 for KB.

Takeaway. Bitmap bits = blocks; bytes = blocks / 8; so blocks = 8 × bytes.

OS-U6-Q34MCQeasy

Why is a bitmap usually preferred to a linked free list for tracking free space on a large disk?

  1. A bitmap needs fewer bits per block than a free list needs bytes per block, so it is always the smaller structure on disk.
  2. A bitmap never has to be written back to disk, because it can always be recomputed from the directory structure.
  3. A bitmap is the only structure that allows a file to occupy non-contiguous blocks.
  4. A bitmap can be held in main memory, so a free block is found without any disk I/O, whereas walking a free list costs a disk read for every block considered.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The dominant cost in free-space management is not the size of the structure but how many disk reads it takes to use it. A bitmap is dense and fixed-size, so it fits in memory and supports scanning.

Step by step.

  1. A bitmap uses 1 bit per block; a linked free list uses at least one pointer per free block, so on disk the list is larger, not smaller. Option (A) is therefore backwards.
  2. Because the bitmap is a dense array, it is normally cached in main memory and the first free block is found by scanning words — no disk access at all.
  3. A free list is scattered through the free blocks themselves, so each step of the walk is a disk read.
  4. Options (B) and (C) are simply false: the bitmap is persistent state that must be written back, and every allocation method supports non-contiguous blocks.

Answer: Option (D) — the bitmap is compact and dense, so it lives in memory and costs no I/O to search.

Common misconception. Students often pick the option that says the bitmap is smaller on disk. It is smaller, but the decisive advantage is that it is searchable in memory.

Takeaway. Bitmaps win on search cost, not on disk footprint.

OS-U6-Q38MSQmedium

A file system keeps its free-space bitmap in main memory and writes it to disk lazily, only when the buffer is flushed. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A crash before the bitmap reaches disk can leave blocks marked free that are in fact in use, so a consistency check must rebuild the free list at boot.
  2. Because the bitmap is in memory, a free block is located by scanning words in memory rather than by reading blocks from disk.
  3. A bitmap needs no consistency check at all, because it is a derived structure that the file system can always recompute from the allocation chains.
  4. If the bitmap reaches disk but the corresponding directory update does not, blocks can be marked in use while no file refers to them, which leaks space until the check repairs it.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Caching a metadata structure in memory decouples its on-disk copy from the real allocation state. Every crash between the two writes leaves the pair inconsistent in one of two directions.

Step by step.

  1. Bitmap written, allocation not: blocks are marked used but unreachable — a space leak. So (D) is true.
  2. Allocation written, bitmap not: blocks are marked free while a file points at them, so a later allocation can hand out a live block and corrupt two files. So (A) is true.
  3. The in-memory copy is what makes allocation cheap: the search is a memory scan. So (B) is true.
  4. Option (C) is false in the sense that matters: the bitmap is persistent state, not a view. Rebuilding it is exactly what a consistency check (fsck) does precisely because it can disagree with the chains.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. The tempting answer is (C): “the bitmap is derived, so it can always be rebuilt”. It can be rebuilt — but only by a check that walks every inode, which is why the inconsistency is a real hazard, not a non-issue.

Takeaway. Lazy metadata caching always buys speed with a consistency window; fsck exists to close it.

OS-U6-Q42MCQeasy

Free space on a disk consists of a few very long contiguous runs. Which free-space structure represents this state most compactly?

  1. A bitmap, because one bit per block is the smallest possible per-block record.
  2. A linked free list, because it needs no space outside the free blocks themselves.
  3. The counting method, because one entry describes a whole run of consecutive free blocks.
  4. A grouping list, because it stores several free block addresses in one block.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The counting method is run-length encoding for free space: each entry stores a first free block and the length of the run that starts there. Its cost is proportional to the number of runs, not to the number of free blocks.

Step by step.

  1. A bitmap always costs one bit per block on the disk, however the free blocks are arranged, so it does not exploit long runs.
  2. A linked free list stores one pointer per free block, so a run of a million blocks costs a million pointers — worse than the bitmap.
  3. Counting stores one (address, count) pair per run, so a few long runs collapse to a few entries.
  4. Grouping reduces I/O when allocating many blocks, but it still records addresses individually, so it does not compress a long run.

Answer: Option (C) — the counting method, which is run-length encoding.

Common misconception. The trap is to reason about worst case rather than this case. Counting is excellent for long runs and terrible for a disk of scattered single free blocks, where every run has length one.

Takeaway. Choose the free-space structure by the shape of the free space: runs favour counting, scatter favours a bitmap.

OS-U6-Q45MCQeasy

A disk has 231 blocks and free space is tracked by a bitmap with one bit per block. What is the size of the bitmap?

  1. 128 MB
  2. 256 MB
  3. 512 MB
  4. 2 GB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The bitmap holds one bit per block, so its size in bits equals the block count; convert bits to bytes by dividing by 8, then bytes to MB by dividing by 220.

Step by step.

  1. Bits = 231.
  2. Bytes = 231 / 8 = 228 bytes.
  3. MB = 228 / 220 = 28 = 256 MB.
  4. Sanity check: 231 blocks at 8 blocks per byte is 228 bytes, and 228 bytes is a quarter of a gigabyte. ✔

Answer: Option (B) — 256 MB.

Common misconception. The standard slip is to forget the factor of 8 and answer 2 GB, or to mix powers of 2 with powers of 10.

Takeaway. Bitmap bytes = blocks / 8; keep everything in powers of two.

OS-U6-Q49MCQmedium

In the grouping method of free-space management, a free block stores as many free block addresses as will fit, together with the address of the block holding the next group. With a 4 KB block and 4-byte addresses, how many free blocks can be described by two chained group blocks?

  1. 1024
  2. 1023
  3. 2046
  4. 2047
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution
