Concept. One block of size B with addresses of size P holds B/P slots. One of those slots is spent pointing at the next group block, so B/P − 1 free blocks are described per block.

Step by step.

  1. Slots per block = 4096 / 4 = 1024.
  2. One slot holds the pointer to the next group, leaving 1023 free block addresses per group block.
  3. Two chained blocks describe 1023 + 1023 = 2046 free blocks.
  4. The third block would describe 3069, and so on — the chain is what makes grouping scale.

Answer: Option (C) — 2046 free blocks.

Common misconception. The frequent error is 2048 (1024 slots × 2), which forgets that each group block spends one slot on the link to the next. 2047 comes from deducting the pointer only once.

Takeaway. Grouping: B/P − 1 addresses per block; n chained blocks describe n(B/P − 1) free blocks.

OS-U6-Q58MCQeasy

Which one of the following free-space structures stores one bit per block, so that a block can be freed in constant time and the whole structure can be held in main memory for a moderately sized disk?

  1. the bitmap
  2. the linked free list
  3. the counting method
  4. the grouping method
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A bitmap gives every block exactly one bit, addressed by block number, so allocating or freeing a known block is a single bit operation.

Step by step.

  1. Bit i of the bitmap is 1 when block i is free and 0 when it is allocated.
  2. Freeing block i is one write to word i / 32, hence O(1).
  3. The size is n / 8 bytes for n blocks, small enough to keep in memory.
  4. A linked list or the counting and grouping methods store addresses, so each operation follows pointers and none of them can free a block without locating it.

Answer: Option (A) — the bitmap.

Common misconception. Believing a bitmap is too large to be practical. One bit per block is the smallest per-block representation there is; a 4 TB disk in 4 KB blocks needs only 128 MB.

OS-U6-Q59MCQeasy

A 64-block disk tracks free space with a bitmap in which bit i records block i, bit 0 being the least significant bit of the first 32-bit word. The first word of the bitmap is 0xF0FF0000. Which block does a first-fit allocator that always starts its search at block 0 choose?

  1. block 8
  2. block 16
  3. block 20
  4. block 24
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A bitmap is read word by word, and the lowest set bit of a word is the first free block in it.

Step by step.

  1. 0xF0FF0000 has zero in its low 16 bits, so blocks 0 to 15 are all allocated.
  2. Bits 16 to 31 hold 0xF0FF, which is not zero, so a free block exists in the upper half.
  3. The lowest set bit of 0xF0FF0000 is bit 16, since the low byte of the upper half (0xFF) occupies bits 16 to 23.
  4. First fit therefore returns block 16.

Answer: Option (B) — block 16.

Common misconception. Reading the word left to right. Bit 0 is the least significant bit, so the numbering of blocks inside a word runs from the right-hand end.

OS-U6-Q60MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about free-space management are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A bitmap uses one bit per disk block and is small enough to be held in main memory for a moderate volume.
  2. A linked free list can be searched for a run of contiguous free blocks only by following the list.
  3. The counting method records, for each run of contiguous free blocks, the first block and the length of the run.
  4. The grouping method stores the addresses of every free block of the volume in a single block.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The four methods differ in what they store: bits (bitmap), addresses chained one at a time (linked list), runs (counting), and addresses packed many per block with a link to the next group (grouping).

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: n blocks need n/8 bytes, which fits in memory for volumes of ordinary size.
  2. (B) is true: the list gives no index, so finding k consecutive free blocks means walking until such a run appears.
  3. (C) is true: that pair is exactly the record the counting method keeps per run.
  4. (D) is false: grouping fills one block with as many free addresses as fit, together with the address of the block holding the next group, so a chain of blocks is needed.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Mixing up grouping and counting. Grouping stores many addresses per block and links blocks; counting stores one (block, count) pair per run of contiguous blocks.

OS-U6-Q61NATmedium

In the grouping method of free-space management, a free block holds 127 free-block addresses together with one pointer to the block that holds the next group. How many free-block addresses can a chain of 3 group blocks describe in total?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 381

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Grouping packs as many free-block addresses into one block as will fit and uses one slot for the link to the next group; the chain is read group by group.

Step by step.

  1. Each group block describes 127 free blocks; the 128th slot is the link, not an address.
  2. A chain of 3 group blocks therefore describes 3 × 127 addresses.
  3. 3 × 127 = 381.

Answer: 381 free-block addresses.

Common misconception. Counting the link slot as an address, which gives 384. The pointer to the next group occupies one of the block's slots and describes no free block.

OS-U6-Q62MCQhard

A bitmap allocator keeps a roving pointer to the block it allocated last and starts every search from there instead of from block 0. Compared with always starting at block 0, which one of the following is the effect?

  1. allocation becomes slower, because every search may have to wrap around the end of the bitmap
  2. consecutive allocations are spread across the disk, so free space stays evenly distributed and the length of each search is amortised, at the price of longer seeks between logically adjacent blocks
  3. the bitmap can no longer be held in main memory
  4. runs of contiguous free blocks can no longer be found
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A roving pointer turns first fit into next fit. The pointer is an optimisation for the search and a policy for placement at the same time.

Step by step.

  1. Always starting at block 0 makes the search scan the same already-allocated prefix on every call, so the total scanning cost grows with the number of allocations.
  2. Starting where the last allocation ended means the scan resumes immediately after the busy prefix, so the amortised scan cost is small.
  3. Because successive files are placed in different regions, free space stays spread over the volume rather than being consumed from one end.
  4. The price is locality: two files written one after the other are no longer adjacent, so reading them in sequence costs more seeks, and large contiguous runs become rarer over time.

Answer: Option (B) — better search cost and distribution, worse locality.

Common misconception. Treating the roving pointer as a pure speed-up. It also changes where blocks are placed, which is why real allocators pair it with policies that prefer to keep a file's blocks together.

OS-U6-Q63NATeasy

A disk has 2¹⁶ blocks and its free-space bitmap is held as an array of 32-bit words. How many words does the bitmap occupy?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 2048

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A bitmap is one bit per block, packed into machine words, so the number of words is the number of blocks divided by the word size.

Step by step.

  1. Blocks: 2¹⁶ = 65536.
  2. Bits per word: 32.
  3. Words = 65536 / 32 = 2048, which is 8 KB of memory.

Answer: 2048 words.

Common misconception. Dividing by 8 (bits per byte) and calling the result words, or forgetting that the last word is used even when the block count is not a multiple of the word size.

OS-U6-Q97NATeasy

A free-space bitmap is held as 32-bit words. Bit i of word w records block 32w + i, bit 0 of a word is its least significant bit, and a 1 means the block is in use. Word 0 holds 0x0000FFFF and every later word is zero. What is the number of the first free block?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 16

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A bitmap is read bit by bit, and the convention for which bit is which decides the answer; here the low bit of a word is the low-numbered block.

Step by step.

  1. 0x0000FFFF has its low 16 bits set and its high 16 bits clear.
  2. With bit 0 the least significant bit, the set bits are blocks 0 to 15, all of them in use.
  3. Bits 16 to 31 are zero, so block 16 is the first free block.
  4. Every later word is zero, so no earlier free block exists and word 0 settles the question.

Answer: 16.

Common misconception. Reading the hexadecimal digits left to right and answering 0, or treating a 1 as free. Both invert the convention the question states.

OS-U6-Q80MCQeasy

In the linked-list method of free-space management, where is the head of the free list kept?

  1. In the first free block of the volume, which is found by scanning the disk.
  2. In the volume's superblock, at a known location on disk, and copied into memory when the volume is mounted.
  3. In the inode of the most recently deleted file.
  4. In the boot block, so that the loader can read it.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The free list is a chain threaded through the free blocks themselves, so only its head must be stored somewhere fixed: it lives in the file-system metadata and is cached in memory while the volume is mounted.

Step by step.

  1. Each free block stores the address of the next free block.
  2. The address of the first free block cannot be stored in a free block, because nothing would point to it.
  3. It is kept in the superblock, a fixed structure at a known offset on the volume, and loaded at mount time.
  4. The boot block holds bootstrap code, not file-system metadata.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Believing the list is self-starting. Without the head pointer in the superblock the whole free list would be unreachable after a reboot.

OS-U6-Q87MCQmedium

A file system keeps its free-space bitmap in main memory and writes it back to disk only when the buffer is evicted. The machine crashes after several blocks were allocated but before the bitmap reached the disk. Which is the most serious consequence?

  1. The blocks that were allocated are lost for ever, so the volume slowly shrinks.
  2. On the next mount those blocks still look free in the disk copy, so they can be handed out a second time while the files that already use them are intact, corrupting data.
  3. The superblock is overwritten by the in-memory bitmap.
  4. Every file on the volume becomes unreadable.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. After a crash the bitmap on disk is the authority. Allocation updates only the memory copy, so a crash can leave blocks that are in use still marked free on disk.

Step by step.

  1. Allocation sets bits to 1 in the memory copy; the disk copy still shows 0 for those blocks.
  2. The crash destroys the memory copy, so the stale disk copy is what gets loaded next.
  3. The allocator sees those blocks as free and may give them to another file, so two files share blocks and both are damaged.
  4. The opposite error — bits set to 1 for blocks that are actually free — only leaks space, which is harmless by comparison.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Assuming a stale bitmap merely leaks blocks. Leaked space costs capacity; a block marked free while in use is a correctness failure.

OS-U6-Q90MCQhard

A journaling file system runs in ordered mode: the data blocks of a file reach their final location before the metadata that points at them is committed to the journal. Which failure is this ordering designed to prevent?

  1. Loss of the journal itself during a crash.
  2. Metadata that points at blocks whose contents were never written, so stale or garbage data appears as the file's content after recovery.
  3. Two processes being given the same free block at the same time.
  4. An inode number being reused before the file that held it is deleted.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Journaling makes metadata updates atomic, but atomicity alone still allows a committed pointer to a data block that was never written. Ordered mode adds the rule that the data lands first.

Step by step.

  1. In writeback mode data and metadata are journaled independently, so after a crash the metadata may be committed while the data block still holds old contents.
  2. Ordered mode writes the data blocks to their final location before the metadata commit.
  3. So a committed pointer always finds real file data, and recovery cannot expose another file's stale blocks.
  4. Concurrent allocation is handled by locking, and inode reuse by the link count; neither is a journaling ordering property.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Believing journaling protects file data. It protects metadata consistency; ordered mode is the extra rule that keeps the data from being garbage.

disk-scheduling-fcfs-sstf-scan-cscan-look 25
OS-U6-Q03MCQeasy

Which disk-scheduling policy services requests strictly in the order of their arrival, so that the head may sweep back and forth across the disk?

  1. SSTF
  2. FCFS
  3. SCAN
  4. C-SCAN
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A disk-scheduling policy decides the order in which pending requests are served. Only one of the standard policies ignores the current head position altogether: FCFS, which serves the queue as it stands.

Step by step.

  1. FCFS takes the requests in arrival order, so the head can jump from cylinder 98 to 183 and back to 37 — sweeping in both directions as the queue dictates.
  2. SSTF always takes the nearest request, so the head moves monotonically toward a locality and does not sweep the whole disk.
  3. SCAN and C-SCAN impose a direction on the sweep by construction.
  4. Hence the only policy whose order is fixed by arrival time alone is FCFS.

Answer: Option (B) — FCFS.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) SSTF reorders the queue by distance from the head on every step.
  • (C) SCAN sweeps to the end of the disk in one direction before reversing.
  • (D) C-SCAN sweeps in one direction only and returns to the start without servicing.

Common misconception. Assuming FCFS is “fair but useless”. It is the baseline: it can be very expensive in head movement, but its behaviour is easy to predict and it never reorders requests.

Takeaway. FCFS = arrival order; SSTF = nearest first; SCAN/C-SCAN = sweep with a direction.

OS-U6-Q07NATeasy

A disk has 200 cylinders numbered 0 to 199. The head is at cylinder 53, and the pending queue in arrival order is 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. Under FCFS, what is the total head movement, in cylinders?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 640

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Head movement is the sum of the absolute differences between consecutive cylinders visited, starting from the current head position. Under FCFS the visit order is the arrival order.

Step by step.

  1. 53 → 98 = 45
  2. 98 → 183 = 85
  3. 183 → 37 = 146
  4. 37 → 122 = 85
  5. 122 → 14 = 108
  6. 14 → 124 = 110
  7. 124 → 65 = 59
  8. 65 → 67 = 2
  9. Total = 45 + 85 + 146 + 85 + 108 + 110 + 59 + 2 = 640.

Answer: 640 cylinders.

Common misconception. Summing the request positions (710) instead of the gaps between consecutive positions. Movement is about travel, not about where the requests are.

Takeaway. Under FCFS the head zig-zags across the queue; the 146-cylinder jump from 183 back to 37 is most of the waste.

OS-U6-Q11MCQmedium

The head is at cylinder 53 on a 200-cylinder disk (0 to 199), and the pending queue is 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. Which one of the following is the order in which SSTF services these requests?

  1. 53, 65, 67, 37, 14, 98, 122, 124, 183
  2. 53, 37, 14, 65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183
  3. 53, 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67
  4. 53, 65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183, 14, 37
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. SSTF always serves the pending request nearest to the current head position, recomputing the nearest after every service. It is a greedy policy, not a sweep.

Step by step. From 53 the distances are 45 (98), 130 (183), 16 (37), 69 (122), 39 (14), 71 (124), 12 (65), 14 (67).

  1. 53 → 65 (12 cylinders). Nearest remaining to 65 is 67.
  2. 65 → 67 (2). From 67 the nearest is 37 (30), then 14 (23).
  3. 67 → 37 → 14. From 14 the nearest is 98 (84).
  4. 14 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183, each step taking the closest of what remains.
  5. Total movement = 12 + 2 + 30 + 23 + 84 + 24 + 2 + 59 = 236.

Answer: Option (A) — 53, 65, 67, 37, 14, 98, 122, 124, 183, total 236 cylinders.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is LOOK moving toward cylinder 0, which goes to 14 before turning; total 208.
  • (C) is the FCFS arrival order; total 640.
  • (D) is an outward sweep from 53 that ignores 37 and 14 until the end, which SSTF would never do.

Common misconception. Sweeping outward from the head and calling it SSTF. SSTF reverses direction whenever the other side becomes nearer — here it turns at 67 and heads down to 14.

Takeaway. SSTF: at each step, take the nearest; the path may zig-zag.

OS-U6-Q15NATmedium

The head is at cylinder 53 on a 200-cylinder disk (0 to 199) and is moving toward cylinder 0. The pending queue is 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. Under SCAN, and counting the travel all the way to cylinder 0 and all the way to cylinder 199, what is the total head movement in cylinders?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 236

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. SCAN, the elevator algorithm, serves every request in the current direction, travels to the end of the disk, reverses, and then serves what is left. The end-of-disk travel is part of the movement.

Step by step.

  1. Moving toward 0 from 53, the requests below the head are 37 and 14, taken in decreasing order: 53 → 37 (16) → 14 (23).
  2. SCAN continues to the end of the disk: 14 → 0 (14).
  3. It reverses and serves the rest in increasing order: 0 → 65 (65) → 67 (2) → 98 (31) → 122 (24) → 124 (2) → 183 (59).
  4. Total = 16 + 23 + 14 + 65 + 2 + 31 + 24 + 2 + 59 = 236.

Answer: 236 cylinders.

Common misconception. Answering 208 by stopping at 14 and calling that SCAN. Reversing at the last request is LOOK, not SCAN; the 28 cylinders of travel to 0 and back to 14 are exactly the difference between 236 and 208.

Takeaway. SCAN pays for the full sweep to the disk edge; LOOK does not. Read the question for which one is named.

OS-U6-Q19MCQmedium

Which one of the following statements about C-SCAN is TRUE?

  1. It serves requests in one direction only, and when the head reaches the last cylinder it returns to the first cylinder without serving requests on the way.
  2. It reverses direction at the last pending request instead of at the end of the disk.
  3. It gives a longer maximum wait than SCAN to a request that lies just behind the head.
  4. It is identical to LOOK except that the request queue is sorted first.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. C-SCAN, the circular SCAN, treats the disk as a ring: it sweeps in one direction only, and on reaching the end it jumps back to the start without servicing anything on the return.

Step by step.

  1. Requests ahead of the head are served in increasing cylinder order.
  2. At the last cylinder the head returns to cylinder 0. The return is travel, not service, so requests passed on the way wait.
  3. Serving then continues in the same direction from 0 upward.
  4. Because every request waits for at most one sweep plus the return, the spread of waiting times is more uniform than under SCAN, where requests just behind the head wait almost two sweeps.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) describes LOOK, which turns at the last request.
  • (C) reverses the truth: C-SCAN is the policy that removes that long wait, at the cost of a full return sweep.
  • (D) confuses C-SCAN with LOOK; the defining feature is the unserviced return, not the sorting.

Common misconception. Thinking C-SCAN is strictly better than SCAN. It equalises waiting time but moves the head over the whole disk on every cycle, so total movement is usually larger.

Takeaway. SCAN = sweep both ways. C-SCAN = sweep one way, fly back empty.

OS-U6-Q23MCQhard

On a 200-cylinder disk (0 to 199) the head is at cylinder 53 and the pending queue is 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. FCFS moves the head 640 cylinders, which is the least of the four policies named in the other options.
  2. LOOK, moving first toward cylinder 0, moves the head 208 cylinders, which is less than SSTF's 236 and less than SCAN's 236.
  3. SCAN, moving toward 0 and travelling to cylinder 0, moves the head 208 cylinders.
  4. SSTF moves the head 640 cylinders, because it reverses direction at every request.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The four policies produce four different orders on the same queue, so their total movements must be computed separately. Only the comparison is common to them.

Step by step.

  1. FCFS, arrival order: 45 + 85 + 146 + 85 + 108 + 110 + 59 + 2 = 640.
  2. SSTF, nearest first: 12 + 2 + 30 + 23 + 84 + 24 + 2 + 59 = 236, order 53, 65, 67, 37, 14, 98, 122, 124, 183.
  3. SCAN toward 0: down to 14, on to 0 (53 cylinders), then up through 65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183 (183 cylinders) = 236.
  4. LOOK toward 0: down to 14 (53 cylinders), then straight up to 183 without going to 0: 16 + 23 + 51 + 2 + 31 + 24 + 2 + 59 = 208.
  5. So LOOK is the cheapest of the four here, and it beats both SSTF and SCAN on this queue.

Answer: Option (B) — LOOK toward 0 gives 208, less than SSTF's and SCAN's 236.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) FCFS does give 640, but that is the largest of the four totals, not the least.
  • (C) SCAN gives 236; 208 is LOOK, which does not travel to cylinder 0.
  • (D) 640 is the FCFS figure, and SSTF does not reverse at every request.

Common misconception. Assuming SSTF is always best. It is greedy on the next step only: here LOOK's single sweep serves the same requests with less travel, because SSTF wastes movement diving to 14 and climbing back.

Takeaway. Compute, do not rank. On this queue the four totals are 640, 236, 236 and 208.

OS-U6-Q25MSQhard

Which of the following statements about disk-scheduling policies are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. SSTF can starve a request that lies far from the head if nearer requests keep arriving.
  2. SCAN bounds the waiting time of any request, because the head sweeps the whole disk in each direction.
  3. C-SCAN gives a more uniform waiting time than SCAN, because it always sweeps in one direction and returns without servicing requests.
  4. LOOK differs from SCAN only in that LOOK never reverses its direction of travel.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each policy is defined by a victim rule for the next request, and each rule has a fairness consequence. Greedy policies can starve; sweep policies bound the wait; the circular variant equalises it.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. SSTF always takes the nearest pending request. If a steady stream of near requests arrives, the far one is never nearest and may wait indefinitely.
  2. (B) True. SCAN passes every cylinder once per sweep, so a request waits at most the time for the head to reach it — one full sweep plus the return leg. That is a bound, unlike SSTF.
  3. (C) True. Under SCAN a request just behind the head waits for almost two full sweeps, while one just ahead waits very little; under C-SCAN every request waits between zero and one sweep plus the fixed return, so the spread is narrower.
  4. (D) False. LOOK reverses at the last pending request in each direction, exactly as SCAN reverses at the end of the disk. Both reverse; they differ in where they reverse.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C) are true; (D) is false.

Common misconception. Believing a smarter policy cannot starve. SSTF is the classic starvation example on disks, just as shortest-job-first is on the CPU. Fairness comes from the sweep, not from the greedy choice.

Takeaway. Greedy = fast average, possible starvation. SCAN = bounded wait. C-SCAN = bounded and uniform wait, at the cost of the return sweep.

OS-U6-Q28MCQeasy

Which one of the following statements about the LOOK disk-scheduling policy is TRUE?

  1. LOOK travels to the physical end of the disk in each direction, so its total head movement always equals that of SCAN for the same queue.
  2. LOOK reverses direction at the last pending request in the current direction, so the head never travels past the outermost request.
  3. LOOK serves requests strictly in arrival order, but only while the head is moving in the same direction as the request.
  4. LOOK is C-SCAN with the return sweep removed, so its waiting time is unbounded.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. SCAN and LOOK are both elevator policies. SCAN goes all the way to the disk edge (cylinder 0 or the last cylinder) before turning; LOOK turns as soon as no further request lies ahead.

Step by step.

  1. In SCAN the head reaches the physical end of the disk even when the last request is far short of it, and that empty travel is wasted movement.
  2. LOOK examines the queue: if nothing lies beyond the current position in the direction of travel, it reverses at the last request it has just served.
  3. So LOOK's movement is never larger than SCAN's for the same queue, and it is strictly smaller whenever the outermost request is not at the disk edge.
  4. Option (C) describes FCFS, not LOOK.

Answer: Option (B) — LOOK turns back at the last request, not at the disk edge.

Common misconception. Students often think LOOK and SCAN are the same algorithm. They differ exactly in where the turn happens, and that difference changes the head-movement total whenever the outermost request is inside the edge.

Takeaway. SCAN = elevator to the wall. LOOK = elevator to the last passenger.

OS-U6-Q31NATeasy

A disk has 200 cylinders numbered 0 to 199. The head is at cylinder 100 and the pending requests, in arrival order, are 55, 58, 39, 18, 90, 160, 150, 38, 184. Under FCFS, what is the total head movement, in cylinders?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 498

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. FCFS serves the queue in arrival order and ignores where the head is, so the total is the sum of the absolute differences between consecutive positions, starting from the initial head position.

Step by step.

  1. 100 → 55 = 45
  2. 55 → 58 = 3
  3. 58 → 39 = 19
  4. 39 → 18 = 21
  5. 18 → 90 = 72
  6. 90 → 160 = 70
  7. 160 → 150 = 10
  8. 150 → 38 = 112
  9. 38 → 184 = 146
  10. Sum = 45 + 3 + 19 + 21 + 72 + 70 + 10 + 112 + 146 = 498.

Answer: 498 cylinders.

Common misconception. The frequent error is to sort the queue first, which is what SSTF or SCAN would do; FCFS keeps arrival order. A second error is to omit the move from the initial head position to the first request.

Takeaway. FCFS total = Σ |positioni+1 − positioni| in arrival order, beginning at the head.

OS-U6-Q35MCQmedium

The head is at cylinder 100 on a 200-cylinder disk (0 to 199), and the pending queue is 55, 58, 39, 18, 90, 160, 150, 38, 184. In which order does SSTF service these requests?

  1. 90, 58, 55, 39, 38, 18, 150, 160, 184
  2. 90, 150, 160, 184, 58, 55, 39, 38, 18
  3. 55, 58, 39, 18, 90, 160, 150, 38, 184
  4. 90, 58, 55, 39, 38, 18, 184, 160, 150
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. SSTF always serves the pending request nearest the current head position, recomputing the nearest after each service. It is greedy and ignores direction of travel and arrival order.

Step by step.

  1. From 100 the distances are: 90 → 10, 58 → 42, 55 → 45, 39 → 61, 18 → 82, 150 → 50, 160 → 60, 184 → 84, 38 → 62. Nearest is 90.
  2. From 90: 58 → 32 is nearest, then from 58 the nearest is 55 (3).
  3. From 55: 39 → 16, then from 39 the nearest is 38 (1), then from 38 the nearest is 18 (20).
  4. From 18 the remaining requests are 150, 160, 184: nearest is 150 (132), then 160 (10), then 184 (24).
  5. Order: 90, 58, 55, 39, 38, 18, 150, 160, 184. Total movement 10 + 32 + 3 + 16 + 1 + 20 + 132 + 10 + 24 = 248 cylinders.

Answer: Option (A) — 90, 58, 55, 39, 38, 18, 150, 160, 184.

Common misconception. The trap is to sweep to one side and then the other (option B), which is SCAN-like, or to keep arrival order (option C), which is FCFS. SSTF interleaves: it can reverse direction at every step.

Takeaway. SSTF recomputes the nearest neighbour after every service; the path may zig-zag freely.

OS-U6-Q39MCQmedium

On a 200-cylinder disk (0 to 199) the head is at cylinder 100 and the pending queue is 55, 58, 39, 18, 90, 160, 150, 38, 184. The head is moving toward cylinder 0. Under SCAN, counting the travel to cylinder 0 and the full sweep back, what is the total head movement?

  1. 208 cylinders
  2. 248 cylinders
  3. 284 cylinders
  4. 314 cylinders
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. SCAN is the elevator: the head keeps moving in its current direction until it reaches the physical end of the disk, serving every request it passes, then reverses and serves the rest.

Step by step.

  1. Moving toward 0 from 100, the requests passed are 90, 58, 55, 39, 38, 18 in that order.
  2. The head does not stop at 18: SCAN runs on to the physical end of the disk, cylinder 0. That leg costs 100 − 0 = 100 cylinders.
  3. The head then reverses and climbs, serving 150, 160 and finally 184. The upward leg is 184 − 0 = 184 cylinders.
  4. Total = 100 + 184 = 284 cylinders. (The travel stops at the last request; no request lies between 184 and 199, so that stretch is not counted.)

Answer: Option (C) — 284 cylinders.

Common misconception. The two wrong answers come from the two classic slips: 208 forgets the leg to cylinder 0 (LOOK, not SCAN, would give 82 + 166 = 248), and 314 counts the jump back to 199 as if this were C-SCAN.

Takeaway. SCAN pays for the trip to the wall; LOOK turns at the last request and saves that empty travel.

OS-U6-Q44NAThard

On a 200-cylinder disk (0 to 199) the head is at cylinder 100 and the pending queue is 55, 58, 39, 18, 90, 160, 150, 38, 184. The head is moving toward cylinder 0. Under C-SCAN, and counting every cylinder crossed including the return sweep from cylinder 0 to cylinder 199, what is the total head movement?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 314

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. C-SCAN treats the disk as circular: it serves requests while moving in one direction only, then returns from one edge to the other without serving anything, and starts again in the same direction.

Step by step.

  1. Downward leg: from 100 to cylinder 0, serving 90, 58, 55, 39, 38, 18 on the way. Movement = 100.
  2. Return sweep: cylinder 0 to cylinder 199, serving nothing. Movement = 199.
  3. Downward leg again from 199: the remaining requests 184, 160, 150 are served in that order, and the travel counted stops at 184. Movement = 199 − 184 = 15.
  4. Total = 100 + 199 + 15 = 314 cylinders.
  5. For comparison, SCAN on the same queue costs 100 + 184 = 284, because it reverses at 0 and climbs straight to 184 without the trip to 199.

Answer: 314 cylinders.

Common misconception. The classic error is to drop the 199-cylinder return sweep and answer 115, or to treat C-SCAN as SCAN and answer 284. The sweep is real head movement even though it serves nothing.

Takeaway. C-SCAN = one-directional service + a full-edge return sweep; the sweep is what makes waiting times uniform.

OS-U6-Q48MCQhard

On a 200-cylinder disk (0 to 199) the head is at 100 and the pending queue is 55, 58, 39, 18, 90, 160, 150, 38, 184. Which one of the following statements about total head movement is TRUE?

  1. FCFS moves 498 cylinders, which is more than SCAN but less than C-SCAN.
  2. LOOK, moving first toward cylinder 0, moves 248 cylinders — exactly the same total as SSTF for this queue.
  3. SCAN, moving toward 0 and travelling to cylinder 0, moves 314 cylinders.
  4. C-SCAN moves 284 cylinders, which is less than SCAN.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The four totals have to be computed separately for this queue; the interesting fact is that LOOK and SSTF coincide here even though they are different policies.

Step by step.

  1. FCFS, in arrival order: 45 + 3 + 19 + 21 + 72 + 70 + 10 + 112 + 146 = 498.
  2. SSTF: 90, 58, 55, 39, 38, 18, 150, 160, 184 gives 10 + 32 + 3 + 16 + 1 + 20 + 132 + 10 + 24 = 248.
  3. SCAN toward 0: 100 down to 0, then up to 184 = 100 + 184 = 284.
  4. LOOK toward 0: down to the last request 18 (82 cylinders), then up to 184 (166 cylinders) = 248.
  5. C-SCAN toward 0: 100 + 199 + 15 = 314.
  6. So (A) is false because 498 is greater than C-SCAN's 314; (C) is false because SCAN is 284, not 314; (D) is false because C-SCAN is 314, not 284. (B) is true.

Answer: Option (B) — LOOK and SSTF both total 248 cylinders on this queue.

Common misconception. The coincidence is the trap in reverse: students see 248 twice and assume one of the two figures must be wrong. LOOK and SSTF agree here by accident of the request positions, not by any theorem.

Takeaway. Compute each policy separately; never infer one total from another.

OS-U6-Q50MSQhard

Which of the following statements about disk-scheduling policies are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. C-SCAN bounds the waiting time of every request by roughly one full sweep plus the return sweep, so no request can be starved, whereas SSTF can postpone a distant request indefinitely while nearer ones keep arriving.
  2. LOOK and SCAN differ only when no request lies beyond the current head position in the direction of travel: LOOK turns back at the last request, while SCAN continues to the disk edge.
  3. SSTF minimises the total head movement over the whole pending queue, which is why it is preferred to FCFS.
  4. For the same queue and starting position, C-SCAN always moves the head less than SCAN, because it never has to reverse direction.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A) and (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Fairness and optimality are different questions. Sweeping policies bound waiting time; greedy policies lower the average but can starve.

Step by step.

  1. C-SCAN always moves in one direction for service, so every request waits at most one pass plus the return sweep — a bound independent of the arrival pattern. SSTF, being greedy, can keep a far request waiting while nearer ones arrive. (A) is true.
  2. SCAN and LOOK are identical until the queue runs out in the direction of travel; then SCAN goes on to the disk edge and LOOK turns immediately. (B) is true.
  3. (C) is false. SSTF is greedy, not optimal: choosing the nearest request now can force a long jump later, and the truly minimal tour is a travelling-salesman problem, not a nearest-neighbour walk.
  4. (D) is false. C-SCAN adds the return sweep from one edge to the other, so for a queue whose requests lie away from that edge it usually moves more than SCAN, not less.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. Option (C) is the most common error in the whole topic: SSTF is described everywhere as “shortest seek time first”, which sounds optimal. It minimises the next seek, not the total.

Takeaway. Greedy lowers the average and forfeits the bound; sweeping buys the bound and pays for the trip to the edge.

OS-U6-Q64MCQeasy

Which one of the following disk-scheduling policies can starve a request that lies far from the current head position, because it always serves the pending request nearest to the head?

  1. FCFS
  2. SSTF
  3. C-LOOK
  4. SCAN
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. SSTF is a greedy shortest-seek-first policy: it has no notion of age, only of distance, so a steady supply of near requests keeps a far request waiting indefinitely.

Step by step.

  1. FCFS serves requests in arrival order, so every request is served after finitely many others.
  2. SSTF always picks the nearest pending request; a request at cylinder 199 is postponed as long as nearer requests keep arriving.
  3. SCAN and C-LOOK sweep the disk, so every cylinder is visited within one sweep, which bounds the wait.
  4. SSTF is therefore the policy that needs aging or a sweep to become fair.

Answer: Option (B) — SSTF.

Common misconception. Thinking that a policy with the smallest total head movement is also fair. SSTF minimises movement locally and is precisely the policy that ignores waiting time.

OS-U6-Q65MCQmedium

A 200-cylinder disk (cylinders 0 to 199) has its head at cylinder 60. The pending requests, in arrival order, are 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190, 51. In which order does SSTF serve them?

  1. 51, 43, 24, 16, 82, 140, 170, 190
  2. 51, 43, 24, 16, 190, 170, 140, 82
  3. 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190, 51
  4. 43, 51, 24, 16, 82, 140, 170, 190
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. SSTF repeatedly takes the pending request with the smallest distance from the current head, so the head always makes the shortest possible step.

Step by step.

  1. From 60 the distances are 9 to 51, 17 to 43, 22 to 82, 36 to 24, 44 to 16, 80 to 140, 110 to 170 and 130 to 190; take 51.
  2. From 51: 43 is at distance 8, the smallest; take 43.
  3. From 43: 24 is at 19, 16 at 27, 82 at 39; take 24, then 16 (distance 8).
  4. From 16 the remaining requests are 82, 140, 170 and 190, all to the right, so they are taken in increasing order: 82, 140, 170, 190.
  5. Total movement = 9 + 8 + 19 + 8 + 66 + 58 + 30 + 20 = 218 cylinders.

Answer: Option (A) — 51, 43, 24, 16, 82, 140, 170, 190.

Common misconception. Option (B) reverses the tail because the head has been moving left. SSTF has no direction: once the requests to the left are exhausted, it turns around and takes the nearest one to the right, which is 82.

OS-U6-Q66NATeasy

On a 200-cylinder disk (cylinders 0 to 199) the head is at cylinder 60. The pending requests, in arrival order, are 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190, 51. Under FCFS, what is the total head movement, in cylinders?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 771

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. FCFS serves the queue in arrival order, so the head simply follows the request sequence wherever it goes.

Step by step.

  1. Movement is the sum of the absolute differences between consecutive positions, starting at 60.
  2. |60−82| = 22, |82−170| = 88, |170−43| = 127, |43−140| = 97.
  3. |140−24| = 116, |24−16| = 8, |16−190| = 174, |190−51| = 139.
  4. Total = 22 + 88 + 127 + 97 + 116 + 8 + 174 + 139 = 771.

Answer: 771 cylinders.

Common misconception. Sorting the queue first. That computes SSTF or SCAN, not FCFS; FCFS is defined by arrival order and its whole cost is the zig-zag it produces.

OS-U6-Q67MCQmedium

How does C-LOOK differ from C-SCAN?

  1. C-LOOK reverses direction at the last pending request instead of at the end of the disk, so it never travels to cylinder 0 or 199 unnecessarily
  2. C-LOOK serves requests strictly in arrival order
  3. C-LOOK keeps one queue per cylinder and serves them round robin
  4. C-LOOK never reverses the direction of the head
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The LOOK family stops at the last request in the current direction instead of continuing to the physical end of the disk; C-LOOK adds the circular return of C-SCAN to that economy.

Step by step.

  1. C-SCAN sweeps to the last cylinder, jumps back to cylinder 0 without servicing, and sweeps again, so wait times are uniform.
  2. C-LOOK does the same circular sweep but turns around at the highest (or lowest) pending request, so the empty travel to the disk edge is avoided.
  3. Its total head movement is therefore never larger than that of C-SCAN on the same queue.
  4. It does reverse, and it does not serve in arrival order, so the other options describe FCFS or a multi-queue policy.

Answer: Option (A) — it turns at the last request instead of the disk edge.

Common misconception. Confusing LOOK with SCAN. SCAN goes to the end of the disk because the head has no way of knowing where the last request is; LOOK uses that knowledge, which is what saves the travel.

OS-U6-Q68MSQhard

Which of the following statements about the SCAN, C-SCAN and LOOK policies are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. LOOK reverses direction at the last pending request rather than at the end of the disk.
  2. C-SCAN treats the cylinders as a circular list and returns to the start without servicing, so waiting times are more uniform than under SCAN.
  3. Under SCAN, a request that lies just behind the head's direction of travel waits almost a full sweep.
  4. SSTF always minimises the total head movement over the whole pending queue.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The sweep policies trade optimal movement for bounded waiting: SCAN bounds the wait to about two sweeps, C-SCAN makes it uniform, and LOOK removes the travel beyond the last request.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: LOOK is SCAN that stops at the outermost pending request.
  2. (B) is true: the circular return gives every cylinder roughly one service per revolution, so no region waits much longer than another.
  3. (C) is true: that region is served last on the return leg, after the whole opposite side has been covered.
  4. (D) is false: SSTF is greedy and can be beaten. On the queue 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190, 51 from head 60, SSTF moves 218 cylinders while LOOK also moves 218 but a different order can do better on other queues; optimality would require trying every order, which is the travelling-salesman problem.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Believing SSTF is optimal because each of its steps is optimal. Greedy choices minimise the next seek, not the total; the shortest total is a TSP path and is not computed by any of these heuristics.

OS-U6-Q69MCQhard

On a 200-cylinder disk (cylinders 0 to 199) the head is at cylinder 60 and is moving toward cylinder 0. The pending requests, in arrival order, are 82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190, 51. Under SCAN, and counting the travel to cylinder 0, what is the total head movement in cylinders?

  1. 218
  2. 250
  3. 280
  4. 771
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. SCAN is the elevator: the head finishes the current direction as far as the end of the disk, then reverses and serves everything on the way back.

Step by step.

  1. Moving down from 60, the requests met in order are 51, 43, 24 and 16: 9 + 8 + 19 + 8 = 44 cylinders.
  2. The head continues to cylinder 0 because SCAN does not stop at the last request: 16 more cylinders.
  3. Reversing, it serves 82, 140, 170 and 190 in that order: 82 + 58 + 30 + 20 = 190 cylinders.
  4. Total = 44 + 16 + 190 = 250 cylinders.

Answer: Option (B) — 250 cylinders.

Common misconception. Answering 218, which is LOOK: it omits the 16 cylinders from 16 down to 0. SCAN, unlike LOOK, is defined to reach the edge of the disk.

OS-U6-Q96NATeasy

A disk platter rotates at 6000 revolutions per minute. What is the average rotational latency, in milliseconds?
(Enter the nearest integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 5

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Average rotational latency is the time of half a revolution, because the wanted sector is equally likely to be anywhere on the track.

Step by step.

  1. 6000 revolutions per minute is 100 revolutions per second, so one revolution takes 60/6000 s = 10 ms.
  2. On average the head waits for half a revolution: 10/2 = 5 ms.

Answer: 5 ms.

Common misconception. Using a full revolution (10 ms), or dividing 6000 by 60 and treating the result as a time in milliseconds.

OS-U6-Q81MCQeasy

SCAN (the elevator algorithm) is in use on a disk whose head is moving toward higher cylinder numbers. In what order are the pending requests served?

  1. In ascending cylinder order, up to the highest cylinder of the disk, then in descending order after the head reverses.
  2. In the order in which the requests arrived.
  3. In descending cylinder order, whatever the current direction of travel.
  4. In ascending order only as far as the highest pending request, then reversed.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. SCAN sweeps the head from one end of the disk to the other, serving every request it passes, and then reverses. LOOK is the variant that turns around at the last pending request instead of at the end of the disk.

Step by step.

  1. Requests ahead of the head in the direction of travel are met in ascending order.
  2. The head continues to the last cylinder of the disk even when no request lies there.
  3. It then reverses and serves the remaining requests in descending order.
  4. Option (D) describes LOOK, option (B) is FCFS, and option (C) contradicts the stated direction of travel.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Treating LOOK and SCAN as one policy. They differ exactly in where the head turns around, and that difference shows up in the total head movement.

OS-U6-Q83MCQmedium

A disk has 4 platters, both surfaces of every platter usable, 1024 tracks per surface, 512 sectors per track and 512 bytes per sector. What is its capacity?

  1. 512 MiB
  2. 1 GiB
  3. 2 GiB
  4. 4 GiB
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Capacity = surfaces × tracks per surface × sectors per track × bytes per sector.

Step by step.

  1. 4 platters with both surfaces usable give 8 recording surfaces, one head each.
  2. 8 × 1024 = 8192 tracks.
  3. 8192 × 512 = 4,194,304 sectors.
  4. 4,194,304 × 512 = 2,147,483,648 bytes, which is exactly 2 GiB.

Answer: Option (C) — 2 GiB.

Common misconception. Counting one surface per platter and halving the answer to 1 GiB. A platter has two usable surfaces unless the drive is built single-sided.

OS-U6-Q98NATmedium

A disk has 200 cylinders, numbered 0 to 199. The head is at cylinder 143 and is moving toward cylinder 0. SCAN is used. The pending requests, in arrival order, are 86, 147, 91, 177, 94, 150, 102, 175, 130. What is the total distance, in cylinders, moved by the head while these requests are served?

Show answer & solution

Answer: 320

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Under SCAN the head serves everything in its path, runs to the end of the disk, then reverses. The distance is the sum of the two sweeps, not the sum of the gaps between consecutive requests.

Step by step.

  1. Moving down from 143, the head passes and serves 130, 102, 94, 91 and 86: a travel of 143 − 86 = 57 cylinders.
  2. SCAN continues to the end of the disk, cylinder 0, even though no request lies there: another 86 cylinders, so the downward sweep costs 143 in all.
  3. The head reverses and moves up, serving 147, 150, 175 and 177: 177 − 0 = 177 cylinders.
  4. Total = 57 + 86 + 177 = 320 cylinders.

Answer: 320.

Common misconception. Reversing at the last pending request instead of at the end of the disk. That is LOOK, which would give 57 + 91 = 148.

OS-U6-Q93MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about the time taken to service a disk request are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. The average rotational latency is half the time of one full rotation.
  2. The transfer time of a request is proportional to the number of sectors it asks for.
  3. For a random workload of small requests, seek time and rotational latency usually dominate the transfer time.
  4. FCFS minimises the average seek time over a queue of requests.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Service time is the sum of three parts: seek time to reach the track, rotational latency to reach the sector, and transfer time to move the data.

Step by step.

  1. (A) The wanted sector is uniformly distributed, so the head waits half a revolution on average. TRUE.
  2. (B) Transfer time is sectors × time per sector, so it grows with the size of the request. TRUE.
  3. (C) A few sectors transfer in microseconds while a seek costs milliseconds and a rotation a few more. TRUE.
  4. (D) FCFS ignores positions entirely and gives the largest total head movement of the classical policies; SSTF and SCAN reduce average seek. FALSE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C) are TRUE; (D) is FALSE.

Common misconception. Assuming FCFS is best because it is fair. Ordering by arrival is exactly what costs head movement.

access-control-protection 21
OS-U6-Q04MCQeasy

A Unix-like file has permission mode 640, read as rw- r-- ---. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. The owner may read and write, members of the group may read, and all other users have no access.
  2. The owner may read and write, members of the group may read and write, and all other users may read.
  3. The owner may read only, the group may read and write, and all other users have no access.
  4. The owner may read, write and execute, the group may read, and all other users may read.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A three-digit octal mode gives the rights of the owner, the group and everyone else, one digit each. Within a digit, read = 4, write = 2 and execute = 1, added together.

Step by step.

  1. Owner digit 6 = 4 + 2 = read + write, no execute.
  2. Group digit 4 = read only.
  3. Other digit 0 = no rights at all.
  4. So the file is writable by its owner, readable by the group, and closed to everyone else.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) would be mode 664.
  • (C) would be mode 460, which also gives the group write.
  • (D) would be mode 744.

Common misconception. Reading the digits as counts of users rather than as bit sums. The digit is an octal number, not a quantity.

Takeaway. 6 = rw, 5 = r-x, 4 = r--, 0 = ---. Three digits, three classes of user.

OS-U6-Q08MCQeasy

Which statement correctly distinguishes an access-control list from a capability list?

  1. An access-control list is stored with the object and names the subjects allowed to use it; a capability is held by a subject and names an object together with the rights the subject may exercise on it.
  2. An access-control list is held by the subject and a capability list is stored with the object.
  3. An access-control list can express only read and write rights, while a capability can express any right.
  4. The two are the same mechanism under different names, differing only in whether the list is sorted.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Protection information can be attached to the object or to the subject. Attached to the object it is an access-control list; attached to the subject it is a capability.

Step by step.

  1. An ACL on a file lists pairs (user or group, rights). The check at open time is “does this subject appear in the file's list?”
  2. A capability is a token held by the subject, for example a descriptor that names a file and carries read/write rights. The check is “does the subject hold a token for this object?”
  3. ACLs are easy to inspect and revoke for one object, but hard to answer “what can this user reach?”. Capabilities are the reverse.
  4. The two therefore differ in where the list lives, not in the kind of rights it can express.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) swaps the two placements.
  • (C) both mechanisms can express any right.
  • (D) they are duals, not the same thing: one is per-object, the other per-subject.

Common misconception. Treating a capability as “an ACL entry copied to the user”. A capability is a protected token the user can present; losing control of it means losing the rights it carries.

Takeaway. ACL = column of the access matrix stored with the object. Capability list = row of the access matrix held by the subject.

OS-U6-Q12MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about file protection are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Revoking a capability is expensive, because capabilities are held by subjects and must be found one by one.
  2. An access-control list answers “what may this user do with this file?” easily, but answers “what may this user do with anything?” only by scanning every object.
  3. The three permission classes rwx for owner, group and others carry the same information as a full access-control list over all users of the system.
  4. In Unix, the execute bit on a directory grants the right to traverse that directory in order to reach a named file inside it.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Protection can be organised per object (ACLs) or per subject (capabilities), and the cost of the two operations that matter — checking a right and revoking one — falls differently on each.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. A capability is a token in the subject's own table, so revoking it means locating every holder; there is no single place to delete an entry.
  2. (B) True. An ACL is the natural per-object view; the per-subject question needs a scan of all objects.
  3. (C) False. Three classes cannot express per-user entries: two users in the same group are indistinguishable under the mode bits, and there is no way to name an individual outside the group.
  4. (D) True. On a directory, x means “may pass through”, r means “may list the names”, and w means “may create or delete entries”. Traversal needs x, not r.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are true; (C) is false.

Common misconception. Reading the directory r bit as “permission to open files inside”. Listing and traversal are separate rights; a directory with mode 711 can be traversed by everyone while its contents remain unlistable.

Takeaway. ACLs answer per-object questions cheaply, capabilities answer per-subject questions cheaply; directory x is the traversal right.

OS-U6-Q16MCQmedium

Directory /d has mode 750 and is owned by user ann, with group staff. The file /d/notes.txt has mode 644. User bob, who is neither ann nor a member of staff, tries to read the file. What happens?

  1. The read succeeds, because the file itself is world-readable.
  2. The read fails with permission denied, because bob lacks the execute permission on /d and so cannot resolve the name inside it.
  3. The read succeeds but the file appears empty.
  4. The read fails because bob lacks the read permission on /d.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Reaching a file means walking every directory on its path. On a directory, x is the right to pass through and to look up a name in it; r is only the right to list the names.

Step by step.

  1. Mode 750 gives the owner rwx, the group r-x, and others ---.
  2. Bob is neither the owner nor in the group, so he falls into the “others” class and has no rights on the directory at all.
  3. To open notes.txt, the system must resolve the name inside /d, which requires traverse permission on /d.
  4. That permission is missing, so the lookup fails with permission denied — before the file's own mode 644 is ever consulted.

Answer: Option (B) — denied at the directory, not at the file.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) the file's mode is irrelevant once the path cannot be resolved.
  • (C) a permission failure is an error, not an empty file.
  • (D) the missing right is x, not r; r on the directory would control listing its names, and bob lacks both anyway.

Common misconception. Checking only the file's own permission bits. Every component of the path is a gate, and the first gate that fails stops the operation.

Takeaway. Directory x = traverse and look up; directory r = list. A world-readable file inside an unreachable directory is unreachable.

OS-U6-Q20MCQhard

A program file has mode 4755 and is owned by root. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. The leading 4 is the set-user-ID bit: the program runs with the effective user ID of the file's owner, and the final digit 5 gives read and execute to all other users.
  2. The leading 4 means the file may be opened by four users at the same time.
  3. The set-user-ID bit changes the file's owner to root each time the program runs.
  4. The final digit 5 grants write and execute to all other users.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The fourth octal digit carries the three special bits: set-user-ID (4), set-group-ID (2) and sticky (1). Set-user-ID makes the process adopt the effective user ID of the file's owner for the duration of the run.

Step by step.

  1. Mode 4755 = special digit 4, owner 7, group 5, others 5.
  2. 4 in the special digit sets set-user-ID; owner 7 = read, write, execute.
  3. Group 5 and others 5 are both r-x, so every user may read and execute the program.
  4. When any user runs it, the process gains root's effective user ID, which is why such a program can perform a privileged action for an unprivileged caller — and why it must be written carefully.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) the special digit is not a count of users.
  • (C) ownership is a property of the file's metadata; set-user-ID changes the process, not the file.
  • (D) 5 is r-x, not write — write would need 7 or 3.

Common misconception. Reading the leading digit as part of the owner's permissions. It is a separate field of three bits; 4755 and 755 differ only in set-user-ID.

Takeaway. 4 = set-user-ID, 2 = set-group-ID, 1 = sticky. Set-user-ID elevates the process to the owner's identity, not the file to the caller's.

OS-U6-Q29MCQeasy

A file report.txt is owned by user u1 and its group is g1; its mode is 644. User u2 is a member of both g1 and g2, but is not u1. Which permission class decides what u2 may do with the file?

  1. The group class, because the file's group is g1 and u2 is a member of g1; membership of g2 is irrelevant.
  2. The owner class, because u2 belongs to the file's group and so inherits the owner's rights.
  3. The union of the group class and the other class, since u2 qualifies for both.
  4. The other class, because u2 is not the owner of the file.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Unix checks the three permission classes in the fixed order owner, then group, then other, and applies the first class that matches. Exactly one class applies, and it is the file's group — not the union of the user's groups.

Step by step.

  1. The file records one group, here g1. There is no per-user list in a mode word.
  2. u2 is not the owner, so the owner class does not apply.
  3. u2 is a member of g1, so the group class applies: mode 644 gives the group read only.
  4. The check stops there. The other class is never consulted, and the extra membership in g2 grants nothing, because g2 is not the file's group.

Answer: Option (A) — the group class of the file's own group decides, giving u2 read access only.

Common misconception. The common error is to take the union of every group the user belongs to, or to let a group member be treated as the owner. A mode word names one group and the first matching class wins.

Takeaway. Owner, then group, then other — first match, no union.

OS-U6-Q32MSQeasy

Which of the following statements about Unix file and directory permissions are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A directory needs the read bit for a user to list its entries, and the execute bit to traverse it or to reach a named file inside it.
  2. Clearing the write bit on a file is enough to stop its owner from deleting it, because deleting a file requires write permission on that file.
  3. The sticky bit on a directory restricts deletion of an entry to the owner of that entry, or to the owner of the directory, even when the directory is world-writable.
  4. The set-group-ID bit on a directory makes files created inside it inherit the directory's group rather than the creator's primary group.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A directory is a table mapping names to inode numbers, so its own permission bits govern name lookup (execute), listing (read) and creating or removing entries (write). A file's own bits never govern whether its name may be unlinked.

Step by step.

  1. Read on a directory lets a user list the names; execute lets the user traverse the directory to reach a known name. Both are needed for a full listing that includes attributes. So (A) is true.
  2. Deleting a name edits the directory, not the file: the user needs write and execute on the directory. A file whose own write bit is clear can still be deleted by anyone with write access to its directory. So (B) is false.
  3. The sticky bit on a shared directory such as /tmp stops one user from deleting another user's file there. So (C) is true.
  4. Set-group-ID on a directory is the inheritance rule: new entries take the directory's group. So (D) is true.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (B) is the classic trap: it confuses permission on the file with permission on the name. Removing a name is a directory operation.

Takeaway. On a file the bits guard its contents; on a directory the same three bits guard listing, traversal and name editing.

OS-U6-Q37MCQmedium

The access matrix has one row per subject and one column per object, with the permitted operations in each cell. Which implementation stores the matrix row by row?

  1. An access-control list, because each object carries the set of subjects allowed to use it.
  2. A bitmap of free blocks, because one bit per block records one row of the matrix.
  3. A protection ring, because the ring number of a process is its row in the matrix.
  4. A capability list, because each subject carries, for every object it may use, an unforgeable token naming that object and the rights held on it.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The access matrix can be decomposed by columns or by rows. Column decomposition stores, per object, the subjects and their rights — that is an access-control list. Row decomposition stores, per subject, the objects and its rights — that is a capability list.

Step by step.

  1. A row of the matrix answers “what may this subject do?”. Storing one row per subject gives each subject a list of (object, rights) pairs: a capability list.
  2. A column answers “who may use this object, and how?”. That is an ACL, so option (A) is the opposite decomposition.
  3. A protection ring orders privilege levels; it is not a row of the matrix.
  4. A free-space bitmap has nothing to do with protection.

Answer: Option (D) — capabilities are the row-wise decomposition of the access matrix.

Common misconception. Because both structures ultimately describe the same matrix, students treat them as interchangeable. They are transposes of each other, which is why revocation is cheap for ACLs and expensive for capabilities.

Takeaway. Columns → ACLs (per object). Rows → capabilities (per subject).

OS-U6-Q41NATmedium

A file is to be readable and writable by its owner, readable and executable by its group, and inaccessible to everyone else. What is its permission mode as a three-digit octal number?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 650

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each permission class is one octal digit built from three bits in the order read (4), write (2), execute (1). The digits are given owner, group, other.

Step by step.

  1. Owner: read + write = 4 + 2 = 6.
  2. Group: read + execute = 4 + 1 = 5.
  3. Other: nothing = 0.
  4. Mode = 650, written rw- r-x ---.

Answer: 650.

Common misconception. The usual error is 750 or 640 — swapping the group digit's execute bit for write, or dropping execute from the group when the intent was “may run but not modify”.

Takeaway. 4 = read, 2 = write, 1 = execute; sum per class, concatenate owner-group-other.

OS-U6-Q46MSQhard

Which of the following statements about protection mechanisms are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A capability is held by the subject that owns it, so it can be prevented from being forged only if the system tags it and checks the tag on every use.
  2. An access-control list that grants a right to a group and later denies it to one member of that group gives different results under first-match and deny-precedence semantics, so the system must fix one.
  3. Creating a hard link to a file gives the creator of the link the same access rights as the file's owner.
  4. The set-user-ID bit on a program lets an unprivileged user perform operations allowed to the program's owner, which makes any bug in that program a privilege-escalation risk.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A capability is a token the subject carries, so the system cannot rely on the subject's honesty; an ACL lives with the object and is consulted by the system. Both need well-defined conflict semantics.

Step by step.

  1. Because a capability is presented by the subject, a forged one would grant the rights it names. The system must therefore make it unforgeable — a tagged, protected address space, or a cryptographic signature. So (A) is true.
  2. If entry 1 grants read to group staff and entry 2 denies read to user bob, a first-match list lets bob read and a deny-precedence list refuses him. The two orders genuinely differ, so the semantics must be specified. So (B) is true.
  3. (C) is false. A hard link is a second name for the same inode, so access is still decided by that inode's owner and mode word. The user who creates the link gains no rights at all.
  4. Set-user-ID runs the program with the file owner's effective identity, which is exactly why a buffer overflow in a setuid-root program is a privilege escalation. So (D) is true.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. The trap in (C) is the word “creator”: a hard link adds a name, not a right. Ownership and the mode word belong to the inode and are unchanged by linking.

Takeaway. ACLs are checked by the system on the object; capabilities must be made unforgeable because the subject carries them.

OS-U6-Q70MCQeasy

A file has permission mode 755. Which one of the following describes it?

  1. owner read, write and execute; group read and execute; others read and execute
  2. owner read and write; group read and write; others read
  3. owner, group and others all read, write and execute
  4. owner read; group read and execute; others no permission
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A three-digit octal mode is three 3-bit groups: owner, group and others, each holding read (4), write (2) and execute (1).

Step by step.

  1. 7 = 4 + 2 + 1, so the owner has read, write and execute.
  2. 5 = 4 + 1, so the group has read and execute but not write.
  3. The last 5 gives others the same rights as the group.
  4. 755 is therefore the standard mode of a directory or of an executable that everyone may run but only the owner may change.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Reading 755 as “everyone can write”. The middle digit is a 5, not a 7; group and others can read and execute but not modify.

OS-U6-Q71MCQmedium

The set-group-ID bit is set on a directory. What is its effect?

  1. files created inside the directory inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group
  2. every file in the directory becomes executable by the group
  3. the directory can be listed only by its owner
  4. members of the group may delete any file in the directory
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. On a directory the set-group-ID bit is an inheritance rule for the group of new files; on an executable file the set-user-ID bit is an elevation rule for the effective user ID.

Step by step.

  1. Without the bit, a new file takes the creator's primary group, which may not be the group that owns the directory.
  2. With it, a new file takes the group of the directory, so a shared project directory keeps every file in the project group.
  3. The mode bits of existing files are unchanged; only the group of newly created entries is affected.
  4. Deletion is controlled by write and execute permission on the directory and, in a sticky directory, by ownership of the file.

Answer: Option (A) — new files inherit the directory's group.

Common misconception. Confusing the set-group-ID bit on a directory with the set-user-ID bit on a program. The first changes ownership of new files; the second runs a program with the file owner's privileges.

OS-U6-Q72MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about Unix directory permissions are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Traversing a path through a directory requires execute permission on that directory.
  2. A directory with read but no execute permission can be listed, yet a file inside it cannot be opened even when its name is known.
  3. The sticky bit on a world-writable directory stops users from deleting files they do not own.
  4. The group permission bits apply to every user who is not the owner.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Read permission on a directory means “may list the names in it”, write means “may create or remove entries”, and execute means “may pass through it”. The three are independent.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: each component of a path must be searchable, which is what execute permission grants.
  2. (B) is true: ls needs read, but resolving name inside the directory needs execute, so the open fails with permission denied.
  3. (C) is true: with the sticky bit set, only the file's owner, the directory's owner or root may unlink an entry.
  4. (D) is false: the group bits apply only to members of the file's group; a user who is neither the owner nor in the group falls through to the other bits.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Treating execute on a directory as “may run the directory”. On a directory, x means search, and without it every path that passes through the directory is unusable.

OS-U6-Q73NATeasy

A file must be readable, writable and executable by its owner, readable and executable by its group, and inaccessible to everyone else. What is its permission mode as a three-digit octal number?
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Answer: 750

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each permission triple is one octal digit formed by adding read = 4, write = 2 and execute = 1.

Step by step.

  1. Owner: read + write + execute = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7.
  2. Group: read + execute = 4 + 1 = 5.
  3. Others: nothing = 0.
  4. The mode is therefore 750, which is also the standard mode of a private directory.

Answer: 750.

Common misconception. Writing 755 out of habit. The group digit is 5, and others must be 0 here, so the answer cannot end in a non-zero digit.

OS-U6-Q74MCQhard

An access matrix is implemented with access-control lists, one list per object. Which one of the following questions becomes expensive to answer?

  1. may subject s read object o
  2. which objects may subject s read
  3. who may read object o
  4. may the owner of object o change its mode
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An access-control list is stored with the object, so it answers “who may do what to this object” quickly and the transpose question slowly.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is cheap: look up the object's list and check the entry for s.
  2. (B) is expensive: nothing records the objects per subject, so every object's list must be scanned.
  3. (C) is cheap: the list is already indexed by subject.
  4. (D) is a matter of ownership and mode, not of the matrix at all.
  5. A capability list stores the transpose and reverses the costs, which is why systems keep both views for different operations.

Answer: Option (B) — enumerating all objects a subject may read.

Common misconception. Thinking an ACL is slow for the common check. It is optimised for exactly that check; what it cannot do is answer questions asked from the subject's side.

OS-U6-Q75MCQmedium

What does the umask of a process control?

  1. the maximum size a file created by the process may reach
  2. the permission bits that are removed from the default mode of every file the process creates
  3. the list of users who may log in as the process owner
  4. the group that owns the files the process creates
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The umask is a per-process mask of permission bits. A new file is created with a default mode (0666 for a file, 0777 for a directory) and the mask is subtracted from it bit by bit.

Step by step.

  1. With umask 022, a file created with default 0666 gets 0666 & ~022 = 0644.
  2. With umask 077, the same default gives 0600, a private file.
  3. The mask can only remove bits, never add them, so it can tighten permissions but cannot grant them.
  4. It has nothing to do with size limits, login lists or group ownership, which are controlled by other mechanisms.

Answer: Option (B) — the bits removed from the default mode of new files.

Common misconception. Reading the mask as the permissions granted. It is subtracted from the default; a mask of 022 leaves 644, it does not produce 022.

OS-U6-Q79MCQeasy

A directory has mode 1777 — world-writable with the sticky bit set, as on /tmp. What does the sticky bit do?

  1. It lets any user delete any file in the directory.
  2. It allows a file in the directory to be deleted or renamed only by the file's owner, the directory's owner or the superuser.
  3. It stops users other than the owner from reading files in the directory.
  4. It makes new files in the directory inherit the directory's group.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. On a directory the sticky bit restricts deletion, not creation or reading. The directory's write permission still lets anyone create files, but removal is limited to the owner of the file, the owner of the directory and root.

Step by step.

  1. Write permission on a directory controls creation and deletion of its entries, so on 1777 everyone may create.
  2. Without the sticky bit, that same write permission lets any user delete any entry.
  3. The sticky bit adds the condition that the deleter must own the file, or own the directory, or be root.
  4. Reading is governed by the read and execute bits of the file and the directory, not by the sticky bit.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Confusing the sticky bit with read protection. 1777 still lets everyone list the directory and read whatever the file permissions allow; the bit guards deletion only.

OS-U6-Q85MCQmedium

The set-group-ID bit is set on a regular executable file whose group is proj. A user who is not in proj executes it. What happens?

  1. The process runs with effective group ID proj for the duration of the execution.
  2. The process keeps the real group ID of the invoking user, because the bit has no effect on a file.
  3. The file becomes readable and executable by every user on the system.
  4. The file's group is changed to the group of the user who executed it.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (A)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. On an executable file set-GID makes the process's effective GID the file's group, just as set-UID makes the effective UID the file's owner. On a directory the same bit means something else: new entries inherit the directory's group.

Step by step.

  1. The kernel sets the effective GID from the file's group when the file is executed.
  2. The real GID is untouched, so the invoking user's own identity is still recorded.
  3. The program can therefore touch group-owned resources the user could not reach directly.
  4. Nothing is granted to other users and no ownership changes, so (B), (C) and (D) are false.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Applying the directory meaning of set-GID to an executable, or assuming the invoking user's group replaces the file's group.

OS-U6-Q94MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about the umask of a process are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. The umask is a per-process attribute, inherited by child processes across fork and exec.
  2. The umask clears permission bits from the mode requested when a file is created.
  3. Changing the umask also changes the permissions of files the process already owns.
  4. With umask 077, a file created with requested mode 0666 ends up with mode 0600.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The umask is a set of bits to be removed, not a mode to be applied. It acts once, at creation time, on the mode the creating call asks for.

Step by step.

  1. (A) It is part of the process's attributes and is inherited by children. TRUE.
  2. (B) The resulting mode is the requested mode with the umask bits cleared. TRUE.
  3. (C) It has no effect on existing files; those need chmod. FALSE.
  4. (D) 0666 with 077 removed gives 0600. TRUE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are TRUE; (C) is FALSE.

Common misconception. Reading the umask as the mode that will be set. It is subtracted, so 022 on 0666 gives 0644, not 0022.

OS-U6-Q89MCQhard

A file carries the POSIX ACL entries user::rw-, user:bob:rw-, group::r--, mask::r-- and other::---. bob is not the file's owner and is a member of the file's group. What can bob do with the file?

  1. Read and write it.
  2. Read it only.
  3. Neither read nor write it.
  4. Read, write and execute it.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Option (B)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. In a POSIX ACL the mask entry caps the permissions of every named user entry, every named group entry and the owning-group entry; the effective permission is the entry intersected with the mask.

Step by step.

  1. bob matches the named user entry user:bob:rw-.
  2. That entry is subject to the mask r--, so bob's effective rights are rw- ∩ r-- = r--.
  3. The owner entry user:: is not capped by the mask, but bob is not the owner.
  4. bob can therefore read the file and do nothing else.

Answer: Option (B) — read only.
