Common misconception. Reading the named entry alone and answering read and write. The mask exists precisely to bound named entries, and it reduces them silently.

OS-U6-Q95MSQhard

Which of the following statements about permission checking in a Unix-like system are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Access is decided by the first class that matches — owner, else group, else other — not by the union of the classes that match.
  2. Execute permission on a directory is needed to traverse it and reach a file inside, even when the file itself is world-readable.
  3. A process that owns the file is granted the union of the owner, group and other permission bits.
  4. With POSIX ACLs, the mask entry caps the permissions granted by every named user entry, every named group entry and the owning-group entry.
Show answer & solution

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Detailed solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The check is a sequence of tests, not a combination: the three classes are tried in order and the first one that matches decides. The ACL mask adds a cap on top of that.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Owner, then group, then other; the first match is final, so a restrictive owner entry is not rescued by a permissive other entry. TRUE.
  2. (B) The x bit on a directory gates traversal of the path, independently of the file's own bits. TRUE.
  3. (C) The owner's bits alone apply; the other classes are never consulted for the owner. FALSE.
  4. (D) The mask bounds named user entries, named group entries and the owning-group entry, which is why adding a named user can silently cut the group's rights. TRUE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are TRUE; (C) is FALSE.

Common misconception. Believing the classes combine, so that a file with mode 604 is more permissive for its owner than 600. Only the first matching class counts.

What this test contains

25 questions on Unit 2 (Inter-Process Communication & Synchronization) — the first of the two sets this unit receives on its third pass through the Operating Systems syllabus. All four subtopics are covered: the critical-section problem, including strict alternation, the initial values Peterson’s solution needs, Lamport’s bakery algorithm, a process that halts inside its critical section and the size of the shared state; hardware primitives, including the release side of a test-and-set lock, the bounded-waiting hand-off algorithm, cache-line contention, ticket-lock fairness and the arithmetic of a ticket queue, and a spin lock taken from an interrupt handler; semaphores, including a counting semaphore initialised above 1, signalling against mutual exclusion, a producer–consumer ordering constraint, a printer pool, the value-and-blocked-count identity and the number of drives in use; and the classic problems, including what wrt protects, why the last reader signals it, the asymmetric fork ordering, the state-array dining solution under simultaneous hunger and its semaphore count, and a bounded buffer whose mutex has been left out. Composition: 15 MCQ, 5 MSQ, 5 NAT; difficulty 10 easy, 10 medium, 5 hard; 60 minutes, 35 marks. MCQ carries 1 mark, MSQ and NAT carry 2 marks, there is no negative marking, and an MSQ scores only when the exact set of correct options is selected. This is a practice marking scheme, not the official GATE scheme.

Concept map used to build the questions

  • Every critical-section protocol is judged on three separate questions. Is the section exclusive, can the system stall while the section is free, and can one process be passed over for ever. Mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting fail independently, and a trace that violates one usually leaves the others intact.
  • Exclusion comes from one indivisible step. A software protocol needs atomic reads and writes of single words; a hardware primitive makes one read-modify-write atomic. Both are defeated by a process that stops while it holds the right to enter, which is why liveness has to be argued separately from exclusion.
  • A semaphore is a counter; a lock has an owner. P subtracts and V adds, a negative value counts the blocked processes, and a signal with no waiter is remembered in the count. The initial value is the number of permits, and nothing in the object prevents a stray V.
  • Spin or block is a cost decision, not a correctness decision. Spinning burns cycles and cache coherence traffic and is right for waits shorter than two context switches; blocking deschedules the waiter and is right for longer waits. Spinning inside an interrupt handler on a single CPU cannot end.
  • Fairness is layered on top of exclusion. A ticket taken from an atomic counter, or a cyclic hand-off through an intent array, is what turns exclusion into bounded waiting; the atomic instruction alone gives none.
  • Each classic problem is one shared object plus one rule. The bounded buffer separates counting (how many slots) from exclusion (who may touch the indices); the readers–writers problem trades concurrency against the risk of starving one side; the dining philosophers is a resource-ordering problem where deadlock and starvation are removed by different devices.

Source categories

A question tagged standard textbook is written in the tradition of the standard operating-systems texts (Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne; Tanenbaum) and tests the definitions, invariants and standard arguments those texts develop. A question tagged original gate-style is independently written practice in the GATE pattern. No question on this paper is presented as an official GATE question: the only verified previous-year question in this bank is PYQ-GATE2021S1-Q25, which belongs to Unit 1, and no previous-year question on this unit has been verified against an official paper and answer key.

Provenance: no question here is presented as an official GATE question unless its year, paper and official answer key are recorded in the Question Bank tab. All other items are practice questions written for this series.
